docs.text:
See README.md in this folder: [dart pub get] followed by [webdev serve] for development (including hot reloading), or [dart compile js web/main.dart -o web/main.dart.js] for a production build—the Dart equivalent of [npm run build], without any prior bundler configuration steps.

If the [webdev serve] server is still running for the [http client 3] web application, you must stop it (Ctrl-C in the terminal that launched it). Then, in a terminal within the [html client] directory:

dart pub get
webdev serve

Line 2 starts the web server that will serve the HTML client application:

  • In [1], in a browser, request URL [http://localhost:8080];
  • to [2-3], enter the credentials admin / admin;
  • In [4], submit the page;

  • In [2], fill in the fields;
  • In [3], submit the page;

The tax amount is displayed in [1]. Run several simulations, then request the list in [2];

  • In [1], delete a simulation;

  • in [1], end the session;

docs.title: 6.6. Conclusion
docs.text: The four clients in this chapter illustrate, with Dart, exactly the same progression as with TypeScript: from server-side processing to client-side processing, then from the CLI script to the full web client. The key differences to note are the manual tracking of the session cookie (necessary in CLI, unnecessary in a browser), the [.toJS] conversion enforced by [dart:js_interop] to bridge the Dart/JavaScript boundary in views, and the complete absence of polyfills during web compilation—a clear advantage of the Dart toolchain over the webpack/babel pipeline.

docs.title: 4. Installing a NestJS Server
docs.text:
This chapter is reproduced verbatim from the TypeScript course: installing a web server is not specific to any particular client language, and the server installed here serves as a common target for both courses. The only difference is that the numerous screenshots from the TypeScript document (installation of Laragon, HeidiSQL, Postman—a good hundred images in total) are not reproduced here; the text, however, is reproduced in its entirety. For step-by-step visual instructions, refer to document [Introduction to the TypeScript Language and the NestJS Web Framework], which describes the exact same installation.

Note: In the following, reference is sometimes made to a PHP server, the one referenced in the course [Introduction to the PHP7 Language Through Examples]. The NestJS server implements the same services as this PHP server.

We will cover the HTTP functions in Dart, which allow you to query a web server. For our tests, we need a web server. We will use the one developed for the TypeScript course (Chapter [Case Study: The Tax Calculation Server in NestJS], not covered in this course but whose server is still used as a target). This server hosts a JSON service offering the following services:

  • [init-session] - GET [main.php?action=init-session&type=json] - tells the server that we want responses from JSON;
  • [authenticate-user] - POST [main.php?action=authenticate-user]: the two posted parameters [user, password] determine whether or not to allow connection to the service JSON. By default, the credentials are [admin, admin];
  • [calculate-tax] - POST [main.php?action=calculate-tax]: The posted parameters [married, children, salary] are used to calculate a tax ([married]: “yes” or “no,” [children]: number of the taxpayer’s children, [salary]: the taxpayer’s annual salary);
  • [list-simulations] - GET [main.php?action=list-simulations] - lists the simulations performed since the start of the session;
  • [delete-simulation] - GET [main.php?action=delete-simulation&number=x] - removes simulation No. x from the list of simulations;
  • [get-admindata] - GET [main.php?action=get-admindata] - retrieves the entire database associated with the server into an object named JSON;
  • [end-session] - GET [main.php?action=end-session]: ends the session. To start another session, the user must issue the “init-session” command above.

docs.title: 4.1. Installing Laragon
docs.text:
In September 2026, the Laragon tool is available at URL [Download Laragon – Fast & Modern Dev Environment ]. Laragon includes tools that allow you to install a PHP server and the MySQL DBMS:

  • in [1], an Apache web server;
  • into [2], the MySQL DBMS;
  • to [3], a messaging tool that we will not be using;
  • [4] starts all services (Apache, MySQL, MailPit);
  • [5] displays the web page for URL [http://localhost]. By default, this URL refers to the <laragon-install>\www folder, where <laragon-install> is the Laragon installation folder;
  • in [6], launches the HeidiSQL tool, which allows you to manage MySQL databases. We will use this tool to create the database used by the tax calculation server;
  • In [7], open a terminal; all the binaries needed for Laragon are located in PATH;
  • In [8], open a Windows Explorer window in the folder associated with URL [http://localhost];

The Laragon installation folder contains the following items:

  • In [1], the [bin] folder contains numerous applications:
  • In [1], the Apache web server;
  • in [2], a command-line terminal;
  • in [3], a client for [git] that allows you to manage different versions of a project;
  • in [4], a database manager;
  • [5], an email manager;
  • in [6], the MySQL DBMS;
  • [7], another web server;
  • in [8], [node.js] to run JavaScript scripts;
  • [9], a text editor;
  • [10], the PHP interpreter;
  • [11], the [Python] interpreter;
  • [12], a cache server;

Laragon comes with a comprehensive development environment. In this course, we will only use the MySQL DBMS, [6], and [heidisql] to manage it graphically;

docs.title: 4.2. Installation and Configuration of the NestJS Server
docs.text:
A NestJS server for a highly simplified tax calculation can be found in the nestjs-case-study folder within the script directory for this course:

nestjs-case-study/
├── package.json
├── nest-cli.json
├── .env.example
├── create_dbtaxes.sql
├── src/
│   ├── main.ts
│   ├── main.controller.ts
│   ├── app.module.ts
│   ├── actions/
│   ├── config/
│   ├── entities/
│   ├── filters/
│   ├── model/
│   ├── responses/
│   ├── session/
│   └── utilities/
└── views/

Node.js and npm must be installed for this server (they are not needed for the Dart scripts themselves). Navigate to the nestjs-case-study folder and install its dependencies:

npm install
Note: this installation is needed only once; it creates the `node_modules` folder. You can then proceed to the configuration below.

The server needs a .env file to specify the connection settings for the MySQL database created by Laragon (see above) as well as the listening port. Copy the provided .env.example file to .env and modify it as follows:

PORT=3000
TAX_DATA_SOURCE=mysql
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=3306
DB_NAME=dbtaxes-2019
DB_USER=admtaxes
DB_PASSWORD=pwdtaxes
CORS_ALLOWED=true
SESSION_SECRET=change-me-in-production
  • PORT: the listening port for the NestJS server (default is 3000).
  • TAX_DATA_SOURCE: MySQL to use the database created below;
  • DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME, DB_USER, DB_PASSWORD: the connection parameters for the dbtaxes-2019 database that we will create with HeidiSQL (see below)—same credentials as those defined in the create_dbtaxes.sql script shown in the directory tree above;
  • CORS_ALLOWED: allows calls to CORS from a Dart (browser) client running on a different port.
  • SESSION_SECRET: the key used to sign the session cookie—change it if the server is ever to be made publicly accessible.

docs.title: 4.3. Creating the Database
docs.text:
To create the MySQL database required by the NestJS server, we use a Laragon option:

  • In [1], all services must be started;
  • in [2], the [Database] option allows you to manage the database;

The [Database] option launches a utility called HeidiSQL:

  • In [1], you can select various DBMS options. The default value provided is MySQL DBMS. This is acceptable;
  • in [2], you log in to HeidiSQL;
  • In [1-2], run the SQL file, then select the [create_dbtaxes.sql] file, which you’ll find in the [nestjs-case-study] folder:

Running the [2] file will create the [dbtaxes-2019] database used by the tax calculation server. To view it, run F5 within HeidiSQL to refresh the display:

The database [dbtaxes-2019] has been created.

docs.title: 4.4. Starting the NestJS server
docs.text:
Once the .env file is in place (and the database has been created), open a terminal at the root of the [nestjs-case-study] folder, then compile and start the server:

npm run build
npm run start:prod

For development, with automatic restart after every source code change, use:

npm run start:dev

In both cases, the console displays:

[Nest] ... [NestFactory] Starting Nest application...
[Nest] ... [InstanceLoader] AppModule dependencies initialized
[Nest] ... [RoutesResolver] MainController {/}:
[Nest] ... [RouterExplorer] Mapped {/main.php, ALL} route
[Nest] ... [NestApplication] Nest application successfully started
Tax calculation server (NestJS) started on http://localhost:3000
JSON entry point: http://localhost:3000/main.php?action=init-session&type=json
HTML entry point: http://localhost:3000/main.php?action=init-session&type=html

The NestJS server has a single entry point (main.php, retained for compatibility even though it is actually NestJS) that receives all requests, and an “action” request parameter that selects the processing to be performed:

docs.title: 4.5. HTML tests for the tax calculation server
docs.text:
If you haven't already, start all Laragon services (for MySQL) as well as the NestJS server (npm run start:prod or npm run start:dev; see above). Then, in a browser, request the URL at http://localhost:3000/main.php?action=init-session&type=html — this is the same init-session action as for the PHP server, with the same type=html parameter, but on port 3000:

The credentials are admin/admin, exactly the same as for the PHP server—they are defined in the same way, in the server code rather than in config.json. Enter them:

Fill out the form and then submit it. You’ll see the following page:

The tax calculation result is displayed—this page is indeed using the database we just created. The “List of simulations” link in the left-hand menu displays the history of calculations for this session:

If you get these results, the NestJS tax calculation server is working correctly with its MySQL database. We are now ready to query the server with Dart clients. To do this, we will use version JSON of the server.

docs.title: 4.6. The API and JSON versions of the tax calculation server
4.6.1. Postman Tests
docs.text:
The PHP server was tested using the Postman desktop tool. The same collection of requests (tax-servers-tests.postman_collection.json, provided in the nestjs-course folder of the TypeScript course scripts) works identically against the NestJS server: API and JSON are exactly the same—same actions, same parameters, same status codes. In Postman, simply change the port for each request (80 → 3000), or more simply, the base URL in the collection if you’ve defined it as a variable.

The Postman tool is available at URL [https://www.postman.com/downloads/]. You may need to create an account.

Start all Laragon services, then open the Postman desktop app:

  • In [1-2], create a request HTTP to query the tax calculation server;
  • In [1], you can name your query HTTP. You will be able to save it and retrieve it;
  • In [2]: enter the URL of the server you want to query;
  • In [3]: select the query type HTTP. We’ll use two of them in the following: GET and POST;
  • in [4]: if your query has parameters of the type [?param1=val1&param2=val2&…], you can define them here;
  • in [5]: if the query type is POST, this is where you define the posted values;

In the [nestjs-course] folder of the TypeScript course scripts, you will find a collection of HTTP requests to the tax calculation server that you can import into POSTMAN.

Proceed as follows. In Postman, run [Ctrl-O]:

  • Use the link [1] to import the file [tax-servers-tests.postman_collection.json] from the folder [nestjs-course]:
  • In [1], the name of the imported collection;
  • in [2], its contents. This is a list of requests (HTTP) to the tax calculation server (JSON);

Let’s look, for example, at the request named [init-session-json-700]. It initiates a session JSON with the server:

  • In [1], the request HTTP is a GET;
  • in [2], the queried URL. It requests to initiate a JSON dialogue with the server;
  • in [3-4], we find the parameters from GET;
  • in [5], to send the request to the tax calculation server;

Before sending the request, make sure you have started the Laragon services. The server’s response, JSON, is as follows:

Now use the request named [init-session-703]:

The request [1-3] is invalid. The parameters must be of the type [?action=xx&type=yy], where “type” can be “html,” “xml,” or “json.” The type “x” will not be recognized. The server’s response, JSON, is as follows:

Resend the request [init-session-json-700] to restart a session JSON. Then send the request [authenticate-user-200] to authenticate yourself:

  • In [1], the request is POST;
  • in [2], the authentication request URL;
  • in [3], the body of POST, which contains the posted values;
  • [4-5], the two posted values. These are the application administrator’s credentials. They are defined in the server’s [config.service.ts] file;

The server’s response, JSON, is as follows:

Once you are authenticated, you can perform a tax calculation. To do so, use the query [calculate-tax-300]:

  • In [1], this is a POST request;
  • in [2], the URL query is called;
  • in [3-4], the three values are posted;

The response JSON is as follows:

Run the request several times, changing the posted values each time. Once you’ve done that, run the request [list-simulations-500], which will display the list of simulations you’ve performed:

  • The request GET [1-4] has only one parameter: [action]. The response JSON is as follows:

This is the list of simulations you have performed.

Use the query [delete-simulation-600] to delete a simulation:

  • In [2], the URL is queried with a GET. It includes two parameters: [action, number]. [number] is the number of the simulation you want to delete from the list of simulations. Here, the number 0 refers to the first simulation in the list;

The server’s response, JSON, is as follows:

The response JSON is the remaining list of simulations after deleting one of them;

Finally, you can end the session with the query [end-session-400]:

The query URL [1-2] has only the parameter [action] (3). The response JSON is as follows:

docs.title: 4.6.2. curl Tests
docs.text:
We can also use the [curl] tool to test the server’s JSON services. All of the following requests use the same session, HTTP (the -b/-c cookies.txt option in curl preserves the session cookie between calls, just as a browser or Postman would):

Let’s start a JSON session with the [init-session] action:

curl -c cookies.txt "http://localhost:3000/main.php?action=init-session&type=json"

{
  "action": "init-session",
  "status": 700,
  "response": "session started with type [json]"
}

Status code 700 confirms that the session has started—this is the same code that the PHP server returned. Now let’s authenticate using the [authenticate-user] action—a POST request, with a single parameter in the URL (action) and the credentials posted:

curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -X POST "http://localhost:3000/main.php?action=authenticate-user" \
     -d "user=admin&password=admin"

{
  "action": "authenticate-user",
  "status": 200,
  "response": "Authentication successful [admin, admin]"
}

You can now calculate taxes using the action [calculate-tax], again with POST with the three posted parameters: marital status, children, and salary:

curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -X POST "http://localhost:3000/main.php?action=calculate-tax" \
     -d "married=yes&children=2&salary=45000"

{
  "action": "calculate-tax",
  "status": 300,
  "response": {
    "married": "yes",
    "children": 2,
    "salary": 45000,
    "tax": 502,
    "surcharge": 0,
    "discount": 857,
    "reduction": 126,
    "rate": 0.14
  }
}

The values are exactly the same (€502 in tax, a discount of €857, a reduction of 126 €, and a rate of 14%) as those displayed in the browser in the previous section—the two versions, HTML and JSON, share the same calculation engine. The list of simulations is obtained using action [list-simulations], a simple GET:

curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt "http://localhost:3000/main.php?action=list-simulations"

{
  "action": "list-simulations",
  "status": 500,
  "response": [
    {
      "married": "yes", "children": 2, "salary": 45000,
      "tax": 502, "surcharge": 0, "discount": 857, "reduction": 126, "rate": 0.14
    }
  ]
}

Run the query [calculate-tax] several times by changing the posted values, then use [delete-simulation] to remove a simulation from the list (&number=x refers to its sequence number), and [get-admindata] to retrieve the entire database in the format JSON (tax brackets and calculation constants). Finally, end the session with the action [end-session]:

curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt "http://localhost:3000/main.php?action=end-session"

{
  "action": "end-session",
  "status": 400,
  "response": "session deleted"
}

You now have a good understanding of the API and JSON exposed by the NestJS tax calculation server—which is exactly the same as that of the PHP server. We can now move on to writing Dart scripts that query this server.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is |HERE|.

The document’s codes are |HERE|.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s Claude AI. Its purpose is to transpose the document [Introduction to the TypeScript Language and the NestJS Web Framework] by replacing the TypeScript language with the Dart language.

The Anthropic Claude AI model did the bulk of the work (90%):

  • Code generation: Claude generated all of the code. I simply tested it by following the generated course. No Dart was available in the environment where Claude worked (unlike in the TypeScript course, where each script could be executed and verified by Claude): the scripts for this course were written and reviewed with the same care, checked for syntax (balanced curly braces and parentheses, presence of a [main] entry point in each executable script), but could not be compiled or executed prior to delivery. Note: All delivered code was tested by the course reviewer. Errors were reported to Claude, who corrected them immediately.
  • Course generation in ODT format: Claude generated several versions at my request. This is where I was primarily involved.

Serge Tahé, September 2026

==

This document is an introductory course on the [Dart] language, designed on the same principle as the [Introduction to the TypeScript language and the NestJS web framework through examples (2026)] course: learning a language through a series of small, standalone scripts, commented line by line, rather than through a theoretical exposition of its grammar.

The progression follows exactly that of the TypeScript course: the same concepts, in the same order, with a Dart script alongside each TypeScript script. This symmetry is intentional: it allows you, at any time, to directly compare how Dart and TypeScript address the same need—and to identify, for each difference, what stems from a simple choice of syntax and what stems from a fundamental difference between the two languages (structural typing versus nominal typing, compilation versus transpilation, the presence or absence of implicit coercion, etc.).

Two chapters from the TypeScript course have been intentionally omitted here: [Introduction to the NestJS Web Framework] and [Case Study: The Tax Calculation Server in NestJS]. These two chapters cover a server-side web framework written in TypeScript—a topic not directly related to learning the Dart language itself. The NestJS tax calculation server, on the other hand, is retained: once installed (see the chapter “Installing a NestJS Server”), it serves as a real-world target for testing Dart functions—exactly as it serves as a target for the HTTP and TypeScript clients from the original course.

However, a difference in scope distinguishes this course from the TypeScript course: the [The Fundamentals] section of the TypeScript course devotes three entire sections to recent updates to ECMAScript (2020–2024, 2026) and to the [Temporal] API. These new features are specific to JavaScript/TypeScript and have no direct equivalent in Dart; they are replaced here by a section on [Dart 3.x New Features], dedicated to recent features specific to Dart: [records], [pattern matching], [sealed] classes, and class modifiers.

docs.title: 1.1. Target Audience and Prerequisites
docs.text:
This course is intended for readers who are already familiar with programming—ideally, those who have already taken the TypeScript course, since the constant comparison between the two languages is central to the teaching approach used here. No prior knowledge of Dart is required: each new concept is introduced through a minimal script, commented on in detail.

Contrary to the common misconception that reduces Dart to “the language of Flutter,” this course does not cover Flutter or mobile interfaces at any point: Dart is used here as a general-purpose programming language, run from the command line ([dart run]), exactly as TypeScript was used with [tsx] in the original course.

docs.title: 1.2. Organization of the Sample Project
docs.text:
The scripts for this course are provided in a separate directory structure, [dart-fundamentals/], which mirrors the folder structure of the TypeScript course ([basics/], [arrays/], [objects/], [strings/], [regexp/], [functions/], [exceptions/], [modules/], [async/], [classes/], [http/]...), plus a new folder, [dart3/], for the [Dart 3.x New Features] section. A second directory tree, [dart-databases/], contains the “Database Access” chapter. Each folder contains its own [README.md] and, when necessary, its own [pubspec.yaml] (the Dart equivalent of [package.json] from Node.js; see the following chapter).

Each script is run individually using the command [dart run], followed by the script’s path—for example, [dart run dart-fundamentals/basics/basics_01.dart]. No full installation of the project is required to run a single script: [dart pub get] (equivalent to [npm install]), run once at the root of a folder containing a [pubspec.yaml], is sufficient to install the dependencies for all the scripts it contains.

docs.title: 2. Setting Up a Development Environment
docs.text:
Note: In the following steps, we’ll use the VSCode tool to test the Dart scripts. Open two VSCode windows and use [File / Open Folder] to open the folders for both projects.

The TypeScript course installs Node.js, an npm project ([package.json]), TypeScript itself and its type checker ([tsc]), a script runner that does not require prior compilation ([tsx]), and finally ESLint. The Dart equivalent of this entire toolchain consists of a single component to install: [Dart SDK]—which can be downloaded from [dart.dev] or, more simply, installed via a system package manager ([choco install dart-sdk] on Windows, [brew install dart] on macOS, or the official APT repository on Linux/Debian/Ubuntu).

Whereas TypeScript requires three separate tools (the [tsc] compiler to check types, [tsx] to run a script without compiling it first, and ESLint for style analysis), the Dart SDK provides all of this in a single command, [dart], which includes the following subcommands: [dart run] (runs a script), [dart analyze] (checks the style—the combined equivalent of [tsc] and ESLint), [dart pub] (manages dependencies, equivalent to [npm]), [dart format] (reformats the code, equivalent to Prettier) and [dart test] (runs the tests).

docs.title: 2.1. Verifying Installed Tools
docs.text:
Once SDK is installed, verify the installation in a terminal using VSCode:

PS C:\Data\st-2026\dev\dart\dart-sept-2026-scripts\dart-fundamentals> dart --version
Dart SDK version: 3.12.2 (stable) (Tue Jun 9 01:11:39 2026 -0700) on "windows_x64"

which displays the version of SDK (for example, [Dart SDK version: 3.12.2 (stable)]). Unlike Node.js and TypeScript, which are installed separately (one version of Node, one version of TypeScript), the version number of the Dart SDK covers the language, the compiler, and all the tools controlled by [dart]: there is only one version to track.

docs.title: 2.2. Setting up the VSCode project
docs.text: As with TypeScript, create a project folder and open it in VSCode. Whereas a TypeScript project is declared with two files ([package.json] for dependencies, [tsconfig.json] for compiler options), a Dart project requires only one: [pubspec.yaml].

docs.title: 2.2.1. The pubspec.yaml file
docs.text:
[pubspec.yaml] serves both the role of [package.json] (project name, dependencies) and, to a lesser extent, that of [tsconfig.json] (the key [environment: sdk:] sets the range of accepted Dart SDK versions, much like [target]/[lib] define the version of ECMAScript targeted by [tsc]):

name: dart_fundamentals
description: Scripts of the course "Introduction to the Dart language by example"
publish_to: 'none'
environment:
  sdk: '>=3.3.0 <4.0.0'

dependencies:
  http: ^1.2.0
  dio: ^5.4.0

Unlike [package.json] (in JSON format), [pubspec.yaml] is, strictly speaking, a YAML file—indentation is significant in it, just as it is in Python.

Once this file is written, the command [dart pub get] (equivalent to [npm install]) downloads the declared dependencies and generates a [pubspec.lock] file (equivalent to [package-lock.json]), which locks in the exact versions to be installed.

docs.title: 2.3. First script
docs.text:
A minimal Dart script, [hello.dart]:

void main() {
  print('Hello Dart!');
}

is run with:

dart run hello.dart

Two immediate differences from the first script, TypeScript, in the course: the function [main] is here MANDATORY (an executable Dart script must define a function named [main] at the file level—unlike TypeScript/[tsx], where the top-level code in the file runs directly, without requiring a function to be defined); and [dart run] compiles and executes the script in a single step, without a visible separate transpilation step (like [tsx], but without the need to install any additional tools: [dart run] is part of SDK itself).

docs.title: 2.4. Second script: static analysis
docs.text:
Whereas the TypeScript course distinguishes between a “type checking” step ([tsc --noEmit]) and a separate ESLint step, Dart merges the two into a single command:

dart analyze

When run without arguments from the root of a project containing a [pubspec.yaml] file, it analyzes all [.dart] files in the project: it flags both type errors (the equivalent of [tsc]) and style issues covered by the enabled lint rules (the equivalent of ESLint)—see the following section for information on enabling these rules.

docs.title: 2.5. The linter
docs.text:
ESLint is an external tool that must be installed and configured separately (file [eslint.config.js], selecting a preset, etc.). Dart integrates its own linter directly into [dart analyze]: simply add the official [package:lints] package to the [dev_dependencies] of [pubspec.yaml], then create a [analysis_options.yaml] file at the root of the project:

include: package:lints/recommended.yaml

This single file serves the same purpose as [eslint.config.js] for the TypeScript course: it activates a set of rules recommended by the Dart team (unused variables, suspicious comparisons, preference for [const], etc.), which [dart analyze] then applies automatically.

docs.title: 2.6. VSCode Dart Extension
docs.text: The official [Dart] extension (publisher: Dart Code), installed from the VSCode extension marketplace, serves exactly the same purpose as the ESLint extension from the TypeScript course, but is more comprehensive: syntax highlighting, autocompletion, display of [dart analyze] errors directly in the editor, and running scripts (the [Run]/[Debug] button above each [main] function) without exiting VSCode. Installing this single extension is sufficient to cover what the TypeScript course spreads across multiple extensions.

docs.title: 3. The Fundamentals
docs.text: This chapter follows, script by script, the progression of chapter [The Fundamentals] from the TypeScript course: same sections, same order, with a Dart script corresponding to each TypeScript script.

docs.title: 3.1. The Basics of Dart
docs.text: This first section covers the fundamentals common to all Dart programs: variables, lists, loops, functions, variable scope, basic types, and conversions.

docs.title: 3.1.1. [basics_01] script
docs.text:
// basics_01.dart
// Ports the TypeScript script basics-01.ts: variables, arrays, loops,
// destructuring, functions, dynamic typing, comparison operators.
void main() {
  // constant - in Dart as in TypeScript, [const] declares a constant
  // whose value is known at COMPILE TIME (an even stricter constant
  // than TypeScript's [const], which only requires a value
  // known at run time and not reassigned)
  const String name = "dupont";
  // a screen display - [print] is the Dart equivalent of [console.log]
  print("name : $name");

  // an array (called a "list" in Dart) with elements of different types
  // [dynamic] because this list deliberately mixes several types
  // (demonstration) - it is the equivalent of TypeScript's [any]: Dart
  // then no longer performs any compile-time type checking
  // on the elements of this list
  final List<dynamic> array = ["one", "two", 3, 4];
  // its number of elements
  int n = array.length;
  // a loop
  for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    print("array[$i] = ${array[i]}");
  }

  // initialization of 2 variables with the content of a list
  // Dart has no list destructuring on assignment like
  // TypeScript (const [a, b] = array); since Dart 3, a
  // "list pattern" gives the same result (see dart3/*.dart
  // for a complete presentation of patterns)
  final [string1, string2] = ["string1", "string2"];
  // concatenation of the 2 strings
  final String string3 = string1 + string2;
  // display result
  print([string1, string2, string3]);
  // using a function
  display(string1);
  // the type of a variable can be known with runtimeType
  // (the Dart equivalent of TypeScript's [typeof] operator)
  displayType("n", n);
  displayType("string1", string1);
  displayType("array", array);

  // [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript] in TypeScript, the
  // [any] type allows a variable to change type during execution
  // (n = "has changed" after n = 4 is valid). In Dart, the type of a
  // variable is fixed once and for all by its declaration: [n] was
  // declared [int] above, so n = "has changed" is a COMPILATION
  // ERROR, not a mere oversight tolerated at run time. To
  // get a behaviour comparable to [any], one would have to declare
  // [dynamic n = array.length;] from the start - but this script
  // deliberately does not, in order to highlight the difference.
  // The following line is therefore COMMENTED OUT: uncommenting it causes a
  // compilation error.
  // n = "has changed";
  print('type[variable n]=${n.runtimeType} (Dart forbids assigning it '
      'anything other than an int: see the comment above)');

  // a function can return a result
  int res1 = f1(4);
  print("res1=$res1");

  // a function can return several values: Dart cannot return
  // a heterogeneous JS array directly into separate variables with
  // a syntax [let x, y, z; [x, y, z] = f()] like TypeScript. We use
  // either a Record (see dart3/, the modern typed solution), or here,
  // to stay close to the original script, a value that we destructure
  // with a pattern (Dart 3):
  final (res2, res3, res4) = f2();
  print("(res2,res3,res4)=${[res2, res3, res4]}");

  // we could have retrieved these values in a list
  final List<dynamic> t = f2ListAny();
  for (var i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
    print("t[$i]=${t[i]}");
  }
  // some tests
  for (var i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
    // displays only the strings - [is String] is the Dart equivalent of
    // [typeof(x) === "string"]
    if (t[i] is String) {
      print("t[$i]=${t[i]}");
    }
  }

  // [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Dart's
  // [==] operator ALWAYS corresponds to JavaScript's strict [===]
  // operator: Dart has no comparison operator with
  // implicit type conversion like JavaScript's non-strict [==].
  // The comparison "2" == 2 is therefore always false in Dart, whatever
  // the operator used - the code below therefore deliberately has
  // only one branch (no "with ==" then "with ===" section as
  // in the original TypeScript script, since this distinction does not exist).
  if ("2" == 2) {
    print("the string 2 is equal to the integer 2");
  } else {
    print("in Dart, the string '2' is never equal to the integer 2 "
        "(no implicit conversion like JS's non-strict ==)");
  }

  // other tests
  for (var i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
    // displays only the integers >10
    if (t[i] is int && t[i] > 10) {
      print("t[$i]=${t[i]}");
    }
  }

  // a while loop
  List<num> t2 = [8, 5, 0, -2, 3, 4];
  var i = 0;
  num sum = 0;
  while (i < t2.length && t2[i] > 0) {
    print("t2[$i]=${t2[i]}");
    sum += t2[i];
    i++;
  }
  print("sum=$sum");
}

// the main program stops here because there is no more executable code

// display
// ----------------------------------
void display(String string) {
  // displays string
  print("string=$string");
}

// displayType
// ----------------------------------
void displayType(String name, dynamic variable) {
  // displays the type of variable - [runtimeType] is the Dart equivalent of
  // [typeof]: unlike [typeof], which returns a generic string
  // ("number", "string"...), [runtimeType] returns the name of the REAL Dart
  // type of the value (int, String, List<dynamic>...)
  print("type[variable $name]=${variable.runtimeType}");
}

// ----------------------------------
int f1(int param) {
  // adds 10 to param
  return param + 10;
}

// ----------------------------------
// returns 3 values as a Record (Dart 3) - the modern, typed Dart type
// for what TypeScript would do with a heterogeneous array [any[]]
(String, int, int) f2() {
  return ("one", 0, 100);
}

// same result as f2(), but as a [dynamic] list to stay
// as close as possible to the [any[]] style of the original TypeScript script
List<dynamic> f2ListAny() {
  return ["one", 0, 100];
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 9: [const String name]: In Dart, [const] requires a value known at the time of COMPILATION — a stricter constraint than [const] for TypeScript, which only requires a value that has not been reassigned at runtime.
  • Line 18: [List<dynamic> array]: Dart calls the JavaScript “array” a [list], and [dynamic] plays the role of [any] in TypeScript to disable type checking on the elements.
  • Line 31: [final [string1, string2] = [...]]: Dart does not support destructuring assignments like TypeScript; the Dart 3 version LIST PATTERN, used here, yields the same result (a complete overview of the patterns is provided in the chapter [Dart 3.x New Features]).
  • Line 56: [n.runtimeType] replaces the [typeof] operator from TypeScript, with one difference: it returns a REAL Dart type name ([int], [List<dynamic>]...), not just a generic string (["number"], ["string"]).
  • The line [n = "has changed";] is intentionally commented out: unlike a variable [any] of type TypeScript, a Dart variable retains the type specified at its declaration—this assignment would result in a COMPILATION ERROR.
  • line 69: [final (res2, res3, res4) = f2();]: a Dart function cannot “return multiple values” into separate variables as a heterogeneous array TypeScript would; [f2] returns a RECORD (Dart 3) here, which is immediately destructured by a list pattern.
  • line 94: [if ("2" == 2)]: Dart’s [] operator corresponds to the strict [=] of JavaScript - There is no Dart equivalent for the non-strict [==] of JavaScript, so there is no second case to show here, unlike in the original TypeScript script.

As a reminder, to run a Dart script, you can type the following command in a terminal:

dart run path_to_script.dart

For example, as shown below:

dart run basics_01.dart

if your terminal is set to the folder containing the script [basics_01.dart]. You can also click on the term [Run] in the text editor, which appears above the function [main]:

The result of running [basics_01] is as follows:

name : dupont
array[0] = one
array[1] = two
array[2] = 3
array[3] = 4
[string1, string2, string1string2]
string=string1
type[variable n]=int
type[variable string1]=String
type[variable array]=List<dynamic>
type[variable n]=int (Dart forbids assigning it anything other than an int: see the comment above)
res1=14
(res2,res3,res4)=[one, 0, 100]
t[0]=one
t[1]=0
t[2]=100
t[0]=one
in Dart, the string '2' is never equal to the integer 2 (no implicit conversion like JS's non-strict ==)
t[2]=100
t2[0]=8
t2[1]=5
sum=13

docs.title: 3.1.2. script [basics_02]
docs.text:
// basics_02.dart
// Ports basics-02.ts: var/let/const in TypeScript, var/final/const in Dart.
void main() {
  // to initialize a variable, we use [var] (inferred type) or an
  // explicit type (like [int] here) for MUTABLE variables -
  // the equivalent of TypeScript's [let]
  int x = 4;
  x++;
  print(x);
  // [final] for a variable assigned ONLY ONCE at run time -
  // the equivalent of TypeScript's [const] (a value known only at
  // run time, but not reassignable afterwards)
  final int y = 10;
  x += y;
  // forbidden - x is mutable but y is not: y++ causes a
  // compilation error, exactly as in TypeScript
  // y++;

  // [NEW compared to TypeScript] Dart offers a second keyword,
  // [const], stricter than [final]: a [const] constant must be
  // known at COMPILE TIME (as at the very beginning of basics_01.dart). There
  // is no equivalent of this final/const distinction in
  // TypeScript, where [const] only means "not reassigned".
  const int z = 100; // known at compile time: valid
  print(z);
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • A mutable variable is declared with an explicit type (or [var]): this is equivalent to [let] from TypeScript.
  • [final] is the equivalent of [const] in TypeScript: a value assigned only once, but whose value is not known until runtime.
  • Line 19: [NEW] Dart adds a second keyword, [const], which is stricter than [final]: a value [const] must be known at the time of COMPILATION. TypeScript does not have this two-level distinction.

The result of the execution is as follows:

5
100

docs.title: 3.1.3. script [basics_03]
docs.text:
// basics_03.dart
// Ports basics-03.ts: variable scope - a file-level variable
// ("top-level" scope, the Dart equivalent of TypeScript's module
// scope) is visible from the functions of the same file.

// top-level variable (outside any function/class), like the top-level
// [let] of the TypeScript script
int count = 1;

void doSomething() {
  // count is known here: a function sees the top-level variables of
  // the file containing it, exactly as in TypeScript
  print("count=$count");
}

void main() {
  // call
  doSomething();
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • A variable declared outside any function (scope [top-level]) is visible from all functions in the same file—exactly the role of a module-scope variable in TypeScript.

The result of execution is as follows:

count=1

docs.title: 3.1.4. script [basics_04]
docs.text:
// basics_04.dart
// Ports basics-04.ts: a variable local to a function hides a top-level
// variable with the same name - the same shadowing principle as in
// TypeScript.

// top-level variable
const int count = 1;

void doSomething() {
  // the local variable hides the top-level variable
  const count = 2;
  print("count inside function=$count");
}

void main() {
  // top-level variable
  print("count outside function=$count");
  // local variable
  doSomething();
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • A local variable within a function, with the same name as a top-level variable—HIDES it ([shadowing])—inside this function—the same principle as in TypeScript.

The result of the execution is as follows:

count outside function=1
count inside function=2

docs.title: 3.1.5. script [basics_05]
docs.text:
// basics_05.dart
// Ports basics-05.ts: a variable declared inside a function
// is not known outside it - same principle as in TypeScript.
void doSomething() {
  // variable local to the function
  const count = 2;
  print("count inside function=$count");
}

void main() {
  // count is not known here: the following line, if uncommented,
  // would cause a compilation error ("Undefined name 'count'"),
  // exactly as in TypeScript
  // print("count outside function=$count");
  doSomething();
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • A variable declared inside a function is not visible outside of it: referencing it outside the function results in a compilation error, just as in TypeScript.

The result of execution is as follows:

count inside function=2

docs.title: 3.1.6. [basics_06] script
docs.text:
This script is shorter than its equivalent TypeScript: see the comment at the top of the file for the reason.

// basics_06.dart
// Ports basics-06.ts: block scope.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] TypeScript has
// THREE declaration keywords with different scopes: [let] and [const]
// are BLOCK-scoped, but [var] (inherited from JavaScript) is
// FUNCTION-scoped - a [var] variable declared in a {...} block "leaks"
// outside that block, which is precisely what this script shows with [count3].
// Dart has NO equivalent of this [var]: [var], [final] and [const] are
// ALWAYS block-scoped in Dart, without exception. This script is therefore
// shorter than the original: there are only two cases to show, not three,
// and both behave like TypeScript's [let]/[const] cases.
void main() {
  // [var] (inferred type) defines a block-scoped variable
  {
    // the variable [count] is only known in this block
    var count = 1;
    print("count=$count");
  }
  // the variable [count] is not known here: the following line, if
  // uncommented, would cause a compilation error
  // count++;

  // [final] defines a (non-reassignable) block-scoped variable
  {
    // the variable [count2] is only known in this block
    final count2 = 1;
    print("count=$count2");
  }
  // the variable [count2] is not known here either
  // count2++;

  // there is no 3rd case in Dart: no declaration keyword
  // lets a variable "leak" outside the block where it is declared,
  // unlike the TypeScript/JavaScript [var] used for [count3]
  // in the original script.
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • [var] and [final] are ALWAYS BLOCK-scoped in Dart, without any exceptions.
  • This script shows only the TWO cases, whereas the TypeScript script showed three: Dart has no equivalent to [var] from JavaScript, whose scope is that of FUNCTION (not the block) and which “leaks” out of a [{...}] block—a classic source of bugs in JavaScript, but structurally impossible in Dart.

The result of the execution is as follows:

count=1
count=1

// basics_07.dart
// Ports basics-07.ts: the main basic data types and their
// introspection with runtimeType (the Dart equivalent of typeof).
void main() {
  const int var1 = 10;
  const String var2 = "abc";
  const bool var3 = true;
  const List<int> var4 = [1, 2, 3];
  const Map<String, String> var5 = {'name': 'axèle'};
  // a variable of function type - Dart types functions with the
  // notation [ReturnType Function(parameters)]
  int Function() var6 = () => 3;

  // displaying the types with runtimeType
  print("var1.runtimeType=${var1.runtimeType}");
  print("var2.runtimeType=${var2.runtimeType}");
  print("var3.runtimeType=${var3.runtimeType}");
  print("var4.runtimeType=${var4.runtimeType}");
  print("var5.runtimeType=${var5.runtimeType}");
  print("var6.runtimeType=${var6.runtimeType}");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 12: [int Function() var6 = () => 3;]: In Dart, functions are defined using the notation [ReturnType Function(parameters)]—a function is a type like any other, assignable to a variable.
  • lines 15–20: [runtimeType] displays, for each variable, its real Dart type ([int], [String], [List<int>], [Map<String, String>] (line 9), [() => int]...).

The result of the execution is as follows:

docs.title: 3.1.8. script [basics_08]
docs.text:
This script differs in nature from its equivalent, TypeScript: whereas basics-08.ts illustrated the conversions IMPLICIT from JavaScript, this script shows the conversions EXPLICIT that must be written instead, since Dart does not perform any such conversions (see the comment at the top of the file for details on the three relevant rules).

// basics_08.dart
// Ports basics-08.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] this script
// completely changes nature compared to the original. JavaScript (and
// therefore TypeScript, which only adds types checked at
// COMPILE TIME but keeps JavaScript's behaviour at RUN TIME)
// performs many IMPLICIT type conversions at run time:
// - in a test [if (data) ...], any value is converted to a
//   boolean ("" and 0 are "falsy", "abcd" and [1,2,3] are "truthy"...);
// - the [+] operator performs an addition IF BOTH operands are
//   numbers, otherwise a string concatenation ("12" * 1 is 12, but
//   "12" + 1 is "121");
// - true/false convert to 1/0 in a calculation...
// Dart has NONE of these implicit conversions:
// - the condition of an [if] must be a [bool], period: [if
//   ("abcd")] is a COMPILATION ERROR, not an automatic conversion;
// - [+] requires operands of the SAME type (String+String, or num+num): "12"
//   + 1 is a compilation error;
// - a [bool] is never implicitly converted to a number.
// This script therefore shows, unlike the original TypeScript script, the
// EXPLICIT conversions that must be written instead of each of these
// implicit conversions.
void main() {
  print("---------------[No implicit conversion to a boolean]------"
      "------------------------------");
  // in TypeScript, [showBool(value)] directly tests the "truthiness" of
  // any value. In Dart, you must write yourself the explicit
  // test matching what you really want to check: an empty
  // string, an empty list, a null value... [showBool] below
  // therefore deliberately accepts only an [Object?] (nullable) and documents,
  // for each family of types, the equivalent EXPLICIT conversion
  showBoolEquivalent("abcd", (v) => (v as String).isNotEmpty);
  showBoolEquivalent("", (v) => (v as String).isNotEmpty);
  showBoolEquivalent([1, 2, 3], (v) => (v as List).isNotEmpty);
  showBoolEquivalent(<int>[], (v) => (v as List).isNotEmpty);
  showBoolEquivalent(null, (v) => v != null);
  showBoolEquivalent(0.0, (v) => (v as double) != 0.0);
  showBoolEquivalent(0, (v) => (v as int) != 0);
  showBoolEquivalent(4.6, (v) => (v as double) != 0.0);

  print("---------------[Explicit conversion of a string to a number]"
      "------------------------------");
  showNumber("12");
  showNumber("45.67");
  showNumber("abcd");

  print("---------------[Explicit conversion to a boolean]------------"
      "------------------------------");
  // unlike Boolean(data) in JavaScript (which applies the
  // "truthiness" rules), there is no equivalent generic Dart function:
  // each type must provide its own notion of "empty/non-empty" (shown
  // above with showBoolEquivalent)

  print("---------------[Explicit conversion to a number]-------------"
      "-----------------------------");
  showNumber2("12.45");
  showNumber2(true); // this case is handled separately below
  showNumber2(null);

  print("---------------[Explicit conversion to a string]-------------"
      "-----------------------------");
  showString(5);
  showString(6.7);
  showString(false);
  showString(null);

  print("---------------[Other cases]------------------------------");
  const String string1 = '1000.78';
  // in Dart, [+] between a String and a num is a compilation error:
  // one of the two operands must be converted explicitly
  // conversion of string1 to a number, then addition
  final double data1 = double.parse(string1) + 1.034;
  print("data1=$data1 (explicit conversion required, unlike "
      "'1000.78' + 1.034 in JS which concatenates into a string)");
  // reverse conversion: the number to a string, then concatenation
  final String data2 = (1.034).toString() + string1;
  print("data2=$data2 (here we knowingly choose concatenation, by "
      "converting the number)");
  // true/false are NEVER implicitly converted to a number in Dart -
  // you must write the desired mapping yourself. [boolValue] is a
  // variable (and not the literal [true] directly): with a literal,
  // dart analyze would see the [: 0.0] branch as dead code (always
  // false), since the condition would then be known at compile time.
  // (deliberately [final], not [const]: a [const] would remain a compile-time
  // constant, and dart analyze would still detect the dead code)
  final bool boolValue = true;
  final double data3 = boolValue ? 1.0 : 0.0;
  print("data3=$data3 (explicit equivalent of JS's 'true * 1.18', "
      "combined with the multiplication below)");
  print("true converted then multiplied by 1.18 = ${data3 * 1.18}");
}

// displays, for a given value, the EXPLICIT boolean conversion that
// replaces JavaScript's implicit conversion - [tester] encodes the
// "right" way to test this particular value
void showBoolEquivalent(Object? data, bool Function(Object?) tester) {
  print("[data=$data], [type(data)]=${data.runtimeType}, "
      "[equivalent explicit test]=${tester(data)}");
}

void showNumber(String data) {
  // unlike [data * 1] in JS (which silently fails with NaN if
  // data is not numeric), [double.parse] throws an explicit
  // [FormatException] on failure - we catch it here to illustrate the
  // "abcd" case of the original script
  try {
    final number = double.parse(data);
    print("[data=$data], [number]=$number, [type(number)]="
        "${number.runtimeType}");
  } on FormatException {
    print("[data=$data] : FormatException, this is not a valid number "
        "(unlike Number('$data') in JS, which would return NaN without "
        "throwing an error)");
  }
}

void showNumber2(Object? data) {
  // explicit conversion according to the actual type of the data - there is no
  // single Dart function equivalent to Number(...) that would accept
  // a num, a bool or null indifferently
  double? number;
  if (data is num) {
    number = data.toDouble();
  } else if (data is String) {
    number = double.tryParse(data);
  } else if (data is bool) {
    number = data ? 1.0 : 0.0;
  }
  print("[data=$data], [type(data)]=${data.runtimeType}, [number]=$number, "
      "[type(number)]=${number.runtimeType}");
}

void showString(Object? data) {
  // toString() exists on (almost) every Dart object, including null
  // (returns "null") - quite close, here, to the behaviour of String(data)
  final String string = data.toString();
  print("[data=$data], [type(data)]=${data.runtimeType}, [string]=$string, "
      "[type(string)]=${string.runtimeType}");
}

Let's discuss this code:

  • [showBoolEquivalent]: Dart does not have an implicit conversion to [bool]—a condition of type [if] requires a REAL [bool]; Each type family (string, list, number) must explicitly provide its own “empty/non-empty” test.
  • Line 126: [double.parse]/[double.tryParse] replace the implicit conversion [Number(string)] from JavaScript: [parse] raises an explicit [FormatException] on failure; [tryParse] returns [null]—never a silent [NaN].
  • Line 73: [double.parse(string1) + 1.034]: [+] between a [String] and a [num] is a COMPILATION error in Dart - unlike ['1000.78' + 1.034] to JavaScript, which concatenates silently.
  • [true ? 1.0 : 0.0]: [bool] is not implicitly converted to a number in Dart—you must write the desired mapping yourself, whereas [true * 1.18] is valid in JavaScript.

The result of the execution is as follows:

---------------[No implicit conversion to a boolean]------------------------------------
[data=abcd], [type(data)]=String, [equivalent explicit test]=true
[data=], [type(data)]=String, [equivalent explicit test]=false
[data=[1, 2, 3]], [type(data)]=List<int>, [equivalent explicit test]=true
[data=[]], [type(data)]=List<int>, [equivalent explicit test]=false
[data=null], [type(data)]=Null, [equivalent explicit test]=false
[data=0.0], [type(data)]=double, [equivalent explicit test]=false
[data=0], [type(data)]=int, [equivalent explicit test]=false
[data=4.6], [type(data)]=double, [equivalent explicit test]=true
---------------[Explicit conversion of a string to a number]------------------------------
[data=12], [number]=12.0, [type(number)]=double
[data=45.67], [number]=45.67, [type(number)]=double
[data=abcd] : FormatException, this is not a valid number (unlike Number('abcd') in JS, which would return NaN without throwing an error)
---------------[Explicit conversion to a boolean]------------------------------------------
---------------[Explicit conversion to a number]------------------------------------------
[data=12.45], [type(data)]=String, [number]=12.45, [type(number)]=double
[data=true], [type(data)]=bool, [number]=1.0, [type(number)]=double
[data=null], [type(data)]=Null, [number]=null, [type(number)]=Null
---------------[Explicit conversion to a string]------------------------------------------
[data=5], [type(data)]=int, [string]=5, [type(string)]=String
[data=6.7], [type(data)]=double, [string]=6.7, [type(string)]=String
[data=false], [type(data)]=bool, [string]=false, [type(string)]=String
[data=null], [type(data)]=Null, [string]=null, [type(string)]=String
---------------[Other cases]------------------------------
data1=1001.814 (explicit conversion required, unlike '1000.78' + 1.034 in JS which concatenates into a string)
data2=1.0341000.78 (here we knowingly choose concatenation, by converting the number)

docs.title: 3.1.9. [basics_09] script
docs.text:
Unlike the new features in ECMAScript, which will be replaced by chapter [Dart 3.x New Features], this script remains in place: most of these operators have existed natively in Dart for a long time, sometimes well before 2020.

// basics_09.dart
// Ports basics-09.ts (the modern ECMAScript 2020-2021 operators).
// Unlike the "ECMAScript new features", which will be replaced further on
// by the Dart 3.x New features chapter, this script stays HERE: most of
// these operators have existed natively in Dart for a long time (sometimes
// since Dart 2.0/2.12, well before 2020), so they are part of the
// Dart fundamentals just like the rest of this chapter.
void main() {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 1) the null-coalescing operator [??] - has existed in Dart for
  //    a long time (Dart 2.0), and behaves EXACTLY as in TypeScript:
  //    it only triggers the default value if the value is null (Dart
  //    has no [undefined] value separate from [null])
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // typed [int?] (nullable), not [int]: with a non-nullable type,
  // dart analyze would rightly see that [?? 10] can never
  // trigger (the type already guarantees that quantity1 is not null) - whereas
  // the goal here is precisely to compare the behaviour of [??] on
  // a non-null value (quantity1) and on a null value (quantity2)
  const int? quantity1 = 0;
  // in Dart, there is no [||] operator for this use: Dart's logical
  // [||] only accepts [bool] operands, so "quantity1 ||
  // 10" would be a compilation error - there is therefore only one
  // operator to show here, [??], without the risk of bug illustrated by the
  // original TypeScript script (0 is an [int] anyway, never
  // interpreted as "false")
  print("quantity1 ?? 10 = ${quantity1 ?? 10}"); // -> 0 (quantity1 is not null)

  const int? quantity2 = null;
  print("quantity2 ?? 10 = ${quantity2 ?? 10}"); // -> 10 (quantity2 is null)

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) optional chaining [?.] - has also existed in Dart for a long time
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  final person1 = PersonWithOptionalAddress(
    name: "Dupont",
    address: Address(city: "Nantes"),
  );
  final person2 = PersonWithOptionalAddress(name: "Martin"); // no address!

  // [?.] stops evaluation and returns [null] as soon as a step is null,
  // instead of throwing a "NoSuchMethodError" exception on null
  print("person1 city = ${person1.address?.city}");
  print("person2 city = ${person2.address?.city}"); // -> null, no error

  // [?.] and [??] can be combined to provide a fallback value
  print("person2 city (with default) = ${person2.address?.city ?? "unknown city"}");

  // [?.] also works on method calls...
  final objectWithMethod = ObjectWithMethod();
  print("existing method call : ${objectWithMethod.sayHello()}");
  // ...and on access to a list element (via the [?[ ]] operator)
  final List<int>? listOrNull = null;
  print("element of a missing list : ${listOrNull?[0]}"); // -> null

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) the logical assignment operators [??=]
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [a ??= b] is equivalent to [a = a ?? b]: assigns b only if a is null -
  // this one exists in Dart, with exactly the same syntax as in
  // TypeScript
  final config = Configuration(delay: 0, page: null);
  config.delay ??= 1000; // delay is already 0 (valid value) -> stays unchanged
  config.page ??= 1; // page is null -> becomes 1
  print("config after ??= : delay=${config.delay}, page=${config.page}");

  // [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript] Dart DOES NOT HAVE
  // the [||=] and [&&=] operators: Dart's [||] and [&&] only accept
  // [bool] values (as seen in point 1), and there is no assignment
  // shortcut for this case - the test must be written explicitly
  String displayedMessage = "";
  // explicit equivalent of [displayedMessage ||= "default message"]:
  // in Dart, you must write yourself the meaningful "false" test (here:
  // empty string) rather than relying on a generic notion of "false"
  if (displayedMessage.isEmpty) {
    displayedMessage = "default message";
  }
  print("displayedMessage after the if equivalent to ||= : $displayedMessage");

  // explicit equivalent of [a &&= b] (assigns b only if a is already
  // "true"): again, a simple if, [a] having to be a real boolean
  bool loggedInUser = true;
  if (loggedInUser) {
    loggedInUser = true; // the "b" of a &&= b
  }
  print("loggedInUser after the if equivalent to &&= : $loggedInUser");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 4) numeric separators [_] in literals
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] Dart does NOT accept the [_]
  // character as a visual separator in a numeric literal: "1_000_000"
  // is a syntax error in Dart. The number must be written "in full",
  // possibly formatting it for display with the [intl] package
  // (NumberFormat) if readability on display is the goal.
  const int oneMillion = 1000000;
  print("oneMillion = $oneMillion");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 5) BigInt
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] JavaScript's
  // [number] type is a double-precision float, which loses its
  // precision beyond about 2^53 - hence the need for a separate [BigInt]
  // type for very large exact integers (bank card numbers,
  // identifiers...). Dart's [int] type, on the other hand, is a REAL signed
  // 64-bit integer on all native platforms (VM, AOT): it remains
  // exact up to 2^63-1, well beyond JavaScript's [Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER]
  // (2^53-1) - most uses that would require a
  // BigInt in JavaScript therefore simply do not need one in Dart.
  print("the Dart equivalent of Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER does not exist: "
      "int is exact up to 9223372036854775807 (2^63-1)");
  const int bigNumber = 9007199254740993; // > 2^53, imprecise in JS, exact here
  print("bigNumber = $bigNumber (exact, whereas it would lose its "
      "precision stored in a JavaScript Number)");
  // for a truly unlimited need (beyond 64 bits, e.g. cryptographic
  // calculation), Dart does NOT offer a BigInt type in its
  // standard library (dart:core): you must then turn to a
  // third-party package such as package:fixnum, or implement your own calculation -
  // a much rarer need than in JavaScript, given the above.
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// utility classes for the optional chaining demonstration
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
class Address {
  final String city;
  Address({required this.city});
}

class PersonWithOptionalAddress {
  final String name;
  final Address? address; // address is optional (nullable)
  PersonWithOptionalAddress({required this.name, this.address});
}

class ObjectWithMethod {
  String sayHello() => "hello!";
}

class Configuration {
  int? delay;
  int? page;
  Configuration({this.delay, this.page});
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • [??] and [?.] (null coalescing, optional chaining) have been part of Dart for a long time and behave exactly as they do in TypeScript.
  • Line 63: [config.delay ??= 1000;]: The logical assignment [??=] exists in Dart, with the same syntax as in TypeScript.
  • Dart has no equivalent for the operators [||=] and [&&=]: its [||]/[&&] only accepts [bool], so there is no generic concept of “false” to bypass—a simple explicit [if] replaces them.
  • [1_000_000] is a SYNTAX ERROR in Dart: unlike TypeScript, no visual separators are allowed in a numeric literal.
  • [int] is a valid 64-bit integer EXACT SIGNED on any native Dart platform, up to 2^63-1 —well beyond [Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER] (2^53-1): most use cases that would require a JavaScript [BigInt] simply do not need them in Dart, which, incidentally, does not offer [BigInt] in its standard library.

The result of the execution is as follows:

quantity1 ?? 10 = 0
quantity2 ?? 10 = 10
person1 city = Nantes
person2 city = null
person2 city (with default) = unknown city
existing method call : hello!
element of a missing list : null
config after ??= : delay=0, page=1
displayedMessage after the if equivalent to ||= : default message
loggedInUser after the if equivalent to &&= : true
oneMillion = 1000000
the Dart equivalent of Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER does not exist: int is exact up to 9223372036854775807 (2^63-1)
bigNumber = 9007199254740993 (exact, whereas it would lose its precision stored in a JavaScript Number)

docs.title: 3.1.10. Conclusion
docs.text: This first section laid the groundwork: strict typing without implicit coercion, the distinction between [final] and [const], systematic block scope, and the absence of destructuring assignment (compensated for by Dart 3 patterns). These differences will come up throughout the course.

docs.title: 3.2. Arrays
docs.text: In Dart, an “array” is called a [list] ([List]). This section covers classic list operations: reference vs. value, iteration, methods on the ends, functional methods, and the recent “immutable” methods of JavaScript.

docs.title: 3.2.1. script [arr_01]
docs.text:
// arr_01.dart
// Ports arr-01.ts: a list is an object handled through its reference,
// exactly like a JavaScript/TypeScript array.
void main() {
  final List<int> arr1 = [1, 2, 3];
  // REFERENCE copy, not content copy
  final List<int> arr2 = arr1;
  // arr1 and arr2 point to the same list - [identical] is the Dart
  // equivalent of [===] applied to object IDENTITY (instead of [==], which for
  // Lists compares the content; see the remark below)
  print("identical(arr1, arr2) : ${identical(arr1, arr2)}");
  // the list can be modified through either arr1 or arr2
  arr2[1] = 10;
  print("arr1=$arr1");
  print("arr2=$arr2");

  // [Dart-specific remark] unlike JavaScript where [arr1 === arr2]
  // and [arr1 == arr2] are equivalent for arrays (reference comparison
  // in both cases), Dart's [==] operator on a List
  // object also compares the REFERENCE by default (not the content): []
  // == [] is therefore false in Dart, as the following line shows
  print("[1, 2] == [1, 2] (two different lists) : ${[1, 2] == [1, 2]}");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 7: [final List<int> arr2 = arr1;] copies the REFERENCE, not its contents: [arr1] and [arr2] refer to the same list, exactly as in JavaScript.
  • Line 11: [identical(arr1, arr2)] is the Dart equivalent of [===] applied to objects (IDENTITY test).
  • Line 22: [[1, 2] == [1, 2]] is FALSE in Dart: unlike JavaScript, where [===] and [] are equivalent on arrays (reference comparison in both cases), the Dart operator [] applied to a [List] ALSO compares, by default, the reference, not the content.

The result of the execution is as follows:

identical(arr1, arr2) : true
arr1=[1, 10, 3]
arr2=[1, 10, 3]
[1, 2] == [1, 2] (two different lists) : false

docs.title: 3.2.2. script [arr_02]
docs.text:
An important difference to note before this script: see the comment at the top of the file regarding the absence of sparse lists in Dart.

// arr_02.dart
// Ports arr-02.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] a JavaScript
// array is "sparse": you can write arr[3] = 100 on an
// empty array, which automatically extends its length to 4, leaving
// "holes" (indexes without a value, different from undefined). A Dart
// List is NOT sparse: its valid indexes always go from 0 to length-1
// without holes, and writing arr[3] on a list of length 0 throws a
// [RangeError] (index out of bounds) - the list never grows by
// itself through indexed assignment. To grow, use [add] (at the end)
// or one of the methods of the next section (arr_03.dart, arr_04.dart).
void main() {
  // [dynamic] because this list will contain values of different types
  final List<dynamic> arr = [];
  print("arr=$arr, length=[${arr.length}]");
  print("-------------------------------");

  // no direct equivalent of arr[3] = 100 on an empty list: we build
  // the same visual result ("holes") by explicitly filling with
  // null up to the desired index, which makes the holes VISIBLE (nulls),
  // where JavaScript leaves them invisible (neither value, nor explicit
  // undefined)
  while (arr.length <= 3) {
    arr.add(null);
  }
  arr[3] = 100;
  arr[1] = "eight";
  print("arr=$arr, length=[${arr.length}]");
  print("-------------------------------");

  // toString
  print("arr.toString=[${arr.toString()}]");
  print("-------------------------------");

  // the keys of a Dart list are always 0..length-1: no separate [keys()]
  // method, the indexes are used directly with a [for]
  for (var key = 0; key < arr.length; key++) {
    print("key=[$key], value=[${arr[key]}]");
  }
  print("-------------------------------");

  // the values of the list - [arr] IS already the iterable of its values,
  // unlike JavaScript where arr.values() returns a separate iterator
  for (var value in arr) {
    print("value=[$value]");
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • A Dart list is NEVER sparse: its valid indices always range from 0 to [length-1] without any gaps.
  • Line 10: Writing [arr[3]] to an empty list raises a [RangeError]—unlike JavaScript, where writing [arr[3] = 100] to an empty array automatically extends it by creating invisible “gaps.”
  • The script explicitly fills in values from [null] up to the desired index to recreate, VISIBLY, the same visual effect as the holes in JavaScript.
  • Line 45: [for (var value in arr)]: a Dart [List] that is already an iterable over its values—no need for a separate method like in JavaScript.

The result of the execution is as follows:

arr=[], length=[0]
-------------------------------
arr=[null, eight, null, 100], length=[4]
-------------------------------
arr.toString=[[null, eight, null, 100]]
-------------------------------
key=[0], value=[null]
key=[1], value=[eight]
key=[2], value=[null]
key=[3], value=[100]
-------------------------------
value=[null]
value=[eight]
value=[null]
value=[100]

docs.title: 3.2.3. script [arr_03]
docs.text:
// arr_03.dart
// Ports arr-03.ts: iterating over a list, and its manipulation methods
// at both ends (pop/push/shift/unshift) as well as splice.
void main() {
  // a list can contain different types of data
  final List<dynamic> arr = [
    1,
    2,
    "one",
    "two",
    true,
    [10, 20],
    {'prop1': 10, 'prop2': "abc"},
  ];
  // print can display the content of a list
  show(1);
  print("arr=$arr");
  show(2);
  // iterating over the list with forEach
  arr.forEach((element) {
    print("element=$element ${element.runtimeType}");
  });
  show("2b");
  // iterating with for-in, more idiomatic in Dart than forEach for a
  // simple iteration (forEach does not accept break/continue, for-in does)
  for (final element in arr) {
    print("element=$element ${element.runtimeType}");
  }
  show(3);
  // iterating over the list with a classic indexed for
  for (var i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    print("i=$i arr[i]=${arr[i]}");
  }
  show(4);
  // modification arr[i]
  arr[5] = [];
  print("arr=$arr");
  show(5);
  // we remove the last element of the list - removeLast() is
  // the Dart equivalent of pop()
  var element = arr.removeLast();
  print("element=$element arr=$arr");
  show(6);
  // we add an element at the end of the list - add() is the equivalent of
  // push() (for a single element)
  arr.add('xyz');
  print("arr=$arr");
  show(7);
  // we add an element at the beginning of the list - insert(0, ...) is
  // the equivalent of unshift()
  arr.insert(0, 1000);
  print("arr=$arr");
  show(8);
  // we remove the 1st element - removeAt(0) is the equivalent of shift()
  element = arr.removeAt(0);
  print("element=$element arr=$arr");
  show(9);
  // we remove element no. 2 from the list - there is no [splice]
  // method in Dart; we first retrieve the relevant subset with
  // [sublist], then remove it with [removeRange]
  var elements = arr.sublist(2, 3);
  arr.removeRange(2, 3);
  print("element(s)=$elements arr=$arr");
  show(10);
  // we remove two elements from the list starting at element no. 1
  elements = arr.sublist(1, 3);
  arr.removeRange(1, 3);
  print("element(s)=$elements arr=$arr");
}

// function
void show(Object param) {
  print("[$param :::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::"
      ":::::::::::::: ]");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Line 20: [arr.forEach(...)] exists, but [for (final element in arr)] (line 26) is preferred in Dart for a simple loop: unlike [forEach], a [for-in] accepts both [break] and [continue].
  • Line 41: [arr.removeLast()] replaces [pop()]; [arr.add(...)] (line 46) replaces [push()] (for a single element); [arr.insert(0, ...)] (line 51) replaces [unshift()], and [arr.removeAt(0)] (line 55) replaces [shift()].
  • Dart does not have a method named [splice]: first, retrieve the relevant subset using [sublist], then remove it using [removeRange]—two steps instead of a single call.

// arr_04.dart
// Ports arr-04.ts: the functional list manipulation methods -
// map, reduce, filter (where), find (firstWhere), findIndex (indexWhere),
// indexOf, lastIndexOf, sort.
void main() {
  // a list
  final List<int> arr = List.generate(10, (i) => i * 10);
  print("arr=$arr");

  // map - returns a (lazy) Iterable; .toList() materializes it as a list,
  // as JavaScript's .map() always does
  final arr2 = arr.map((element) => {'prop1': element, 'prop2': element * element}).toList();
  print("arr=$arr");
  print("arr2=$arr2");

  // reduce WITHOUT initial value - same signature as in JavaScript
  final sum = arr.reduce((accumulator, currentValue) => accumulator + currentValue);
  print("sum arr=$sum");

  // [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] Dart has no reduce() WITH an
  // initial value: that is the role of a separate method, [fold], whose
  // 1st parameter is precisely the initial value
  final sum2 = arr.fold(10, (accumulator, currentValue) => accumulator + currentValue);
  print("sum2 arr=$sum2");

  // filter -> where (returns an Iterable; .toList() to get a list)
  final arr4 = arr.where((element) => element > 50).toList();
  print("arr4=$arr4");

  // find -> firstWhere
  final element1 = arr.firstWhere((element) => element > 20);
  print("element1=$element1");

  // findIndex -> indexWhere
  final index1 = arr.indexWhere((element) => element == 20);
  print("index1 20=$index1");

  // indexOf - identical to JavaScript
  final index2 = arr.indexOf(30);
  print("index2 30=$index2");
  final index3 = arr.indexOf(31);
  print("index3 31=$index3");

  // lastIndexOf - identical to JavaScript
  final index4 = [4, 5, 4, 2].lastIndexOf(4);
  print("index4 4=$index4");

  // sort - [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] unlike JavaScript's
  // sort(), which returns the sorted array (in addition to modifying it in
  // place), Dart's sort() returns NOTHING (void): it only
  // modifies the list in place. So you must sort THEN read the list again.
  final arr5 = [4, 5, 4, 2];
  arr5.sort();
  print("arr5=$arr5");

  // reverse sort, with a comparator - same principle as in JavaScript: the
  // comparator returns a negative, zero, or positive number
  final arr6 = [4, 5, 4, 2];
  arr6.sort((e1, e2) {
    if (e1 > e2) {
      return -1;
    } else if (e1 == e2) {
      return 0;
    } else {
      return 1;
    }
  });
  print("arr6=$arr6");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Line 12: [arr.map(...)] returns a LAZY [Iterable] (evaluated on demand)—[.toList()] materializes it as a list.
  • line 17: [arr.reduce(...)] (with no initial value) has the same signature as JavaScript.
  • [WARNING] Dart's [reduce] does NOT accept an initial value: this is the role of a separate method, [fold], whose first parameter is precisely this initial value.
  • [filter] -> [where], [find] -> [firstWhere], [findIndex] -> [indexWhere] - [where] returns, like [map], a lazy [Iterable].
  • Line 53: [WARNING] [arr5.sort()] returns NOTHING ([void]): unlike [sort()] from JavaScript, which returns the sorted array IN ADDITION to modifying it in place, Dart’s [sort()] simply modifies the list in place—you must sort, THEN re-read the list.
