docs.title: 3.2.5. script [arr_05]
docs.text:
The original TypeScript script contained array methods added between 2022 and 2023 ([at], [findLast], [toSorted]...). Dart did not follow the same schedule: this script shows the current Dart equivalent for each one.

// arr_05.dart
// Ports arr-05.ts.
// The original TypeScript script presented array methods
// ADDED to JavaScript between 2022 and 2023 (at, findLast, toSorted...).
// Dart did not follow exactly the same schedule of new features: some
// of these needs have long been covered (differently), others not
// at all. This script therefore shows, for each, the current Dart equivalent.
void main() {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 1) access to the last element: no [at(index)] method with a negative
  //    index in Dart, but dedicated shortcuts already exist
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  final List<int> arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];
  print("arr[arr.length - 1] = ${arr[arr.length - 1]}"); // works as in JS
  print("arr.last = ${arr.last}"); // -> last element, more readable (equivalent of at(-1))
  print("arr[arr.length - 2] = ${arr[arr.length - 2]}"); // no shortcut for the second-to-last
  print("arr.first = ${arr.first}"); // -> equivalent to arr[0] / arr.at(0)
  // no equivalent of "hello".at(-1) on String: we use
  // classic indexing
  const string = "hello";
  print("string[string.length - 1] = ${string[string.length - 1]}");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) findLast() and findLastIndex()
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // findLast() -> lastWhere(), which has always existed in Dart (not a
  // recent addition as in JavaScript)
  final List<int> numbers = [5, 12, 8, 21, 3, 17];
  final lastEven = numbers.lastWhere((n) => n % 2 == 0);
  print("last even number = $lastEven"); // -> 8

  // [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] Dart has no ready-made
  // findLastIndex(); we rebuild it with an explicit backwards loop
  var lastEvenIndex = -1;
  for (var i = numbers.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    if (numbers[i] % 2 == 0) {
      lastEvenIndex = i;
      break;
    }
  }
  print("index of the last even number = $lastEvenIndex");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) the "immutable" methods (toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with)
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // sort() and removeRange()/insert() (see arr_03.dart, arr_04.dart) modify
  // the list in place, exactly as in JavaScript.
  // [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] Dart does NOT offer dedicated
  // "to..." methods: the same result is obtained by copying the list
  // FIRST (with [List.of] or [[...original]]), then applying
  // the mutating operation to the COPY - the principle remains simple, just a
  // bit more explicit than in JavaScript.
  final List<Object> original = [4, 5, 4, 2];

  // toSorted -> copy, then sort the copy
  final sorted = List.of(original)..sort();
  print("original = $original (unchanged)");
  print("sorted = $sorted");

  // toReversed -> .reversed is already NON-MUTATING in Dart (it returns a
  // new lazy Iterable, unlike reverse(), which does not even exist
  // on List in Dart): .toList() materializes it
  final reversed = original.reversed.toList();
  print("reversed = $reversed, original still = $original");

  // toSpliced -> copy, then apply removeRange + insertAll to the copy
  final modified = List.of(original);
  modified.removeRange(1, 3);
  modified.insertAll(1, ["a", "b", "c"]);
  print("modified = $modified, original still = $original");

  // with(index, value) -> copy, then assign the index on the copy
  final replaced = List.of(original);
  replaced[0] = 999;
  print("replaced = $replaced, original still = $original");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // why it is useful: the same argument as in JavaScript applies in
  // Dart, notably with Flutter, where a [State] must never be modified
  // in place but replaced by a new state to trigger a new
  // display.
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 10: There is no [at(index)] method with a negative index in Dart, but dedicated shortcuts already exist: [arr.last] (equivalent to [at(-1)]) and [arr.first] (equivalent to [at(0)]).
  • [findLast] -> [lastWhere], which has always existed in Dart (not a recent addition like JavaScript). There is no ready-made equivalent for [findLastIndex]: an explicit reverse traversal reconstructs it.
  • [WARNING] Dart does not provide dedicated “immutable” methods ([toSorted], [toSpliced], [with]): you get the same result by copying the list ([List.of(original)]), then applying the MUTATING operation to the copy.
  • Line 63: [original.reversed] is an exception: it is already NON-MUTATING in Dart (it returns a new lazy [Iterable]), whereas Dart doesn’t even offer a mutant [reverse()] for [List].

The result of the execution is as follows:

arr.last = 50
arr[arr.length - 2] = 40
arr.first = 10
string[string.length - 1] = o
last even number = 8
index of the last even number = 2
original = [4, 5, 4, 2] (unchanged)
sorted = [2, 4, 4, 5]
reversed = [2, 4, 5, 4], original still = [4, 5, 4, 2]
modified = [4, a, b, c, 2], original still = [4, 5, 4, 2]
replaced = [999, 5, 4, 2], original still = [4, 5, 4, 2]

docs.title: 3.2.6. Conclusion
docs.text: Dart lists are manipulated using method names that often differ from their JavaScript equivalents ([removeLast] for [pop], [where] for [filter]...), but the same principles apply: shared references, multiple traversals, and the distinction between mutating and non-mutating operations.

docs.title: 3.3. The objects
docs.text: Dart has no direct equivalent to the literal object JavaScript, whose properties can be freely created at any time. Depending on whether the object’s SHAPE is known in advance or not, this section uses either a [Map<String, dynamic>] (free form) or a true Dart class (fixed form)—a conscious choice that does not exist in TypeScript.

docs.title: 3.3.1. [obj_01] script
docs.text:
See the comment at the top of the file: the fundamental difference between a [Map] and a class is the reason for this entire script.

// obj_01.dart
// Ports obj-01.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] a JavaScript
// object literal can receive NEW properties at any time
// (obj1.prop1 = "abcd"), which the TypeScript interface only announces
// in advance. A Dart class, on the other hand, has a set of fields FIXED at
// compile time: impossible to add a field to an instance afterwards.
// For an object whose properties are built dynamically (as
// here), the natural Dart equivalent is therefore a [Map<String, dynamic>], not
// a class.
void main() {
  // an empty Map, with dynamic properties ("keys")
  final Map<String, dynamic> obj1 = {};
  // the properties of the object can be created dynamically
  obj1['prop1'] = "abcd";
  print('obj1=$obj1');
  // another property
  obj1['prop2'] = [1, 2, 3];
  print("obj1=$obj1");
  // in Dart, there is only ONE notation to access a property
  // of a Map (the one with square brackets): no separate "dot"
  // notation (obj1.prop3) as in JavaScript, since precisely a Map
  // is not an object with fixed fields
  obj1['prop3'] = true;
  print("obj1=$obj1");

  // obj1 is a reference to the Map (like a pointer), not the Map
  // itself
  final Map<String, dynamic> obj2 = obj1;
  // obj2 and obj1 point to the same Map
  obj2['prop1'] = "xyzt";
  print("obj1=$obj1");
  print("obj2=$obj2");

  // keys can be variables
  const String var1 = 'prop1';
  print('prop1=${obj1[var1]}');
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 14: [Map<String, dynamic> obj1 = {};]: for an object whose properties are constructed dynamically, the natural Dart equivalent is a [Map], not a class—a Dart class has a set of fields FIXED at compile time.
  • line 16: [obj1['prop1'] = "abcd";]: there is only one notation for accessing a property of a [Map] (brackets) — no separate dot notation ([obj1.prop1]) as in JavaScript.
  • Line 30: [obj2 = obj1;] copies the REFERENCE: [obj1] and [obj2] refer to the same [Map], following exactly the same principle as for lists (see arr_01.dart).

The result of the execution is as follows:

obj1={prop1: abcd}
obj1={prop1: abcd, prop2: [1, 2, 3]}
obj1={prop1: abcd, prop2: [1, 2, 3], prop3: true}
obj1={prop1: xyzt, prop2: [1, 2, 3], prop3: true}
obj2={prop1: xyzt, prop2: [1, 2, 3], prop3: true}
prop1=xyzt

docs.title: 3.3.2. script [obj_02]
docs.text:
// obj_02.dart
// Ports obj-02.ts: a multi-level object.
//
// [difference with obj_01.dart] here, unlike obj-01, the SHAPE of
// the object is known and fixed in advance (first name, age, father, mother always
// present): this is exactly the case where Dart prefers a real class to
// a Map - safer (the compiler checks each field) and more readable
// (person.father.firstName rather than person['father']['firstName']).
import 'dart:convert';

class SubPerson {
  final String firstName;
  // not final: the script modifies the mother's age further down
  // (person.mother.age = 40), which requires a mutable field.
  int age;
  SubPerson({required this.firstName, required this.age});

  factory SubPerson.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) =>
      SubPerson(firstName: json['firstName'] as String, age: json['age'] as int);
  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() => {'firstName': firstName, 'age': age};
}

class PersonWithFamily {
  final String firstName;
  int age;
  final SubPerson father;
  SubPerson mother;
  PersonWithFamily({
    required this.firstName,
    required this.age,
    required this.father,
    required this.mother,
  });

  factory PersonWithFamily.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => PersonWithFamily(
        firstName: json['firstName'] as String,
        age: json['age'] as int,
        father: SubPerson.fromJson(json['father'] as Map<String, dynamic>),
        mother: SubPerson.fromJson(json['mother'] as Map<String, dynamic>),
      );
  Map<String, dynamic> toJson() =>
      {'firstName': firstName, 'age': age, 'father': father.toJson(), 'mother': mother.toJson()};

  @override
  String toString() => toJson().toString();
}

void main() {
  final person = PersonWithFamily(
    firstName: "martin",
    age: 12,
    father: SubPerson(firstName: "paul", age: 45),
    mother: SubPerson(firstName: "micheline", age: 42),
  );
  // accessing the properties
  print("person first name=${person.firstName}");
  print("mother first name=${person.mother.firstName}");
  person.mother.age = 40;
  print("mother age=${person.mother.age}");
  // print can display an object IF toString() has been defined (see above)
  // - unlike JavaScript's console.log, which inspects the structure
  // of an object even without a custom toString()
  print("person=$person");
  print("mother=${person.mother.toJson()}");

  // we can also display the jSON string of the object - jsonEncode/jsonDecode
  // (from the standard package dart:convert) are the Dart equivalents of
  // JSON.stringify/JSON.parse; they require the object to provide a
  // toJson() (see above), unlike JSON.stringify, which can
  // serialize any JavaScript object without configuration
  final String json = jsonEncode(person);
  print("jSON=$json");
  // the jSON can be read back - jsonDecode returns a generic
  // Map<String, dynamic> (not directly a PersonWithFamily): you must go
  // explicitly through fromJson again, unlike JSON.parse, which returns
  // a JavaScript object directly usable as is
  final PersonWithFamily person2 = PersonWithFamily.fromJson(jsonDecode(json));
  print("father=${person2.father.toJson()}");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Since the object’s SHAPE is known and fixed in advance, this script prefers a real class to a [Map]—it’s safer (each field is checked at compile time) and more readable ([person.father.firstName] rather than [person['father']['firstName']]).
  • Line 71: [jsonEncode(person)]/[jsonDecode(json)] (line 77) (dart:convert) are equivalent to [JSON.stringify]/[JSON.parse], but require the class to provide a [toJson()] —unlike [JSON.stringify], which serializes any JavaScript object without configuration.
  • [jsonDecode] returns a generic [Map<String, dynamic>], never directly a [PersonWithFamily]: you must explicitly go through [fromJson], unlike [JSON.parse], which directly returns a JavaScript object that can be used as-is.
  • Line 63: [print("person=$person")] displays something useful ONLY because [toString()] has been redefined —unlike [console.log], which inspects an object’s structure even without a custom [toString()].

mother first name=micheline
mother age=40

mother={firstName: micheline, age: 40}
jSON={"firstName":"martin","age":12,"father":{"firstName":"paul","age":45},"mother":{"firstName":"micheline","age":40}}
father={firstName: paul, age: 45}

docs.title: 3.3.3. script [obj_03]
docs.text:
// obj_03.dart
// Ports obj-03.ts: getters and setters.
// Here, a Dart getter/setter is defined exactly as in a TypeScript
// class ([get]/[set] keywords) - the only difference is that in Dart
// they necessarily live in a class (never in a Map).
class PersonWithName {
  String? _name;

  // getter
  String get name {
    print("name getter");
    return _name!;
  }

  // setter
  set name(String aName) {
    print("name setter");
    _name = aName;
  }
}

void main() {
  final person = PersonWithName();
  // setter
  person.name = "Hercule";
  // getter
  print(person.name);
  // [difference with TypeScript] the field [_name] is REALLY private here
  // (the [_] prefix is a real rule of the Dart language, applied at
  // the FILE/library level), whereas the [_name] of obj-03.ts
  // is only a naming convention: nothing prevented, in TypeScript,
  // writing person._name = "xyz" from outside the object. In Dart,
  // inside this same file, direct access remains possible (we
  // are in the same library):
  person._name = "xyz";
  print("person._name=${person._name}");
  // ... but from ANOTHER file that would import this class,
  // person._name would be inaccessible: only the get/set name pair
  // would remain usable. This point is taken up and developed
  // in classes/class_05.dart (truly private fields).
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • A Dart getter/setter is written using the same keywords: [get]/[set] as in TypeScript—the only difference is that they must be defined within a class, never in a [Map].
  • Line 7: [String? _name;]: the [_name] field is private here—the [_] prefix is a valid Dart rule (at the file/library level), whereas [_name] from TypeScript is merely a naming convention with no actual effect.
  • Line 35: [person._name = "xyz";] remains possible HERE within the same file (same library)—but would be inaccessible from ANOTHER file that imports this class (explored in detail in classes/class_05.dart).

The result of the execution is as follows:

name setter
name getter
Hercule
person._name=xyz

// obj_04.dart
// Ports obj-04.ts: property name notation and shorthand notation.
class FullName {
  final String lastName;
  final String firstName;
  const FullName({required this.lastName, required this.firstName});
}

void main() {
  // [difference with TypeScript] a Dart class has only ONE notation
  // for its fields (never surrounded by single or double quotes like
  // the properties of a JavaScript object literal): this point of the
  // original script therefore only applies to [Map]s, shown below.
  const obj1 = FullName(lastName: "martin", firstName: "jean");
  print("firstName=${obj1.firstName}");

  // on a Map, however, the key is always a character string,
  // surrounded by single or double quotes - there is no "literal"
  // notation like {lastName: "martin"} without quotes on a Dart Map
  final Map<String, String> obj2 = {'lastName': "martin", 'firstName': "jean"};
  print("lastName=${obj2['lastName']}");

  final Map<String, String> obj3 = {"lastName": "martin", "firstName": "jean"};
  // only one possible notation to access a Map key (square
  // brackets) - no separate "dot" notation (obj3.lastName)
  print("lastName=${obj3["lastName"]}");

  // [difference with TypeScript] Dart has no shorthand notation
  // equivalent to {obj1, obj2} to build a Map from variables
  // with the same name as the desired keys: the key must always be written
  // explicitly
  final obj4 = {'obj1': obj1, 'obj2': obj2};
  // obj1 will be displayed as "Instance of 'FullName'": without a custom
  // toString() (see obj_02.dart), Dart only displays the name of the
  // class, where JavaScript's console.log would have inspected every detail
  print("obj4=$obj4");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • A Dart class has only one notation for its fields—never enclosed in quotes—so this point in the original script boils down to ONE notation.
  • In a [Map], the key is always a string enclosed in quotes: there is no literal notation without quotes, such as [{lastName: "martin"}] in JavaScript.
  • Dart does not have a shorthand notation equivalent to [{obj1, obj2}] for constructing a [Map] from variables with the same names as the desired keys: you must always write the key explicitly.

The result of the execution is as follows:

lastName=martin
lastName=martin
obj4={obj1: Instance of 'FullName', obj2: {lastName: martin, firstName: jean}}

// obj_05.dart
// Ports obj-05.ts: an object can carry a method (toString).
import 'dart:convert';

class PersonWithToString {
  final String firstName;
  final int age;
  final Map<String, dynamic> father;
  final Map<String, dynamic> mother;

  PersonWithToString({
    required this.firstName,
    required this.age,
    required this.father,
    required this.mother,
  });

  // method - in Dart, overriding toString() is done with the
  // [override] keyword, which explicitly documents that we override a method
  // inherited from the [Object] class (the common ancestor of all Dart
  // classes) - there is no equivalent of this annotation in TypeScript
  @override
  String toString() => jsonEncode({
        'firstName': firstName,
        'age': age,
        'father': father,
        'mother': mother,
      });
}

void main() {
  final person = PersonWithToString(
    firstName: "martin",
    age: 12,
    father: {'firstName': "paul", 'age': 45},
    mother: {'firstName': "micheline", 'age': 42},
  );

  // usage - print() automatically calls toString(), as would
  // a string interpolation "$person"
  print("person=$person");
  print("person.toString=${person.toString()}");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • [@override String toString() => ...]: Redefining [toString()] is done using the keyword [@override], which explicitly documents that a method inherited from [Object] (the common ancestor of all Dart classes) is being redefined - There is no equivalent of this annotation in TypeScript.
  • Line 41: [print("person=$person")] automatically calls [toString()], just as any string interpolation in ["$person"] would.

The result of the execution is as follows:

This script only makes sense in Dart for a [Map]: a Dart class has fixed fields, known at compile time, and therefore never needs to be traversed dynamically.

// obj_06.dart
// Ports obj-06.ts: dynamic iteration over the properties of an object.
//
// [difference with TypeScript] this script only makes sense, in Dart, for a
// [Map]: a Dart class has fixed fields, known at compile time, and
// therefore never needs to be "iterated over" dynamically like a JavaScript
// object. We go back here to a Map<String, dynamic>, as in obj_01.
void main() {
  final Map<String, dynamic> person = {
    'firstName': "martin",
    'age': 12,
    'father': {'firstName': "paul", 'age': 45},
    'mother': {'firstName': "micheline", 'age': 42},
  };

  print(person);
  print("-----------------------");

  // [difference with TypeScript] a Dart Map has no "prototype
  // chain" like a JavaScript object: ALL its keys are its
  // own, so there is no equivalent of the risk of
  // iterating over an INHERITED property (which hasOwnProperty avoids in
  // JavaScript). A simple for-in on .entries is enough, without any
  // additional test:
  for (final entry in person.entries) {
    print("${entry.key} = ${entry.value}");
  }

  // another equivalent syntax, with forEach
  print("-----------------------");
  person.forEach((key, value) {
    print("$key = $value");
  });

  // or again, if we only want the keys (equivalent of Object.keys)
  print("-----------------------");
  for (final key in person.keys) {
    print("$key = ${person[key]}");
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 25: [for (final entry in person.entries)]: A Dart [Map] does not have a “prototype chain” like a JavaScript object—all its keys belong to it directly, so there is no equivalent to the risk of iterating over a INHERITED property (which [hasOwnProperty] avoids in JavaScript).
  • Line 31: [person.forEach((key, value) => ...)] and [person.keys] (line 37) (equivalent to [Object.keys]) offer the same traversals, with no additional testing required.

// obj_07.dart
// Ports obj-07.ts: destructuring.
// [NEW, Dart 3] object destructuring ("object patterns") is a
// RECENT feature in Dart (3.0, 2023) - developed in the chapter
// Dart 3.x New features (dart3/patterns.dart). We use it here, ahead
// of that chapter, since it is the direct equivalent of what this
// TypeScript script does.
class FullName {
  final String lastName;
  final String firstName;
  const FullName({required this.lastName, required this.firstName});
}

void main() {
  const obj1 = FullName(lastName: "martin", firstName: "jean");

  // destructuring obj1 into the variables [n, p]: the syntax
  // [:lastName] means "extract the lastName field, and name it lastName"; it can
  // then be renamed with an [alias] as here
  final FullName(lastName: n, firstName: p) = obj1;
  print("n=$n p=$p");

  // [difference with TypeScript] the PARAMETERS of a Dart function do not
  // directly support writing a pattern (unlike
  // TypeScript, where function f({lastName, firstName}: FullName) destructures
  // directly in the parameter list). Destructuring must be done in
  // the BODY of the function, with a pattern variable declaration:
  void f(FullName obj) {
    final FullName(lastName: n2, firstName: p2) = obj;
    print("f-n2=$n2 f-p2=$p2");
  }

  f(obj1);

  // shorthand notation [:lastName] (equivalent to [lastName: lastName]) - the
  // pattern name directly becomes the name of the created variable, exactly
  // like TypeScript's shorthand notation {lastName, firstName}
  void h(FullName obj) {
    final FullName(:lastName, :firstName) = obj;
    print("h-lastName=$lastName h-firstName=$firstName");
  }

  h(obj1);
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 20: [final FullName(lastName: n, firstName: p) = obj1;]: object pattern extraction is a feature of Dart (3.0, 2023), used here ahead of the chapter on [Dart 3.x New Features] because it directly corresponds to what this TypeScript script does.
  • [WARNING] The PARAMETERS of a Dart function do NOT directly support a pattern—unlike TypeScript ([function f({lastName, firstName})]): you must use destructuring within the function’s BODY.
  • Line 39: [final FullName(:lastName, :firstName) = obj;]: The shorthand notation [:lastName] (equivalent to [lastName: lastName]) makes the field name directly the name of the created variable—the exact equivalent of the shorthand notation [{lastName, firstName}] for TypeScript.

The result of execution is as follows:

n=martin p=jean
f-n2=martin f-p2=jean
h-lastName=martin h-firstName=jean

// obj_08.dart
// Ports obj-08.ts: shallow cloning with the spread operator.
void main() {
  // the spread operator [...] exists in Dart, but ONLY in a
  // collection literal (List, Set or Map) - never to "spread" the
  // fields of an arbitrary class instance (there is, by the way, no
  // notion of "enumerable fields" in Dart, unlike JavaScript).
  // On a Map, however, it behaves exactly as in JavaScript:
  final Map<String, String> obj1 = {'lastName': "martin", 'firstName': "jean"};

  // shallow clone of obj1 with the spread operator
  final Map<String, String> obj2 = {...obj1};

  // checks - identical() is the Dart equivalent of === applied to
  // object identity (see arr_01.dart); obj2 points to a COPY of obj1
  print("identical(obj1, obj2) : ${identical(obj1, obj2)}");
  print("obj2=$obj2");

  // -------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [Dart-specific complement] for a CLASS (rather than a Map), the Dart
  // idiom for clone-with-modifications is a hand-written [copyWith]
  // method (widely used with Flutter, to never modify a state
  // in place - see arr_05.dart):
  // -------------------------------------------------------------------
  final p1 = _FullName(lastName: "martin", firstName: "jean");
  final p2 = p1.copyWith(firstName: "paul"); // copy of p1, first name changed
  print("p1=$p1, p2=$p2");
}

class _FullName {
  final String lastName;
  final String firstName;
  const _FullName({required this.lastName, required this.firstName});

  _FullName copyWith({String? lastName, String? firstName}) =>
      _FullName(lastName: lastName ?? this.lastName, firstName: firstName ?? this.firstName);

  @override
  String toString() => '{lastName: $lastName, firstName: $firstName}';
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • The spread operator [...] exists in Dart, but ONLY in a collection literal ([List], [Set], or [Map])—never to spread the fields of any class instance (Dart has no concept of “enumerable fields”).
  • Line 12: [{...obj1}] superficially clones a [Map], exactly as in JavaScript; [identical(obj1, obj2)] (line 16) confirms that [obj2] points to a COPY.
  • For a CLASS, the Dart idiom for “clone-with-modification” is a hand-written [copyWith] method (widely used with Flutter)—there is no generic equivalent of the spread operator for classes.

The result of the execution is as follows:

identical(obj1, obj2) : false
obj2={lastName: martin, firstName: jean}
p1={lastName: martin, firstName: jean}, p2={lastName: martin, firstName: paul}

// obj_09.dart
// Ports obj-09.ts.
import 'dart:convert';

void main() {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 1) Object.hasOwn(object, property)
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [difference with TypeScript] as explained in obj_06.dart, a Dart Map
  // has no prototype chain: any key present in the Map
  // necessarily belongs to it as its "own". [containsKey] has therefore always
  // been the only test needed - there was no need to add a
  // late [Map.hasOwn] like JavaScript's [Object.hasOwn] of 2022.
  final Map<String, dynamic> person = {'lastName': "Dupont", 'firstName': "Jean"};

  print("person.containsKey('lastName') = ${person.containsKey('lastName')}");
  print("person.containsKey('age') = ${person.containsKey('age')}");

  // typical use in an iteration over properties
  print("-----------------------");
  for (final key in person.keys) {
    print("$key = ${person[key]}");
  }

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) deep cloning
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // obj_08.dart shows shallow cloning with the
  // spread operator [...obj] - but a spread only clones the 1st level: the
  // sub-Maps remain shared!
  final Map<String, dynamic> original = {
    'lastName': "Dupont",
    'address': {'city': "Nantes", 'postalCode': "44000"},
  };

  // shallow cloning with spread
  final Map<String, dynamic> shallowCopy = {...original};
  (shallowCopy['address'] as Map)['city'] = "Angers"; // also modifies the address of [original]!
  print("shallow copy modified the original : "
      "${(original['address'] as Map)['city'] == "Angers"}");

  // reset for the next test
  (original['address'] as Map)['city'] = "Nantes";

  // [difference with TypeScript] Dart has no native structuredClone()
  // function. For a structure made entirely of "JSON" types
  // (Map, List, String, num, bool, null - exactly the case here), the simplest
  // Dart idiom is a round trip through jsonEncode/jsonDecode:
  // this forces a complete copy, at every level
  final Map<String, dynamic> deepCopy = jsonDecode(jsonEncode(original));
  (deepCopy['address'] as Map)['city'] = "Angers";
  print("deep copy did not modify the original : "
      "${(original['address'] as Map)['city'] == "Nantes"}");
  print("original = $original");
  print("deepCopy = $deepCopy");
  // NB: this detour through jsonEncode/jsonDecode only works for
  // "JSON-serializable" data; to deep-clone an arbitrary
  // class, you must write your own cloning (e.g. a recursive
  // copyWith, see obj_08.dart), as Dart offers no generic equivalent.

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) optional chaining + nullish on nested accesses
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // a very frequent combination in practice to read a partial
  // configuration - identical to TypeScript, these two operators having existed in
  // Dart for a long time (see basics_09.dart)
  displayTheme(null);
  displayTheme({'appearance': {'theme': "dark"}});
  displayTheme({'appearance': <String, dynamic>{}});
  displayTheme(<String, dynamic>{});
}

void displayTheme(Map<String, dynamic>? configuration) {
  // if configuration, configuration['appearance'] or
  // configuration['appearance']['theme'] is missing, we fall back on "light"
  // without ever crashing
  final theme = (configuration?['appearance'] as Map?)?['theme'] ?? "light";
  print("theme = $theme");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 16: [person.containsKey('lastName')]: just like [Map], Dart has no prototype chain (see obj_06.dart), [containsKey] has always been the only necessary test—there’s no need for a later equivalent of the 2022 [Object.hasOwn] in JavaScript.
  • Line 50: [jsonDecode(jsonEncode(original))]: Dart does not have a native [structuredClone()] function. For a structure that is entirely “JSON” ([Map], [List], [String], [num], [bool], [null]), this round-trip forces a complete copy at all levels—unlike the superficial spread of obj_08.dart, which clones only the first level.
  • line 77: [configuration?['appearance'] as Map?)?['theme'] ?? "light"]: The optional chaining [?.]/[?[ ]] combined with [??] works exactly as in TypeScript; these two operators have long existed in Dart (see basics_09.dart).

The result of the execution is as follows:

person.containsKey('lastName') = true
person.containsKey('age') = false
-----------------------
lastName = Dupont
firstName = Jean
shallow copy modified the original : true
deep copy did not modify the original : true
original = {lastName: Dupont, address: {city: Nantes, postalCode: 44000}}
deepCopy = {lastName: Dupont, address: {city: Angers, postalCode: 44000}}
theme = light
theme = dark
theme = light
theme = light

docs.title: 3.3.10. Conclusion
docs.text: The choice between [Map] and a class is the central issue of this section: use [Map<String, dynamic>] for a free-form or unknown structure (such as an ordinary JavaScript object), and a class for a fixed structure verified by the compiler. Dart 3 patterns (obj_07.dart) already demonstrate that this choice does not prevent you from retaining most of the convenience of TypeScript destructuring.

// Ports str-01.ts: strings are read-only.
void main() {

  const String string1 = "abcd ";
  // type - runtimeType is the Dart equivalent of typeof
  print("string1.runtimeType=${string1.runtimeType}");
  // character no. 2 - [] indexing works as in TypeScript
  print("string1[2]=${string1[2]}");

  // only offers [] indexing for READING. Unlike TypeScript, there
  // is not even a []= operator for String: the following line is
  // a COMPILATION error ("The operator '[]=' isn't defined for the
  // class 'String'"), whether or not one first tries to type it
  // dynamically.
  // string1[2] = "0";
}

Let's discuss this code:

  • [string1[2]]: Bracket indexing works the same way as in TypeScript, but only for READING.
  • [WARNING] Dart doesn't even have an operator for [[]=] for [String]: [string1[2] = "0";] is a COMPILATION ERROR ([The operator '[]=' isn't defined for the class 'String']), whereas TypeScript simply results in a type error during write indexing.

docs.title: 3.4.3. script [str_02]
docs.text:
See the comment at the top of the file: this script is shorter than the original because there is no equivalent to the primitive/object distinction in JavaScript.

// str_02.dart
// Ports str-02.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] JavaScript has
// TWO ways of representing a string: the primitive type [string]
// (literal "xyzt"), and the object type [String] (built with [new
// String("xyzt")]), which is a real object, distinct from its value (`new
// String("a") === new String("a")` is actually false!). Dart has
// only ONE [String] type: there is no separate "boxed object" variant
// to compare with the primitive type. This script is therefore shorter than
// the original; the only common point shown is that toString (here Dart only has
// "length") works the same in all cases.
void main() {
  // a string literal
  const String string1 = "abcd ";
  print("string1.runtimeType=${string1.runtimeType}");

  // no equivalent of "new String(...)": an explicitly built string
  // remains the same String type, with the same value
  final String string2 = String.fromCharCodes("xyzt".codeUnits);
  print("string2.runtimeType=${string2.runtimeType}");

  // another syntax (without new) - still the same type
  const String string3 = "12 34";
  print("string3.runtimeType=${string3.runtimeType}");

  // lengths behave identically in all cases,
  // since in Dart this is one and the same type
  print("string1.length=${string1.length}");
  print("string2.length=${string2.length}");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Dart has only ONE string type: no distinction between a primitive type [string] and an object type [String] constructed with [new String(...)], as in JavaScript.
  • Line 20: [String.fromCharCodes(...)] explicitly constructs a string, but remains the same, unique type [String], with the same value—there is no equivalent to the trap [new String("a") === new String("a")] (false in JavaScript).

The result of the execution is as follows:

string1.runtimeType=String
string2.runtimeType=String
string3.runtimeType=String
string1.length=5
string2.length=4

// str_03.dart
// Ports str-03.ts: string interpolation and extraction of a substring.
void main() {
  const String string = "Introduction to Dart by example";
  // Dart has, like TypeScript, native string interpolation (no
  // third-party library needed) - with $variable or ${expression}
  // (unlike TypeScript, which reserves `` for templates and keeps ""
  // or '' for simple strings, $"..." Dart always accepts $/${})
  //
  // [difference with TypeScript] substr(start, length) is an OLD,
  // deprecated JavaScript method (deprecated well before
  // TypeScript uses it here, to stay faithful to the original script).
  // Dart never had it: its equivalent is substring(start, end) - the
  // 2nd parameter is an END position, not a LENGTH.
  final String str =
      "[$string].substring(3, 5)=" + string.substring(3, 5); // 2 characters starting at no. 3
  print(str);
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • String interpolation ([$variable], [${expression}]) is native to Dart, as is TypeScript, but works with ["..."] and ['...'] interchangeably—there is no reserved [...] syntax as in JavaScript.
  • Line 16: [string.substring(3, 5)]: Dart has never had a [substr(start, length)] (deprecated method of JavaScript)—its equivalent is [substring(start, end)], whose second parameter is an END position, not a LENGTH.

// str_05.dart
// Ports str-05.ts: the classic sprintf format specifiers.
import 'dart:convert';
import 'package:sprintf/sprintf.dart';

void main() {
  const String string = "Dart";
  // character strings
  print(sprintf("[%s, %%s]=>[%s]", [string, string]));
  print(sprintf("[%s, %%20s]=>[%20s]", [string, string]));
  print(sprintf("[%s, %%-20s]=>[%-20s]", [string, string]));
  // integers
  print(sprintf("[%d, %%d]=>[%d]", [10, 10]));
  print(sprintf("[%d, %%4d]=>[%4d]", [10, 10]));
  print(sprintf("[%d, %%-4d]=>[%-4d]", [10, 10]));
  print(sprintf("[%d, %%04d]=>[%04d]", [10, 10]));
  // reals
  print(sprintf("[%f, %%f]=>[%f]", [-10.5, -10.5]));
  print(sprintf("[%f, %%10.2f]=>[%10.2f]", [-10.5, -10.5]));
  print(sprintf("[%f, %%-10.2f]=>[%-10.2f]", [-10.5, -10.5]));
  print(sprintf("[%f, %%010.3f]=>[%010.3f]", [-10.5, -10.5]));

  // [difference with TypeScript] the npm package [sprintf-js] adds
  // JavaScript-specific specifiers, absent from the "classic" sprintf:
  // %j (JSON), %T (type), %t (boolean). The Dart package [sprintf] only
  // supports the standard C/POSIX specifiers (%s, %d, %f...) - we
  // get the same result for %j and %T with the equivalent Dart
  // tools (jsonEncode, runtimeType), combined with %s:
  final person = {'name': "mathieu", 'age': 34};
  // json (equivalent of sprintf-js's %j)
  print(sprintf("person (%%j equivalent)=%s", [jsonEncode(person)]));
  // type (equivalent of sprintf-js's %T)
  print(sprintf("person type (%%T equivalent)=%s", [person.runtimeType]));
  // boolean (equivalent of sprintf-js's %t - %s is enough, a Dart bool
  // is already displayed as "true"/"false", exactly the expected format)
  print(sprintf("boolean (%%t equivalent)=%s", [4 == 4]));
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • The standard C/POSIX format specifiers ([%s], [%d], [%f], width, alignment, leading zeros) work exactly like their [sprintf-js] equivalents.
  • [WARNING]: The Dart package [sprintf] does NOT include the extensions specific to [sprintf-js] ([%j], [%T], [%t]): the same result is obtained by combining [%s] with the equivalent Dart tools—[jsonEncode] for [%j], [.runtimeType] for [%T], and a simple Boolean (already shown as [true]/[false]) for [%t].

// str_06.dart
// Ports str-06.ts: the usual string manipulation methods.
import 'package:sprintf/sprintf.dart';

void main() {
  const String string = "  Introduction to Dart ";
  // substring(10, 12): 2 characters starting at no. 10 (substring(start,
  // end), not substr(start, length) - see str_03.dart)
  print(sprintf("[%s].substring(10,12)=[%s]", [string, string.substring(10, 12)]));
  // trim: removal of leading and trailing blanks - identical to
  // TypeScript
  print(sprintf("[%s].trim()=[%s]", [string, string.trim()]));
  // toLowerCase: conversion to lowercase
  print(sprintf("[%s].toLowerCase=[%s]", [string, string.toLowerCase()]));
  // toUpperCase: conversion to uppercase
  print(sprintf("[%s].toUpperCase=[%s]", [string, string.toUpperCase()]));
  // indexOf: position of a searched string in the string, -1 if absent
  print(sprintf("[%s].indexOf('Dart')=[%s]", [string, string.indexOf('Dart')]));
  print(sprintf("[%s].trim().indexOf('abcd')=[%s]", [string, string.indexOf('abcd')]));
  // includes -> contains: true if the searched string is in the string
  print(sprintf("[%s].contains('Dart')=[%s]", [string, string.contains('Dart')]));
  // length: length of the string - a property, as in TypeScript
  print(sprintf("[%s].length=[%s]", [string, string.length]));
  // slice(7,10) -> substring(7,10): the same parameters (start, end) have
  // exactly the same meaning here as in slice, unlike substr (see
  // str_03.dart)
  print(sprintf("[%s].substring(7,10)=[%s]", [string, string.substring(7, 10)]));
  // match: RegExp.firstMatch(string) is the Dart equivalent of
  // string.match(/regexp/) - "intro" in uppercase or lowercase
  // (caseSensitive: false is the equivalent of the /i/ flag)
  final RegExp pattern = RegExp('intro', caseSensitive: false);
  print(sprintf("[%s].match(intro,i)=[%s]", [string, pattern.firstMatch(string)?.group(0)]));
  // replace: replaces string1 with string2 in string
  // replaceFirst: only replaces the 1st occurrence of i with x
  print(sprintf("[%s].replaceFirst('i','x')=[%s]", [string, string.replaceFirst('i', 'x')]));
  // [difference with TypeScript] replaceAll ALREADY REPLACES ALL the
  // occurrences in Dart, and always has (no need for a regular
  // expression with a /g/ flag like the replace(/i/g,'x') of str-06.ts, nor
  // to wait for ECMAScript 2021 as in plain JavaScript - see str_07.dart)
  print(sprintf("[%s].replaceAll('i','x')=[%s]", [string, string.replaceAll('i', 'x')]));
  // split: splits the string into words separated by the split parameter -
  // returns the list of these words
  // RegExp(r'\s*'): words separated by 0 or more spaces
  print(sprintf("[%s].split(RegExp(r'\\s*'))=[%s]", [string, string.split(RegExp(r'\s*'))]));
  // RegExp(r'\s+'): words separated by one or more spaces
  print(sprintf("[%s].split(RegExp(r'\\s+'))=[%s]", [string, string.split(RegExp(r'\s+'))]));
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 9: [string.substring(10, 12)], [.trim()], [.toLowerCase()] (line 14), [.toUpperCase()] (line 16), [.indexOf(...)], [.length] (line 23) behave like their equivalents TypeScript.
  • Line 21: [string.contains('Dart')] replaces [includes]; [string.substring(7, 10)] (line 27) replaces [slice(7, 10)]—the parameters (start, end) have exactly the same meaning here as in [slice], unlike in [substr].
  • Lines 31–32: [RegExp('intro', caseSensitive: false).firstMatch(string)]: the Dart equivalent of [string.match(/regexp/i)], with the [caseSensitive: false] option serving the same purpose as the [/i/] flag.
  • Line 40: [WARNING] [string.replaceAll('i', 'x')] ALREADY replaces ALL the occurrences in Dart, and this has always been the case—no need for a regular expression with a flag like JavaScript's [/g/], nor to wait for a recent version of the language (see str_07.dart).

docs.title: 3.4.8. script [str_07]
docs.text:
// str_07.dart
// Ports str-07.ts.
void main() {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 1) replaceAll(search, replace)
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [difference with TypeScript] as noted in str_06.dart, replaceAll()
  // already replaces ALL the occurrences in Dart, without this ever having
  // required an addition to the language (unlike ECMAScript 2021, where
  // this method had to be added to avoid the detour through a
  // regular expression with the /g/ flag)
  const String string = "one cat, two cats, three cats";
  print("replaceFirst (only 1 occurrence) : ${string.replaceFirst("cat", "dog")}");
  print("replaceAll (all the occurrences) : ${string.replaceAll("cat", "dog")}");
  // replaceAll also accepts a regular expression (without needing
  // any particular flag, unlike JavaScript's mandatory /g/)
  print("replaceAll with regexp : ${string.replaceAll(RegExp('cat'), "dog")}");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) allMatches(string) - the Dart equivalent, present from the start, of
  //    matchAll() added to JavaScript in 2020
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  const String text = "Jean is 30 years old, Marie is 25 years old, Paul is 40 years old";
  final RegExp pattern = RegExp(r'(\w+) is (\d+) years old');

  // allMatches returns an Iterable<RegExpMatch>, each giving access to the
  // captured groups AND to their position - exactly like matchAll()
  print("-----------------------");
  for (final result in pattern.allMatches(text)) {
    print("name = ${result.group(1)}, age = ${result.group(2)}, "
        "position = ${result.start}");
  }

  // the Iterable can be turned into a List with .toList()
  final allResults = pattern.allMatches(text).toList();
  print("number of matches = ${allResults.length}");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) isWellFormed() / toWellFormed()
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // [difference with TypeScript] Dart has no direct equivalent of these
  // two ECMAScript 2024 methods. A Dart String is, like a JavaScript
  // string, a sequence of UTF-16 code units (the same isolated "half-
  // characters" are therefore theoretically possible), but the
  // problem arises much less often in practice: Dart strings
  // almost always come from an already validated UTF-8 decoding (.dart
  // source files, dart:convert.utf8.decode...), which precisely rejects
  // malformed sequences at the source, rather than letting through an
  // invalid character as a naive split can do in
  // JavaScript. The closest everyday Dart concern, by the way, is
  // not "well formed in the UTF-16 sense" but "a single displayed
  // character (grapheme) can take up SEVERAL code units" (emoji,
  // combined accents...) - a different subject, handled by the
  // [characters] package (pub.dev/packages/characters), outside the scope of this
  // script.
  const String validString = "café ☕";
  print("validString.runes.length (number of code points) = "
      "${validString.runes.length}");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • [string.replaceAll(...)] also accepts a regular expression without requiring any specific flags—confirming the point raised in str_06.dart.
  • [pattern.allMatches(text)] is the Dart equivalent, available ALWAYS, of [matchAll()], added to JavaScript in 2020: it returns a [Iterable<RegExpMatch>], each providing access to the captured groups AND their respective positions.
  • [WARNING] Dart has no direct equivalent to [isWellFormed()]/[toWellFormed()] (ECMAScript 2024): this issue arises much less frequently in practice, as Dart strings almost always originate from a previously validated UTF-8 decoding—see the comment at the top of the file for the distinction regarding the [characters] package.

docs.title: 3.4.9. Conclusion
docs.text: Manipulating Dart strings is similar to their TypeScript equivalents, with method names that are sometimes different ([substring] instead of [substr]/[slice], [contains] instead of [includes]), and a consistent absence of the pitfalls associated with recent changes in JavaScript ([replaceAll], [matchAll]), as Dart made these choices from the outset.

docs.title: 3.5. Regular expressions
docs.text: The syntax of regular expressions itself is identical to that of JavaScript (Dart uses, like JavaScript, the PCRE/ECMA-262 syntax): only the API for using them from within the code changes.

// regexp_01.dart
// Ports regexp-01.ts: regular expressions in Dart - retrieving the
// different fields of a string with captured groups.
void main() {
  // the pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
  // we only want to retrieve the sequence of digits - the syntax of
  // regular expressions itself is identical to JavaScript's
  // (Dart uses, like JavaScript, the PCRE/ECMA-262 syntax)
  RegExp pattern = RegExp(r'(\d+)');
  print("type of a regular expression : ${pattern.runtimeType}");
  // we match the string against the pattern
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "xyz1234abcd");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "12 34");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "abcd");

  // the pattern: a sequence of digits surrounded by any characters
  // we want the sequence of digits as well as the fields that follow and precede it
  pattern = RegExp(r'^(.*?)(\d+)(.*?)$');
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "xyz1234abcd");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "12 34");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "abcd");

  // the pattern - a date in dd/mm/yy format
  pattern = RegExp(r'^\s*(\d\d)/(\d\d)/(\d\d)\s*$');
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "10/05/97");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "  04/04/01  ");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "5/1/01");

  // the pattern - a decimal number
  pattern = RegExp(r'^\s*([+|-]?)\s*(\d+\.\d*|\.\d+|\d+)\s*$');
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "187.8");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "-0.6");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "4");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, ".6");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, "4.");
  comparePatternToString(pattern, " + 4");
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------------
void comparePatternToString(RegExp pattern, String string) {
  // compares the string [string] to the pattern [pattern]
  print("----------- string=$string, pattern=$pattern");
  // [difference with TypeScript] Dart has only ONE method to obtain
  // the first detailed result (captured groups): [firstMatch] - there
  // is no distinction between a RegExp-side method (exec) and a
  // String-side method (match) as in JavaScript, the Dart API being
  // organized solely around RegExp
  final RegExpMatch? result = pattern.firstMatch(string);
  if (result == null) {
    print("comparison with firstMatch= no match");
  } else {
    // rebuilds the list of groups, like the array returned by exec()
    final groups = List.generate(
      result.groupCount + 1,
      (i) => result.group(i),
    );
    print("comparison with firstMatch= $groups (position=${result.start})");
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Line 9: [RegExp(r'(\d+)')]: The template syntax is identical to JavaScript; the prefix [r] (RAW string) avoids having to double the backslashes, an added convenience unique to Dart.
  • Line 48: [pattern.firstMatch(string)]: Dart has only one method for obtaining the first detailed result—there is no distinction, as in JavaScript, between a method on the [RegExp] side ([exec]) and a method on the [String] side ([match]), as Dart is organized solely around [RegExp].
  • Line 55: [result.group(i)]/[result.groupCount] (line 54) reconstruct the list of captured groups, like the array returned by [exec()].

docs.title: 3.6.2. [func_01]
docs.text:
// func_01.dart
// Ports func-01.ts: how parameters are passed to a function.
// The general principle is the same as in TypeScript: a "primitive" type
// (int, String, bool - immutable) SEEMS passed by value (modifying it in
// the function does not change the caller's variable), while a mutable
// object (List, Map, class instance) is passed by REFERENCE (
// modifying it in the function IS visible to the caller). In reality, Dart
// (like JavaScript) ALWAYS passes the reference itself by value: what
// changes is only that reassigning the local PARAMETER (param =
// something else) never affects the caller's variable, whereas
// MODIFYING the pointed object (param.push(...), param[i] = ...) always
// affects it, if that object is mutable.
void main() {
  // ----------------------- number - seems passed by value (immutable)
  // [WARNING, difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] a Dart nested function
  // can NOT reference a local variable declared further down in
  // the same block, even if the call happens after that declaration: unlike
  // JavaScript, where the scope of a closure is resolved at runtime, Dart
  // requires the variable to be already declared at the point where the compiler reads
  // the reference. We therefore declare [count] BEFORE the function that uses it.
  int count = 10;
  void doSomethingWithNumber(int param) {
    param++;
    print("[param inside function]=$param [type]=${param.runtimeType} "
        "[same variable as the caller]=${identical(param, count)}");
  }

  doSomethingWithNumber(count);
  print("[count outside function]=$count");

  // --------------------- string - seems passed by value (immutable)
  void doSomethingWithString(String param) {
    param += " xyz";
    print("[param inside function]=$param [type]=${param.runtimeType}");
  }

  String text = "abcd";
  doSomethingWithString(text);
  print("[text outside function]=$text");

  // --------------------- boolean - seems passed by value (immutable)
  void doSomethingWithBoolean(bool param) {
    param = !param;
    print("[param inside function]=$param [type]=${param.runtimeType}");
  }

  bool boolean = true;
  doSomethingWithBoolean(boolean);
  print("boolean [outside function]=$boolean");

  // --------------------- list - passed by reference (mutable)
  // same remark as above: [arr] is declared before the function that
  // references it in its body.
  final List<int> arr = [10, 20, 30];
  void doSomethingWithList(List<int> param) {
    param.add(1000);
    print("[param inside function]=$param [type]=${param.runtimeType} "
        "[same list as the caller]=${identical(param, arr)}");
  }

  doSomethingWithList(arr);
  print("[arr outside function]=$arr");

  // --------------------- object (Map) - passed by reference (mutable)
  // same remark as above: [obj] is declared before the function that
  // references it in its body.
  final Map<String, dynamic> obj = {};
  void doSomethingWithMap(Map<String, dynamic> param) {
    param['aNewProperty'] = "xyz";
    print("[param inside function]=$param [type]=${param.runtimeType} "
        "[same Map as the caller]=${identical(param, obj)}");
  }

  doSomethingWithMap(obj);
  print("[obj outside function]=$obj");

  // --------------------- function
  // [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] a JavaScript
  // function IS an object: new properties can be dynamically assigned
  // to it (f.aNewProperty = "xyz"), which is what the
  // original script does. A Dart function IS NOT an extensible object: it
  // is impossible to attach a property to a variable of function
  // type. What IS possible, and achieves a comparable result
  // (remembering a state associated with a function), is a CLOSURE
  // in other words, a function that "captures" an outer variable.
  int callCounter = 0;
  int Function() f = () {
    callCounter++; // captures [callCounter] by reference
    return callCounter;
  };
  print("f() = ${f()}, callCounter = $callCounter");
  print("f() = ${f()}, callCounter = $callCounter");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • The general principle is the same as in TypeScript: an immutable type ([int], [String], [bool]) SEEMS passed by value, a mutable object ([List], [Map], class instance) is passed by REFERENCE.
  • Line 58: [identical(param, arr)] confirms that [param], within the function, refers to the same list as [arr] in the caller—modify [param] ([.add(...)] (line 56)) IS visible to the caller.
  • [WARNING] a JavaScript function IS an object, extensible with new properties; a Dart function IS NOT. The Dart equivalent for storing a state associated with a function is a CLOSURE: the variable [callCounter] is captured BY REFERENCE by the function [f].

[text outside function]=abcd

// func_02.dart
// Ports func-02.ts: a function can be assigned to a variable.
void main() {
  // an anonymous function can be assigned to a variable - the syntax of the
  // type [int Function(int, int)] reads "a function that takes two ints
  // and returns an int", the Dart equivalent of the arrow signature
  // [(a: number, b: number) => number] in TypeScript
  int Function(int, int) variable1 = (a, b) {
    return a + b;
  };
  print("variable1.runtimeType=${variable1.runtimeType}");
  // the variable is then used like a function
  print("variable1(10,12)=${variable1(10, 12)}");

  // in Dart, a function with a { ... } body can also be written with an
  // arrow [=>] IF its body is a single expression - the arrow
  // syntax is therefore, as in TypeScript, just a shorthand
  int Function(int, int, int) variable2 = (a, b, c) {
    return a - b + c;
  };
  print("variable2(10,12,14)=${variable2(10, 12, 14)}");

  // shorthand with =>, when there is only one expression in the
  // code of the function - this expression is then the return value
  int Function(int, int, int) variable3 = (a, b, c) => a + b + c;
  print("variable3(10,12,14)=${variable3(10, 12, 14)}");
}

Let's comment on this code:

  • lines 8–10: [int Function(int, int) variable1 = (a, b) { ... };]: the notation [ReturnType Function(parameters)] describes the type of a function—the Dart equivalent of the arrow signature [(a: number, b: number) => number] for TypeScript.
  • line 25: [(a, b, c) => a + b + c]: The arrow syntax exists in Dart whenever a function has only a single expression as its body—exactly the same principle as in TypeScript.

// func_03.dart
// Ports func-03.ts: a function can receive a function as a parameter.
void main() {
  // function g with a function f as parameter - the type [int Function(int,
  // int)] denotes the type of a function, exactly like the signature
  // [(a: number, b: number) => number] in TypeScript
  int g(int param1, int param2, int Function(int, int) f) {
    return f(param1, param2) + 100;
  }

  // uses of g
  print(g(0, 10, f1));
  print(g(0, 10, f2));
  // the actual parameter of function type can be passed directly -
  // arrow notation
  print(g(0, 10, (param1, param2) {
    return param1 + param2 + 30;
  }));
  // or, equivalently, with the body between braces
  print(g(0, 10, (param1, param2) {
    return param1 + param2 + 40;
  }));
}

// function f1
int f1(int param1, int param2) {
  return param1 + param2 + 10;
}

// function f2
int f2(int param1, int param2) {
  return param1 + param2 + 20;
}

docs.title: 3.6.5. script [func_04]
docs.text:
See the comment at the top of the file: this script illustrates the absence of object functions in Dart—as previously mentioned in func_01.dart—and the idiom used in their place.

// func_04.dart
// Ports func-04.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] in JavaScript,
// a function IS an object: properties can be assigned to it after the
// fact (f.prop1 = ...), and a function used with [new] plays the role
// of a constructor, [this] denoting the newly created object. A Dart
// function is NEVER an extensible object (see func_01.dart) and therefore cannot
// play this role. The Dart idiom that comes closest is
// the exact opposite: a CLASS whose INSTANCES behave like
// functions, thanks to a special method named [call] - this is called a
// "callable class".
void main() {
  // a "callable class" equivalent to the function f of the original script:
  // [f] carries a state (prop1), instead of receiving it from the outside after the
  // fact
  final f = _WithStateAndDisplay("val1");
  // f(...) actually calls f.call(...) - Dart automatically translates
  // "instance(arguments)" into "instance.call(arguments)"
  f.show();

  // a class g which, like a JavaScript constructor, initializes its
  // own state - this is exactly the normal role of a Dart
  // CONSTRUCTOR, no trick needed here at all: "new (g as any)()" in
  // TypeScript is just a classic Dart constructor
  final g = _LikeAClass();
  g.show();
}

class _WithStateAndDisplay {
  final String prop1;
  const _WithStateAndDisplay(this.prop1);

  // special method [call]: an instance of this class can be
  // "called" like a function (here without parameters, a bit like
  // "f()" would in JavaScript once show is attached to f)
  void call() => show();

  void show() => print(prop1);
}

class _LikeAClass {
  final String prop2 = "val2";
  void show() => print(prop2);
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 37: [void call() => show();]: the special method [call] makes an INSTANCE callable as a function ([f()] automatically becomes [f.call()])—this is the “callable class,” the Dart idiom closest to a JavaScript object function.
  • [_LikeAClass]: Unlike a constructor JavaScript (a function called with [new]), a Dart constructor requires no special tricks—that is its normal role.

val1
val2

// func_05.dart
// Ports func-05.ts (the "rest" operator ...otherArgs).
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Dart has NO
// "rest" operator allowing an arbitrary number of surplus
// POSITIONAL arguments to be gathered into a list (unlike
// (arg1, ...otherArgs) in TypeScript). The caller must therefore explicitly
// build and pass a list, rather than "spreading" its arguments
// individually at the end of the call.
void main() {
  // call - we gather "the other arguments" into a list ourselves
  // [dynamic] (they are of different types here, as in the original
  // script)
  f(1, ["two", "three", {'x': 2, 'y': 3}]);
}

void f(int arg1, List<dynamic> otherArgs) {
  // 1st argument
  print("arg1=$arg1");
  // the other arguments
  var i = 0;
  for (final element in otherArgs) {
    print("otherArguments[$i]=$element");
    i++;
  }
}

// [addition] for a variable number of NAMED (rather than
// positional) parameters, Dart does offer a real dedicated mechanism: the
// optional named parameters, between braces - void f2({int? a, int?
// b}) - but these must be DECLARED one by one in the signature
// (so their number is not arbitrary either, unlike a rest
// operator).

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 14: [f(1, ["two", "three", {...}]);]: Dart has NO “rest” operator to group an arbitrary number of arguments ([...otherArgs])—the caller must construct and pass the list themselves.
  • Additionally (not shown in this script), Dart provides a true mechanism for a variable number of NAMED parameters—optional named parameters enclosed in curly braces—but these must be declared one by one in the signature.

The result of the execution is as follows:

otherArguments[0]=two
otherArguments[1]=three
otherArguments[2]={x: 2, y: 3}

docs.title: 3.6.7. Conclusion
docs.text: The typing of Dart functions ([ReturnType Function(parameters)]) is very similar to the arrow function signatures of TypeScript. The fundamental difference lies elsewhere: a Dart function is never an extensible object, which rules out an entire set of JavaScript patterns (function-with-properties, constructor function, rest operator) in favor of Dart-specific equivalents (closures, callable classes, named parameters).

// excep_01.dart
// Ports excep-01.ts: the try / catch / finally principle.
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

void main() {
  final DateFormat formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");
  for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    // date - time of the current moment
    final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
    // time formatting to get the milliseconds
    final String time = formatter.format(now);
    // the milliseconds
    final int milli = now.millisecond;
    // display
    print("--------------------iteration no. $i at $time");
    try {
      // random number (here, derived from the current milliseconds)
      final int number = milli % 2;
      if (number == 0) {
        // throw an error msg - in Dart, [throw] can throw any
        // object, exactly as in JavaScript (see excep_02.dart)
        throw "error";
      }
      // if we get here, there was no error
      print("no error");
    } catch (error) {
      // if we get here, there was an error
      print("error1=$error");
    } finally {
      // executed in all cases, error or not
      print("finally");
    }
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 16–23: [try { ... } catch (error) { ... } finally { ... }]: the same mechanism, with the same syntax, as in TypeScript.
  • Line 22: [throw "error";]: [throw] can throw ANY object in Dart, exactly as in JavaScript (explained in more detail in excep_02.dart).
  • Line 3: [import 'package:intl/intl.dart';]/[DateFormat] (line 6) provide the date formatting used to vary the example from one iteration to the next—the Dart equivalent of [moment.js] (already encountered in the TypeScript course).

// excep_02.dart
// Ports excep-02.ts: we can "throw" just about anything
// to signal an error - true in Dart as in JavaScript.
void main() {
  var i = 0;
  print("--------------------attempt no. $i");
  // throw a character string
  try {
    throw "error msg";
  } catch (error) {
    // there was an error
    print("error=[$error], type=${error.runtimeType}");
  }

  // throw a list
  i++;
  print("--------------------attempt no. $i");
  try {
    throw [1, 2, 3];
  } catch (error) {
    print("error=[$error], type=${error.runtimeType}");
  }

  // throw a Map
  i++;
  print("--------------------attempt no. $i");
  try {
    throw {'name': "hercule", 'country': "ancient greece"};
  } catch (error) {
    print("error=[$error], type=${error.runtimeType}");
  }

  // throw an Exception - dart:core provides [Exception], the
  // idiomatic way to signal a "normal" (recoverable) error, the analogue
  // of the JavaScript [Error] used in the original script
  i++;
  print("--------------------attempt no. $i");
  try {
    throw Exception("network connection error");
  } catch (error) {
    print("error=[$error], type=${error.runtimeType}");
  }

  // same error, but reading its message directly
  i++;
  print("--------------------attempt no. $i");
  try {
    throw Exception("network connection error");
  } catch (error) {
    // the message is in [error.message] - unlike TypeScript where
    // the type of a catch variable is [unknown] by default, [catch
    // (error)] without an explicit type in Dart already types [error] as
    // [Object], without having to write [catch (error as any)];
    // but accessing .message still requires knowing that it is
    // an Exception (here we know it, see throw above)
    if (error is Exception) {
      print("error.toString=[$error], type(error)=${error.runtimeType}");
    }
  }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 9: [throw "error msg";], [throw [1, 2, 3];] (line 19), [throw {...};] (line 28): a string, a list, and a [Map] can all be thrown as-is - Dart does not restrict the type of the thrown object, such as JavaScript.
  • [throw Exception("...")]: [Exception] (dart:core) is the idiomatic way to signal a “normal” (recoverable) error, analogous to [Error] and JavaScript.
  • Line 49: [catch (error)] without an explicit type; [error] is already of type [Object] - Unlike TypeScript, where the type of a variable [catch] is [unknown] (line 51) by default and requires explicit type casting to be used.

// excep_03.dart
// Ports excep-03.ts: differentiating the type of error received in a [catch].
void main() {
  // differentiate the type of error received in a [catch]
  for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
    final int milli = now.millisecond;
    print("--------------------iteration no. $i");
    try {
      // random number (derived from the current milliseconds)
      final int number = milli % 3;
      // Dart already has, in dart:core, several ready-to-use error types
      // comparable to JavaScript's ReferenceError/RangeError/EvalError
      // namely [StateError], [RangeError], [FormatException]
      switch (number) {
        case 0:
          throw StateError("error 1");
        case 1:
          throw RangeError("error 2");
        default:
          throw const FormatException("error 3");
      }
    } catch (error) {
      // there was an error - [is] is the Dart equivalent of [instanceof]
      if (error is StateError) {
        print("StateError : ${error.message}");
      } else if (error is RangeError) {
        print("RangeError : ${error.message}");
      } else if (error is FormatException) {
        print("FormatException : ${error.message}");
      }
    }
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • [StateError], [RangeError], [FormatException] (dart:core) are predefined error types, similar to [ReferenceError]/[RangeError]/[EvalError] in JavaScript.
  • Line 25: [if (error is StateError)]: [is] is the Dart equivalent of [instanceof], used here to distinguish the type of error received in a single [catch].

docs.text:
// excep_04.dart
// Ports excep-04.ts (the [cause] property of an error, ECMAScript 2022) and
// custom error classes.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Dart does NOT
// offer a standard [cause] field on its error classes
// (dart:core Exception/Error do not have one). To attach an original
// error to a new error (the same need as in 2022 on the
// JavaScript side), you must add it YOURSELF as an ordinary field of your
// own exception class - which is what this script does.

// it is common to catch a technical (low-level) error and to
// rethrow it as a more explicit (high-level) error

void readConfiguration() {
  // simulates a low-level technical error (e.g.: file not found)
  throw Exception("ENOENT: file 'config.json' not found");
}

// custom error class with a home-made [cause] field - we implement
// [Exception] (the marker interface of dart:core), as
// "extends Error" would on the TypeScript side
class StartupError implements Exception {
  final String message;
  final Object? cause;
  const StartupError(this.message, {this.cause});

  @override
  String toString() => "StartupError: $message";
}

void startApplication() {
  try {
    readConfiguration();
  } catch (technicalError) {
    // the named parameter [cause] makes it possible to attach the original error to
    // the new error, without losing the information
    throw StartupError("unable to start the application", cause: technicalError);
  }
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// another custom error class, with an additional business field
// (fieldInError) - always possible in Dart, without
// any particular notion of "language version" (unlike
// TypeScript, which dates this practice to 2015 via ES2015 classes)
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
class ValidationError implements Exception {
  final String message;
  final String fieldInError;
  const ValidationError(this.message, this.fieldInError);

  @override
  String toString() => "ValidationError: $message";
}

bool validate(Object? age) {
  if (age is! int) {
    throw const ValidationError("the age must be a number", "age");
  }
  if (age < 0 || age > 130) {
    throw const ValidationError("the age must be between 0 and 130", "age");
  }
  return true;
}

void main() {
  try {
    startApplication();
  } catch (error) {
    if (error is StartupError) {
      print("error=${error.message}");
      // error.cause gives access to the original error, very useful for
      // debugging
      print("cause=${error.cause}");
    }
  }

  // some attempts with different values
  for (final Object? value in [25, -5, "thirty", 200]) {
    try {
      validate(value);
      print("value [$value] : validation OK");
    } catch (error) {
      // we can distinguish our business errors from the other errors thanks to [is]
      if (error is ValidationError) {
        print("value [$value] : validation error on "
            "[${error.fieldInError}] - ${error.message}");
      } else {
        // an unexpected error, not anticipated by our code
        rethrow;
      }
    }
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 23: [class StartupError implements Exception]: Implementing [Exception] (the marker interface from dart:core) acts as [extends Error] in TypeScript.
  • Line 5: [WARNING] Dart does not provide the standard [cause] field on its error classes (unlike ECMAScript 2022): The [cause] field of [StartupError] is written manually, like a regular field of the class.
  • Line 48: [class ValidationError implements Exception] with a business field [fieldInError]: this has always been possible in Dart, without needing to know any specific “language version.”
  • Line 91: [rethrow;]: rethrows the captured error as-is when it is not of the expected type, to prevent an unexpected error from being silently swallowed.

The result of the execution is as follows:

error=unable to start the application
cause=Exception: ENOENT: file 'config.json' not found
value [25] : validation OK
value [-5] : validation error on [age] - the age must be between 0 and 130
value [thirty] : validation error on [age] - the age must be a number
value [200] : validation error on [age] - the age must be between 0 and 130

docs.title: 3.7.6. Conclusion
docs.text: Dart’s exception handling adopts the [try]/[catch]/[finally] triplet from TypeScript exactly as is. Two key points to note: the implicit [Object] type of an unannotated [catch] (more convenient than the [unknown] of TypeScript), and the absence of a standard [cause] field, which you’ll need to recreate yourself when the need arises.

docs.title: 3.8. The modules
docs.text: ES and TypeScript modules distinguish a DEFAULT export (one per module, importable under any name) from NAMED exports (multiple per module). Dart does not make this distinction: any top-level declaration in a [.dart] file is automatically exported under its own name. The three [export-01/02/03.ts] scripts from the TypeScript course therefore boil down, in Dart, to a single file, [module_data.dart], imported in three different ways by the following three scripts.

docs.title: 3.8.1. [module_data, import_01] scripts
docs.text:
// module_data.dart
// Ports, on its own, the three scripts export-01.ts / export-02.ts /
// export-03.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] ES modules
// distinguish a "default export" (only one per module, importable under
// any name) and "named exports" (several per module,
// imported by their exact name, possibly renamed with [as]). Dart does NOT have
// this distinction: EVERY top-level declaration (class, function,
// variable) of a .dart file IS automatically exported, and always
// under its own name - there is no notion of an anonymous "default export"
// in Dart. The three variants of the original TypeScript script
// (anonymous default export, named default export, multiple named
// exports) therefore boil down, in Dart, to this one and same file.
class Module {
  final int data;
  const Module(this.data);

  void doSomething() {
    print(data);
  }
}

// a top-level instance, playing the role of the anonymous default export of the
// export-01.ts script
const Module data = Module(2);

// a top-level function, playing the role of the 2nd named export of
// export-03.ts
void doSomething() {
  print("doSomething");
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 26: [const Module data = Module(2);] acts as the default export (ANONYMOUS) for [export-01.ts]; [void doSomething() { ... }] serves as the second named export for [export-03.ts].
  • In Dart, there is no concept of an anonymous “default export”: every top-level declaration is exported under its own name.

[import_01.dart], which imports this module without a prefix:

// import_01.dart
// Ports import-01.ts.
// import WITHOUT prefix: the declarations of module_data.dart (data,
// doSomething, Module) become directly usable under their own
// name - the most common case.
import 'module_data.dart';

void main() {
  // using the imported object
  data.doSomething();
  // [difference with TypeScript] unlike "import data from
  // './export-01.js'" which can freely rename a default export on
  // import, Dart imports [data] UNDER ITS ORIGINAL NAME: to give it
  // another name locally, you must go through a VARIABLE
  // ALIAS (see below), not through the import itself
  final myVariable = data;
  print(myVariable.data);
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 6: [import 'module_data.dart';] WITHOUT a prefix: the declarations become directly usable under their own names—the most common case.
  • line 16: [final myVariable = data;]: unlike [import data from './export-01.js'], which can freely rename a default export upon import, Dart imports [data] UNDER ITS ORIGINAL NAME—to rename them locally, you must use a variable alias.

2

// import_02.dart
// Ports import-02.ts.
// import WITH prefix (as module1): this is the Dart way to "rename" an
// import as a whole - the closest entry point to TypeScript's
// "import a default export under any name",
// even if here it is the entire MODULE that is renamed, not a single value
import 'module_data.dart' as module1;

void main() {
  // using the imported object, via the prefix
  module1.data.doSomething();
  // all the declarations of module_data.dart are accessible behind
  // the prefix [module1] - useful to avoid name collisions between
  // two modules each importing, for example, a [doSomething] function
  print(module1.data.data);
  module1.doSomething();

  • Line 11: [module1.data.doSomething();]: All declarations in the module are accessible behind the prefix, which is useful for avoiding name collisions between two modules that each import, for example, a function named [doSomething].

// import_03.dart
// Ports import-03.ts.
// selective import with [show]: only the listed names are made accessible,
// without prefix - the Dart equivalent of "import {data, doSomething} from
// './export-03.js'"
import 'module_data.dart' show data, doSomething;

// import of the whole module, under a prefix - the Dart equivalent of
// "import * as module from './export-03.js'"
import 'module_data.dart' as module;

void main() {
  // using the selective imports (without prefix)
  data.doSomething();
  doSomething();

  // using the [module] prefix - gives access to ALL the declarations
  // of module_data.dart, including those that were not listed in
  // the [show] above (here, the Module class itself)
  print(module.data.data);
  module.doSomething();

  // [Dart addition] there is also the reverse combinator [hide], which
  // imports everything EXCEPT the listed names - with no direct equivalent in
  // ES/TypeScript modules
}

  • line 10: [import 'module_data.dart' as module;] combined with the [show] above: the equivalent of [import * as module from './export-03.js'], accessible in parallel.
