// remote_config.dart
// Ports remote-config.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Dart DOES NOT HAVE
// "top-level await": it is impossible to use [await] at the top
// level of a .dart file, outside any function. This script therefore cannot,
// like its TypeScript equivalent, itself run an asynchronous
// call as soon as it is loaded and directly export the already resolved
// RESULT: instead it exposes an asynchronous FUNCTION, which the
// calling code (import_04.dart) will have to explicitly await with [await].
// This is, by the way, how async/async_06.dart already worked,
// BEFORE ECMAScript 2022 introduced top-level await on the
// JavaScript side - Dart never needed to depart from it, an explicit async
// function being enough for all cases.
class Configuration {
  final String applicationName;
  final String version;
  const Configuration({required this.applicationName, required this.version});

  @override
  String toString() => '{applicationName: $applicationName, version: $version}';
}

// a function that simulates an asynchronous call (e.g.: reading a remote
// configuration file)
Future<Configuration> loadFromNetwork() async {
  print("[remote_config] loading the configuration...");
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 300));
  print("[remote_config] configuration loaded");
  return const Configuration(applicationName: "Dart course", version: "2026");
}

Let's break down this code:

  • Line 4: [WARNING] Dart does not support "top-level await": it is NOT possible to use [await] at the top level of a file, outside of any function.
  • Lines 26–31: [Future<Configuration> loadFromNetwork() async { ... }] therefore exposes an asynchronous FUNCTION to be explicitly awaited, rather than executing the call as soon as the file is loaded and directly exporting the resolved result.

docs.title: 3.8.5. [import_04] script
docs.text:
// import_04.dart
// Ports import-04.ts.
// As explained in remote_config.dart, Dart has no top-level
// await: the main program of a Dart script is ALWAYS the function
// [main], which you just need to declare [async] to be able to use [await] in it
// - exactly the role that an explicit "main" function already played in
// JavaScript before 2022 (see async/async_06.dart).
import 'remote_config.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  print("[import_04] before calling loadFromNetwork()");

  // unlike the original TypeScript script, where the IMPORT itself
  // triggered the loading (top-level await HIDDEN in
  // remote-config.js), here the wait is explicit and VISIBLE at the call:
  final Configuration configuration = await loadFromNetwork();

  print("[import_04] after the call: the configuration is already available");
  print("configuration = $configuration");

  // we can of course use [await] normally in [main], since
  // it is declared [async] above
  print("[import_04] waiting 200ms...");
  await Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 200));
  print("[import_04] finished");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 10–26: [Future<void> main() async { ... }]: The main program of a Dart script is ALWAYS the function [main], which simply needs to be declared [async] to use [await] —exactly the role of an explicit function [main] in JavaScript BEFORE the introduction of top-level await in 2022.
  • Line 16: [final Configuration configuration = await loadFromNetwork();]: the await is explicit and VISIBLE, unlike the HIDDEN top-level await in the import of the original TypeScript script.

docs.title: 3.8.6. Conclusion
docs.text: The Dart module system is simpler than that of TypeScript: there is no distinction between default exports and named exports, and there is a single import mechanism (which may be prefixed and filtered by [show]/[hide]). The trade-off for this simplicity is the absence of top-level await, which requires exposing explicit asynchronous functions rather than values that are already resolved at load time.

// async_01.dart
// Ports async-01.ts: the principle of an asynchronous action with a timer.
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

void main() {
  // start
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the script], ${time()}");

  // Timer (dart:core, via dart:async) is the Dart equivalent of setTimeout:
  // it arms a 1000 ms timer and immediately returns a [Timer] object
  // (the equivalent of the timer number returned by setTimeout); when the delay
  // has elapsed, the Dart runtime places the function in the
  // microtask/event queue, exactly as Node.js would
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    // this code will be executed when the timer has reached the value 0
    print("[end of the asynchronous action Timer], ${time(scriptStart)}");
  });

  // will be displayed before the msg of the timer's inner function
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

// utility displaying time and duration
String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Lines 18–21: [Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () { ... })] (dart:async) is the Dart equivalent of [setTimeout]: it starts a timer and immediately returns a [Timer] object (the equivalent of the timer number returned by [setTimeout]).
  • Line 24: The message [[end of the main code of the script]] is displayed BEFORE the timer’s message: Dart is, like JavaScript, single-threaded for user code execution—the callback function for [Timer] is queued only after the main code has finished.

The result of the execution is as follows:

[end of the main code of the script], time=18:15:45.163, duration= 0 second(s) and 14 milliseconds
[end of the asynchronous action Timer], time=18:15:46.180, duration= 1 second(s) and 32 milliseconds

docs.title: 3.9.2. [async_02] script
docs.text:
See the comment at the top of the file: Dart has no direct equivalent for [EventEmitter], hence the choice of two separate [StreamController] functions, one for each “event category” in the original script.

// async_02.dart
// Ports async-02.ts.
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Node.js has a
// generic [EventEmitter] class, to which handlers are subscribed
// by any event NAME (character string). Dart has no
// direct equivalent in dart:async: the Dart idiom for a stream
// of events is a [Stream] (possibly "broadcast", to allow
// several subscribers), one per event CATEGORY rather than a generic
// emitter multiplexing string names. Here we create two
// StreamControllers, one for each "named event" of the original script.
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

void main() {
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the script], ${time()}");

  // two single-event "event emitters" - the equivalent, put
  // end to end, of eventEmitter.on('timer1Success', ...) and
  // eventEmitter.on('timer1Failure', ...)
  final StreamController<Map<String, int>> timer1Success = StreamController.broadcast();
  final StreamController<Map<String, int>> timer1Failure = StreamController.broadcast();

  // we subscribe to the [timer1Success] evt - .listen() is the equivalent of .on()
  timer1Success.stream.listen((result) {
    print("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [$result], "
        "${time(scriptStart)}, via the [timer1Success] stream");
  });

  // we subscribe to the [timer1Failure] evt
  timer1Failure.stream.listen((result) {
    print("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [$result], "
        "${time(scriptStart)}, via the [timer1Failure] stream");
  });

  // Timer arms a 1000 ms timer and immediately returns control
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    print("[Timer, end of the 1 s timer], ${time(scriptStart)}");
    // we emit an event to say that a result is available
    timer1Success.add({'success': 4});
    // we emit another event to say that another result is available
    timer1Failure.add({'failure': 6});
  });

  // will be displayed before the msgs of the events emitted by the function associated
  // with the timer
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 24–25: [StreamController<Map<String, int>>.broadcast()] is the Dart idiom for an event stream —one [Stream] per event CATEGORY, rather than a generic emitter multiplexing string names like Node.js's [EventEmitter].
  • Line 28: [timer1Success.stream.listen((result) => ...)]: [.listen()] is equivalent to [.on(...)]; [.add(...)] (based on [StreamController], not [Stream]) triggers an event equivalent to [eventEmitter.emit(...)].

The result of the execution is as follows:

[end of the main code of the script], time=18:16:41.231, duration= 0 second(s) and 18 milliseconds
[Timer, end of the 1 s timer], time=18:16:42.237, duration= 1 second(s) and 24 milliseconds
the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [{success: 4}], time=18:16:42.246, duration= 1 second(s) and 33 milliseconds, via the [timer1Success] stream

// async_03.dart
// Ports async-03.ts: takes up async_02.dart again, adding costly SYNCHRONOUS
// code between arming the timer and the end of the main code -
// exactly as in JavaScript, this code blocks the execution of the timer
// (Dart is, like JavaScript, single-threaded as far as the execution
// of "user" code is concerned: a long synchronous loop delays by as much the
// processing of Timers and Streams, which only run once the
// call stack is back at rest).
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

void main() {
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the script], ${time()}");

  final StreamController<Map<String, int>> timer1Success = StreamController.broadcast();
  final StreamController<Map<String, int>> timer1Failure = StreamController.broadcast();

  timer1Success.stream.listen((result) {
    print("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [$result], "
        "${time(scriptStart)}, via the [timer1Success] stream");
  });
  timer1Failure.stream.listen((result) {
    print("the timer's asynchronous function returned the result [$result], "
        "${time(scriptStart)}, via the [timer1Failure] stream");
  });

  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    print("[Timer, end of the 1 s timer], ${time(scriptStart)}");
    timer1Success.add({'success': 4});
    timer1Failure.add({'failure': 6});
  });

  // somewhat intensive synchronous code, which prevents the main code from
  // finishing before the end of the timer
  for (var i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
    for (var j = 0; j < 10000; j++) {
      i + i ^ 2 + i ^ 3;
    }
  }

  // will be displayed before the msgs of the events emitted by the function associated
  // with the timer
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • A costly synchronous double loop, inserted between the timer being set and the end of the main code, delays the processing of [Timer] and [Stream]—a direct consequence of Dart’s single-threaded nature, as previously mentioned in async_01.dart.

docs.title: 3.9.4. The Future Mechanism
docs.text: [Future<T>] is the Dart class equivalent to [Promise<T>]: an object that represents the result—which may not yet be available—of an asynchronous operation. Whereas TypeScript constructs a [Promise] using a [executor] passed directly to the constructor ([resolve]/[reject]), Dart separates this construction into a separate class, [Completer<T>]: [completer.complete(value)] serves as [resolve], [completer.completeError(error)] acts as [reject], and [completer.future] provides access to [Future] itself, to be distributed to anyone who wishes to receive the result.

docs.text:
// async_04.dart
// Ports async-04.ts: getting the result of an asynchronous action without
// explicitly going through events, thanks to a [Future] - the Dart class
// equivalent to [Promise], which also implicitly uses
// events behind the scenes.
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

void main() {
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");

  // definition of an asynchronous task using a Future - built
  // with [Completer], the Dart class that plays the role of the "executor"
  // (resolve, reject) passed to the Promise constructor in JavaScript
  final DateTime future1Start = DateTime.now();
  final Completer<String> completer1 = Completer<String>();
  print("[start of the asynchronous function of future1], ${time(future1Start)}");
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    // this code is executed after a 1 second delay
    print("[end of the asynchronous function of future1], ${time(future1Start)}");
    // the asynchronous task returns a result with [complete] - the Future is
    // then successful (the Dart equivalent of [resolve])
    completer1.complete('[success]');
  });
  final Future<String> future1 = completer1.future;

  // we can know the result of the Future [future1] once it has
  // finished (successfully or in error) - .then() subscribes to success,
  // .catchError() to failure, .whenComplete() is executed in all cases
  // (the equivalent of then/catch/finally of the Promise class)
  future1
      .then((result) {
    print("[future1.then], ${time(future1Start)}, result=$result");
  }).catchError((result) {
    print("[future1.catchError], ${time(future1Start)}, result=$result");
  }).whenComplete(() {
    print("[future1.whenComplete] ${time(future1Start)}");
  });

  // definition of a second asynchronous task
  final DateTime future2Start = DateTime.now();
  final Completer<String> completer2 = Completer<String>();
  print("[start of the asynchronous function of future2], ${time(future2Start)}");
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 2000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous function of future2], ${time(future2Start)}");
    // the asynchronous task returns an error with [completeError] -
    // the Dart equivalent of [reject]
    completer2.completeError('[failure]');
  });
  final Future<String> future2 = completer2.future;

  future2.then((result) {
    print("[future2.then], ${time(future2Start)}, result=$result");
  }).catchError((result) {
    print("[future2.catchError], ${time(future2Start)}, result=$result");
  }).whenComplete(() {
    print("[future2.whenComplete], ${time(future2Start)}");
  });

  // will be displayed before the msgs of the asynchronous functions and of the
  // associated futures
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 19: [Completer<String> completer1 = Completer<String>();]: the Dart class that acts as the [executor] ([resolve]/[reject]) passed to the [Promise] constructor in JavaScript.
  • Line 26: [completer1.complete('[success]');]/[completer2.completeError('[failure]');] (line 51): the Dart equivalent of [resolve]/[reject].
  • [future1.then(...).catchError(...).whenComplete(...)]: the same sequence as [then]/[catch]/[finally] from a [Promise] TypeScript, with the same method names except for [whenComplete] (equivalent to [finally]).

The result of the execution is as follows:

[start of the asynchronous function of future1], time=18:18:56.247, duration= 0 second(s) and 1 milliseconds
[start of the asynchronous function of future2], time=18:18:56.251, duration= 0 second(s) and 0 milliseconds
[end of the main code of the script], time=18:18:56.251, duration= 0 second(s) and 12 milliseconds
[end of the asynchronous function of future1], time=18:18:57.268, duration= 1 second(s) and 22 milliseconds

[future2.catchError], time=18:18:58.267, duration= 2 second(s) and 16 milliseconds, result=[failure]

// async_05.dart
// Ports async-05.ts: [async] functions that return a [Future], and
// [Future.wait] - the Dart equivalent of [Promise.all].
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

// shape of the result returned by async01 and async02
class AsyncResult {
  final List<int> prop1;
  final String prop2;
  final int prop3;
  const AsyncResult(this.prop1, this.prop2, this.prop3);
  @override
  String toString() => '{prop1: $prop1, prop2: $prop2, prop3: $prop3}';
}

// an asynchronous function can return a Future and then have the keyword
// [async] - exactly as in TypeScript, except that here the [Future] is
// built with a [Completer] rather than an "executor" passed to the
// constructor (see async_04.dart)
Future<AsyncResult> async01(int p1) async {
  final Completer<AsyncResult> completer = Completer();
  print("[start of the asynchronous task async01]");
  final DateTime async01Start = DateTime.now();
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous task async01], ${time(async01Start)}");
    completer.complete(AsyncResult([10, 20, 30], "abcd", p1));
  });
  return completer.future;
}

Future<AsyncResult> async02(int p1, int p2) async {
  final Completer<AsyncResult> completer = Completer();
  print("[start of the asynchronous task async02]");
  final DateTime async02Start = DateTime.now();
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 2000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous task async02], ${time(async02Start)}");
    completer.complete(AsyncResult([11, 21, 31], "xyzt", p1 + p2));
  });
  return completer.future;
}

void main() {
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the script], ${time()}");

  // we launch the two asynchronous functions in parallel and wait
  // until both have finished - Future.wait only completes
  // if ALL succeed (like Promise.all), and fails as soon as one of the
  // two fails
  Future.wait([async01(10), async02(10, 20)]).then((result) {
    // the result is a List [result1, result2]
    print("[future-wait success], ${time(scriptStart)}, result=$result");
  }).catchError((error) {
    print("[future-wait error], ${time(scriptStart)}, error=$error");
  }).whenComplete(() {
    print("[future-wait whenComplete], ${time(scriptStart)}");
  });

  // will be displayed before the msgs of the asynchronous functions and of the
  // associated futures
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 23–28: [Future<AsyncResult> async01(int p1) async { ... }]: an asynchronous function can be declared as [async] and return a [Future<T>], just like in TypeScript — except that here, the [Future] is constructed with an internal [Completer] rather than a [executor] passed to the constructor.
  • Line 53: [Future.wait([async01(10), async02(10, 20)])] is the Dart equivalent of [Promise.all]: it terminates only if ALL the tasks succeed, and fails as soon as any one of them fails.

// async_06.dart
// Ports async-06.ts: parallel or sequential execution of several
// asynchronous tasks with async / await - a syntax practically
// identical to TypeScript's.
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:intl/intl.dart';

final DateFormat _formatter = DateFormat("HH:mm:ss.SSS");

class AsyncResult {
  final List<int> prop1;
  final String prop2;
  const AsyncResult(this.prop1, this.prop2);
  @override
  String toString() => '{prop1: $prop1, prop2: $prop2}';
}

// an asynchronous function returning a Future
Future<AsyncResult> async01(DateTime async01Start) async {
  final Completer<AsyncResult> completer = Completer();
  print("[start of the asynchronous function async01], ${time()}");
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 1000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous function async01], ${time(async01Start)}");
    completer.complete(const AsyncResult([11, 21, 31], "abcd"));
  });
  return completer.future;
}

Future<AsyncResult> async02(DateTime async02Start) async {
  print("[start of the asynchronous function async02], ${time()}");
  final Completer<AsyncResult> completer = Completer();
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 2000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous function async02], ${time(async02Start)}");
    completer.complete(const AsyncResult([12, 22, 32], "xyzt"));
  });
  return completer.future;
}

Future<AsyncResult> async03(DateTime async03Start) async {
  print("[start of the asynchronous function async03], ${time()}");
  final Completer<AsyncResult> completer = Completer();
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 3000), () {
    print("[end of the asynchronous function async03], ${time(async03Start)}");
    // the asynchronous action fails - completeError() is the Dart equivalent
    // of reject()
    completer.completeError(const AsyncResult([13, 23, 33], "failure"));
  });
  return completer.future;
}

// asynchronous function - using async / await, syntax identical to
// TypeScript
Future<void> runSequentiallyAndInParallel() async {
  final DateTime sequentialStart = DateTime.now();
  print("------------ sequential execution of the asynchronous tasks started "
      "------------------------");
  try {
    // execution of [async01], waiting for it
    final DateTime async01Start = DateTime.now();
    final result1 = await async01(async01Start);
    print("[async01 result]=$result1");
    // execution of [async02], waiting for it
    final DateTime async02Start = DateTime.now();
    print("start async02-------------${time()}");
    final result2 = await async02(async02Start);
    print("[async02 result]=$result2");
    // execution of [async03], waiting for it
    final DateTime async03Start = DateTime.now();
    print("start async03-------------${time()}");
    final result3 = await async03(async03Start);
    print("[async03 result]=$result3");
  } catch (error) {
    // one of the asynchronous actions failed
    print("[sequential error]= $error, ${time(sequentialStart)}");
  } finally {
    print("[end of the sequential execution of the asynchronous tasks], ${time(sequentialStart)}");
  }

  final DateTime parallelStart = DateTime.now();
  print("------------ parallel execution of the asynchronous tasks started "
      "------------------------");
  try {
    final result = await Future.wait([
      async01(parallelStart),
      async02(parallelStart),
      async03(parallelStart),
    ]);
    print("[parallel success], ${time(parallelStart)}, result=$result");
  } catch (error) {
    print("[parallel error], ${time(parallelStart)}, error=$error");
  } finally {
    print("[end of the parallel execution of the asynchronous tasks], ${time(parallelStart)}");
  }

  print("[end of the function runSequentiallyAndInParallel], "
      "${time(sequentialStart)}");
}

void main() {
  final DateTime scriptStart = DateTime.now();
  print("[start of the main code of the script], ${time()}");

  // [difference with TypeScript] just like "main();" in TypeScript,
  // which runs an async function WITHOUT waiting for it (it continues in
  // the background), the Dart call below does exactly the same thing:
  // runSequentiallyAndInParallel() is indeed launched, but [main]
  // does not wait for it (no [await] here) - the behaviour is therefore
  // identical
  runSequentiallyAndInParallel();

  // will be displayed before the various msgs of the asynchronous functions and of
  // their futures
  print("[end of the main code of the script], ${time(scriptStart)}");
}

String time([DateTime? start]) {
  final DateTime now = DateTime.now();
  String result = "time=${_formatter.format(now)}";
  if (start != null) {
    final int duration = now.difference(start).inMilliseconds;
    final int milliseconds = duration % 1000;
    final int seconds = duration ~/ 1000;
    result = "$result, duration= $seconds second(s) and $milliseconds milliseconds";
  }
  return result;
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • The syntax [async]/[await] is virtually identical to TypeScript: [final result1 = await async01(async01Start);] suspends execution until [Future] is resolved.
  • Line 46: [completer.completeError(...)] within [async03] triggers an exception that is caught by the enclosing [try]/[catch], - the same behavior as a rejected [Promise] when encountering a [try]/[catch] around a [await].
  • Line 109: [runSequentiallyAndInParallel();] is called WITHOUT [await] from [main]: just like [main();] in TypeScript, the function is indeed launched but [main] does not wait for it—the same behavior, with no difference to note here.

docs.title: 3.9.8. script [async_07]
docs.text:
// async_07.dart
// Ports async-07.ts (additions to the Promise class). Dart has a direct
// equivalent for some of these additions (Completer, Future.any - with
// a different semantics, see below), but not for others
// (allSettled, the "real" any that waits for a first SUCCESS): this script
// rebuilds them by hand, which is also an opportunity to better understand
// what these methods really do.
import 'dart:async';

// small utility function: returns a Future that succeeds or fails
// after [delay]
Future<String> task(String name, int delayMs, bool succeeds) {
  final Completer<String> completer = Completer();
  Timer(Duration(milliseconds: delayMs), () {
    if (succeeds) {
      completer.complete("result of $name");
    } else {
      completer.completeError("failure of $name");
    }
  });
  return completer.future;
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1) the equivalent of Promise.allSettled()
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// [WARNING, difference with TypeScript] Dart's Future.wait(), like
// Promise.all(), GIVES UP at the first error (by default): we lose
// the result of the other Futures which, for their part, would have succeeded. There is
// no Future.allSettled() in dart:async; we rebuild it by
// "capturing" each error BEFORE gathering them with Future.wait (which,
// this way, never sees an error any more: each Future we give it
// always succeeds, with a "success" or "failure" result)
class Result<T> {
  final bool succeeded;
  final T? value;
  final Object? error;
  Result.success(this.value)
      : succeeded = true,
        error = null;
  Result.failure(this.error)
      : succeeded = false,
        value = null;
}

Future<Result<T>> _capture<T>(Future<T> future) {
  return future.then((v) => Result<T>.success(v)).catchError((e) => Result<T>.failure(e));
}

Future<void> demoAllSettled() async {
  print("--- equivalent of Promise.allSettled ---");
  final results = await Future.wait([
    _capture(task("task1", 300, true)),
    _capture(task("task2", 200, false)),
    _capture(task("task3", 100, true)),
  ]);
  for (var i = 0; i < results.length; i++) {
    final r = results[i];
    if (r.succeeded) {
      print("task${i + 1} succeeded : ${r.value}");
    } else {
      print("task${i + 1} failed : ${r.error}");
    }
  }
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2) the equivalent of Promise.any()
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript] Future.any() EXISTS in
// Dart, but with a semantics DIFFERENT from Promise.any(): Future.any()
// completes with the FIRST result, whether it is a success OR
// an error (a kind of raw "race"), whereas Promise.any()
// specifically waits for a first SUCCESS, ignoring failures as long
// as at least one is still in the race. To reproduce the JavaScript
// behaviour, you have to write it yourself, with a Completer and a
// failure counter:
Future<String> promiseAny(List<Future<String>> futures) {
  final Completer<String> result = Completer();
  var failureCount = 0;
  final errors = List<Object?>.filled(futures.length, null);
  for (var i = 0; i < futures.length; i++) {
    futures[i].then((value) {
      if (!result.isCompleted) {
        result.complete(value);
      }
    }).catchError((error) {
      errors[i] = error;
      failureCount++;
      if (failureCount == futures.length && !result.isCompleted) {
        // all the tasks failed
        result.completeError(errors);
      }
    });
  }
  return result.future;
}

Future<void> demoAny() async {
  print("--- equivalent of Promise.any ---");
  try {
    final result = await promiseAny([
      task("slow-mirror", 500, true),
      task("fast-mirror", 100, true),
      task("broken-mirror", 50, false),
    ]);
    print("first available mirror : $result");
  } catch (globalError) {
    // globalError contains the list of all the individual errors
    print("all the mirrors failed : $globalError");
  }
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 3) the equivalent of Promise.withResolvers()
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// [difference with TypeScript] Dart did not need to wait until 2024 to
// have this feature: the [Completer] class, seen throughout
// this WHOLE async chapter (see async_04.dart and following), does exactly
// what Promise.withResolvers() does - "taking out" the
// resolve/reject functions (here .complete/.completeError) from the constructor, from
// the start, without an artificial intermediate variable.
Future<String> demoCompleter() {
  print("--- Completer (native, long-standing equivalent of "
      "Promise.withResolvers) ---");
  final Completer<String> completer = Completer();

  // we can resolve the Future from anywhere, for example in another
  // callback
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 200), () {
    print("[external callback] we trigger the resolution of the Future");
    completer.complete("value passed from an external callback");
  });

  return completer.future;
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 4) cancelling an asynchronous operation
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// [difference with TypeScript] Dart has no generic AbortController
// in dart:core/dart:async (the http package, for its part, offers its own
// approach - see the chapter "Dart's HTTP functions"). We can
// reproduce the same principle with a simple Completer playing the role of the
// cancellation signal, raced against the task itself thanks to
// Future.any() - which, here, is perfectly suitable: we precisely want the
// FIRST result, whether it is the normal end of the task or
// the cancellation (see the remark in point 2 above).
Future<String> cancellableTask(int delayMs, Future<void> cancellationSignal) {
  final Completer<String> completer = Completer();
  final Timer timer = Timer(Duration(milliseconds: delayMs), () {
    if (!completer.isCompleted) {
      completer.complete("finished normally");
    }
  });
  // if the cancellation signal is triggered first, we stop everything and
  // complete with an error
  cancellationSignal.then((_) {
    timer.cancel();
    if (!completer.isCompleted) {
      completer.completeError(Exception("operation cancelled"));
    }
  });
  return completer.future;
}

Future<void> demoCancellation() async {
  print("--- cancellation with a Completer used as a signal ---");
  final Completer<void> cancellationSignal = Completer();
  // we schedule the cancellation in 100 ms, before the normal end of the
  // task (500 ms)
  Timer(const Duration(milliseconds: 100), () => cancellationSignal.complete());
  try {
    final result = await cancellableTask(500, cancellationSignal.future);
    print("result = $result");
  } catch (error) {
    print("error : $error");
  }
}

// successive execution of the demonstrations
Future<void> main() async {
  await demoAllSettled();
  await demoAny();
  print("--- Completer, result --- ${await demoCompleter()}");
  await demoCancellation();
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • [WARNING] Dart has NO [Future.allSettled]: [Future.wait], just like [Promise.all], GIVES UP at the first error—the class [Result<T>] and the function [_capture] rebuild the equivalent by capturing each error BEFORE combining the [Future]s with [Future.wait].
  • Line 70: [WARNING, key difference] [Future.any()] EXISTS in Dart but with a DIFFERENT SEMANTICS from [Promise.any()]: [Future.any()] returns the FIRST result (success OR error), whereas [Promise.any()] specifically waits for a first SUCCESS while ignoring failures—[promiseAny()] recreates this behavior manually, using a [Completer] and a failure counter.
  • [Completer] has always natively served the role of [Promise.withResolvers()] (added in 2024 to JavaScript): [demoCompleter()] “exits” [complete]/[completeError] from the constructor right from the start, without any additional tricks.
  • To cancel an asynchronous operation (there is no generic [AbortController] in Dart), [cancellableTask] starts the task and uses a [Completer] as a cancellation signal, via [Future.any()] —which works perfectly HERE, since we specifically want the first of the two events, whichever it may be.

The result of the execution is as follows:

--- equivalent of Promise.allSettled ---
task1 succeeded : result of task1
task2 failed : failure of task2
task3 succeeded : result of task3
--- equivalent of Promise.any ---
first available mirror : result of fast-mirror
--- Completer (native, long-standing equivalent of Promise.withResolvers) ---
[external callback] we trigger the resolution of the Future
--- Completer, result --- value passed from an external callback
--- cancellation with a Completer used as a signal ---
error : Exception: operation cancelled

docs.title: 3.9.9. Conclusion
docs.text: [Future] and [Completer] together cover everything that [Promise] and its [executor] cover in TypeScript, using a two-step construction rather than a single constructor. The most notable differences concern the recent additions to the [Promise] class: some have never been necessary in Dart ([Completer] has always covered [withResolvers]), while others have no equivalent and must be written by hand ([allSettled], the “real” [any]).

docs.title: 3.10.1. script [class_00]
docs.text:
This script serves as a transition between the previous chapter and this one, showing the simplest possible Dart class—compare this with the detour via a function taken by JavaScript.

// class_00.dart
// Ports class-00.ts.
// This TypeScript script is deliberately a COPY of func-04.ts (already
// ported in functions/func_04.dart): it serves as a transition between the
// "Functions" chapter and the "Classes" chapter, by showing that
// JavaScript SIMULATES a class with a simple function (keyword [new] +
// [this] in the body of the function).
//
// [fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] Dart never needed
// this simulation: a Dart function can NOT play the role of a
// constructor (see func_04.dart), so there is simply nothing to
// "simulate" - we directly write a REAL class, which is what the rest
// of this chapter does (class_01.dart and following). This script therefore only
// shows, side by side, the simplest possible Dart class.
class AVerySimpleClass {
  String prop2 = "val2";

  void show() {
    print(prop2);
  }
}

void main() {
  // instantiation - an automatically generated Dart constructor (here, without
  // parameters) is enough; no special keyword to "make a function
  // play the role of a class" as in JavaScript
  final instance = AVerySimpleClass();
  instance.show();

  // for the "assigning properties/methods afterwards" variant (the
  // 1st example of class-00.ts, with the function [f]), see directly
  // functions/func_04.dart, which details it with "callable classes".
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 27: [final instance = AVerySimpleClass();]: an automatically generated Dart constructor (here with no parameters) is sufficient—no special keyword is needed to “make a function act as a class” as in JavaScript.
  • Dart has never needed to simulate a class with a function (see func_04.dart): a Dart function cannot act as a constructor, so there is simply nothing to simulate.

The result of the execution is as follows:

val2

docs.title: 3.10.2. script [class_01]
docs.text:
// class_01.dart
// Ports class-01.ts: a class with constructor, getters/setters, and
// toString().
//
// [fundamental difference with TypeScript] the original script simulates
// encapsulation through a naming CONVENTION: a field [_lastName] (with an
// underscore), accessed via a getter/setter [lastName] - but nothing prevents,
// in TypeScript, writing person._lastName = "xyz" from outside the
// class (see the comment in obj_03.dart). In Dart, the [_] prefix IS
// NOT a convention: it is a RULE OF THE LANGUAGE that makes the field
// truly private, inaccessible outside the FILE (the library) where
// it is declared. Here, the class and its use are in the same
// file, so _lastName stays visible in this file - but it would no longer be
// from another file that would import this class (see
// person.dart/teacher.dart, separated into distinct files
// precisely to illustrate this point).
class Person {
  String? _lastName;
  String? _firstName;
  int? _age;

  // constructor - the "this.xxx" syntax as a named/positional parameter
  // is only a Dart shortcut to directly assign a field; here we
  // rather go through the setters, to stay faithful to the original script
  Person(String lastName, String firstName, int age) {
    this.lastName = lastName;
    this.firstName = firstName;
    this.age = age;
  }

  // getters and setters
  String get lastName => _lastName!;
  set lastName(String value) => _lastName = value;

  String get firstName => _firstName!;
  set firstName(String value) => _firstName = value;

  int get age => _age!;
  set age(int value) => _age = value;

  // toString - the Dart equivalent of "JSON.stringify(this)" requires an
  // explicit export of the fields (see obj_02.dart): there is no
  // automatic introspection of the fields of a Dart class, unlike
  // a JavaScript object
  @override
  String toString() => '{"lastName":"$lastName","firstName":"$firstName","age":$age}';
}

// using the class
void main() {
  final person = Person("Poirot", "Hercule", 66);
  // [difference with TypeScript] "person instanceof Person" becomes
  // "person is Person" in Dart (see arr_01.dart for identical(), already
  // encountered, not to be confused with [is] which tests the TYPE, not
  // the identity)
  // [expected] dart analyze reports "unnecessary_type_check" here (the
  // static type of [person] is already [Person]): this is deliberate, to
  // show the syntax of [is] - a warning, not an error.
  print("person=${person.toString()} ${person.runtimeType} "
      "${person is Person}");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 18: [String? _lastName;]: the prefix [_] IS NOT a convention in Dart; it is a LANGUAGE RULE that actually makes the field private, inaccessible outside the FILE (the library) where it is declared—unlike the [_lastName] from TypeScript, which is a mere convention with no actual effect (see obj_03.dart).
  • [person is Person]: the Dart equivalent of [person instanceof Person]—not to be confused with [identical()], which tests IDENTITY, not TYPE.
  • [toString()] must be written explicitly: unlike [JSON.stringify(this)], there is no automatic introspection of a Dart class’s fields.

The result of the execution is as follows:

person={"lastName":"Poirot","firstName":"Hercule","age":66} Person true

docs.title: 3.10.3. [person, teacher] scripts
docs.text:
This file extracts the [Person] class from class_01.dart into its own file, to be reused via inheritance —exactly as [classes/Person.ts] is reused by [classes/Teacher.ts] in the TypeScript course.

// person.dart
// Ports classes/Person.ts: the same class as class_01.dart, but
// extracted into its own file to be reused through inheritance
// (teacher.dart) - exactly as classes/Person.ts is
// reused by classes/Teacher.ts.
//
// [fundamental difference with TypeScript] from HERE on, the [_lastName] field
// (as well as _firstName and _age) becomes TRULY inaccessible from any
// other .dart file that would import this class - including from
// teacher.dart, which nevertheless inherits from it (see the remark on this
// in teacher.dart). This is the concrete, and no longer merely
// theoretical, difference with TypeScript's _name convention.
class Person {
  String? _lastName;
  String? _firstName;
  int? _age;

  Person(String lastName, String firstName, int age) {
    this.lastName = lastName;
    this.firstName = firstName;
    this.age = age;
  }

  String get lastName => _lastName!;
  set lastName(String value) => _lastName = value;

  String get firstName => _firstName!;
  set firstName(String value) => _firstName = value;

  int get age => _age!;
  set age(int value) => _age = value;

  @override
  String toString() => '{"lastName":"$lastName","firstName":"$firstName","age":$age}';
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Starting HERE, [_lastName]/[_firstName]/[_age] become inaccessible from any other file [.dart] that imports this class —including from [teacher.dart], which nevertheless inherits from it (see teacher.dart below).
  • This is the CONCRETE difference—which is no longer merely theoretical—from the [_lastName] convention of TypeScript: [person.dart] and [class_01.dart] define the SAME class, but only the version isolated in its own file actually reveals this barrier.

[teacher.dart], which inherits from [Person]:

// teacher.dart
// Ports classes/Teacher.ts: simple inheritance with [extends].
import 'person.dart';

class Teacher extends Person {
  String? _subject;

  // constructor - super(...) calls the constructor of the parent class,
  // exactly as in TypeScript
  Teacher(String lastName, String firstName, int age, String subject)
      : super(lastName, firstName, age) {
    this.subject = subject;
  }

  // getters and setters
  String get subject => _subject!;
  set subject(String value) => _subject = value;

  // [remark, a direct consequence of Dart's true privacy] even as a
  // subclass, Teacher can NOT directly access the
  // _lastName/_firstName/_age fields of Person (they are private to the file
  // person.dart, not only to the Person class): Teacher must
  // go through the inherited PUBLIC getters (lastName, firstName, age), exactly
  // like any other code outside person.dart. This is more
  // strict than TypeScript, where a child class can freely read/write
  // this._lastName inherited from its parent class (the _name convention being
  // only a matter of naming, never a real barrier).
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Line 5: [class Teacher extends Person] and [: super(lastName, firstName, age)]: simple inheritance and a call to the parent constructor, using exactly the same syntax as in TypeScript.
  • [WARNING, direct consequence of true Dart privacy] Even as a subclass, [Teacher] cannot directly access the fields [_lastName]/[_firstName]/[_age] in [Person]: they are private to the FILE [person.dart], not just to the [Person] class. [Teacher] must go through the PUBLIC inherited getters, just like any other external code—which is stricter than TypeScript, where a child class can freely read from or write to the [this._lastName] inherited from its parent class.

docs.title: 3.10.5. script [class_03]
docs.text:
// class_03.dart
// Ports class-03.ts: redefinition (override) of an inherited method.
// Like the original TypeScript script, we start again from [Person] but we
// define a LOCAL variant of Teacher (not the one in teacher.dart),
// to add a redefinition of toString() to it.
import 'person.dart';

class Teacher extends Person {
  String? _subject;

  Teacher(String lastName, String firstName, int age, String subject)
      : super(lastName, firstName, age) {
    this.subject = subject;
  }

  String get subject => _subject!;
  set subject(String value) => _subject = value;

  // redefinition of toString - [override] is essential here (compilation
  // error without it): it is what explicitly indicates that we are
  // redefining a method of the parent class, rather than creating a
  // new one by mistake (a typo in the name, for example) - a
  // safety net that TypeScript does not offer
  @override
  String toString() => "[Teacher]${super.toString()}";
}

void main() {
  final teacher = Teacher("Poirot", "Hercule", 66, "detective");
  // [expected] dart analyze reports "unnecessary_type_check" here (the
  // static type of [teacher] is already [Teacher]): this is deliberate,
  // to show the syntax of [is] - a warning, not an error.
  print("teacher=${teacher.toString()} ${teacher.runtimeType} "
      "${teacher is Teacher}");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Lines 23–25: [@override String toString() => "[Teacher]${super.toString()}";]: [@override] is here INDISPENSABLE (compilation error without it)—an explicit safety net that TypeScript does not provide, guarding against a typo that would create a new method instead of redefining an existing one.
  • Line 25: [super.toString()] calls the parent class version, exactly as in TypeScript.

The result of the execution is as follows:

teacher=[Teacher]{"lastName":"Poirot","firstName":"Hercule","age":66} Teacher true

docs.text:
// class_04.dart
// Ports class-04.ts: polymorphism - a function accepting the base type
// [Person] can also receive any subclass, such as
// [Teacher].
import 'teacher.dart';
import 'person.dart';

// function accepting a Person as parameter (or any subclass)
void show(Person person) {
  // in all cases
  print("parameter=${person.toString()} ${person.runtimeType}");
  // instance of Person - [is] is the Dart equivalent of [instanceof];
  // true for a Person AND for any subclass such as Teacher
  // [expected] dart analyze reports "unnecessary_type_check" here (the
  // static type of the parameter [person] is already [Person]): this is
  // deliberate, to show the base case before the more interesting case
  // below ([person is Teacher]) - a warning, not an error.
  if (person is Person) {
    print("person=${person.toString()}");
  }
  // instance of Teacher - only true if [person] is
  // specifically a Teacher (or a subclass of Teacher)
  if (person is Teacher) {
    print("teacher=${person.toString()}");
  }
}

void main() {
  // calling show with a teacher
  show(Teacher("Poirot", "Hercule", 66, "detective"));
  show(Person("Marple", "Miss", 70));
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Line 9: [void show(Person person)] accepts both [Person] and a subclass such as [Teacher]—polymorphism works exactly as it does in TypeScript.
  • Line 18: [person is Person] is true for a [Person] AND for any subclass; [person is Teacher] is true only specifically for a [Teacher] (or one of its subclasses).

The result of the execution is as follows:

person={"lastName":"Poirot","firstName":"Hercule","age":66}
teacher={"lastName":"Poirot","firstName":"Hercule","age":66}
parameter={"lastName":"Marple","firstName":"Miss","age":70} Person
person={"lastName":"Marple","firstName":"Miss","age":70}

docs.title: 3.10.7. script [class_05]
docs.text:
// class_05.dart
// Ports class-05.ts (private fields and static blocks, ECMAScript 2022).
//
// [fundamental difference with TypeScript/JavaScript] this script shows, on the
// JavaScript side, the LATE (2022) arrival of TRUE private fields ([#] prefix),
// after years when only the [_name] convention existed (see
// class_01.dart). Dart never had this problem: the [_] prefix has been a
// true language-level privacy from the start (see the remark in
// person.dart) - this script therefore has NOTHING new to introduce on this
// specific point, only to illustrate it with a new example (a bank
// account).
class BankAccount {
  // private field: only visible in this FILE (class_05.dart), not
  // only in this class - exactly the same mechanism as
  // person.dart, not a new feature
  double _balance;

  // private field with default value
  final List<String> _history = [];

  // normal public field (no [_]): accessible from the outside
  final String holder;

  BankAccount(this.holder, [double initialBalance = 0]) : _balance = initialBalance;

  // public method giving controlled access to the private field
  double get balance => _balance;

  void deposit(double amount) {
    _balance += amount;
    // _addToHistory is a private method, callable only
    // from this file
    _addToHistory("deposit of $amount");
  }

  void withdraw(double amount) {
    if (amount > _balance) {
      throw Exception("insufficient balance");
    }
    _balance -= amount;
    _addToHistory("withdrawal of $amount");
  }

  // private method: the [_] prefix also works on methods
  void _addToHistory(String operation) {
    _history.add(operation);
  }

  void displayHistory() {
    print("history of $holder : $_history");
  }
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
// private STATIC fields and methods also exist
// ------------------------------------------------------------------------
class IdGenerator {
  // private static field: shared by all instances, invisible
  // outside this file
  static int _lastId = 1000;

  // [difference with TypeScript] Dart has no "static initialization
  // block" ([static { ... }]): a static field is limited to a
  // direct initialization expression (like "= 1000" above). For
  // a more complex (computed) initialization, the Dart idiom is a lazy
  // static GETTER, or (more rarely) a dedicated static method
  // called explicitly - there is no code that runs
  // "by itself" when the class is loaded, as a JavaScript static block
  // would.

  // public static method giving controlled access to the private
  // static field
  static int nextId() {
    _lastId++;
    return _lastId;
  }
}

void main() {
  // normal use
  final account = BankAccount("Dupont", 100);
  account.deposit(50);
  account.withdraw(30);
  print("balance = ${account.balance}"); // via the public getter
  account.displayHistory();

  // we cannot access the private field directly from the outside -
  // but here, this file IS the one where BankAccount is declared, so
  // _balance would in fact remain accessible: it is by importing this class
  // from ANOTHER .dart file that _balance would become truly
  // inaccessible (see the remark in teacher.dart)
  print("nextId() = ${IdGenerator.nextId()}");
  print("nextId() = ${IdGenerator.nextId()}");
  print("nextId() = ${IdGenerator.nextId()}");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 16: [double _balance;]: same masking mechanism as in person.dart - nothing new compared to the previous scripts, unlike JavaScript, where TRUE private fields ([#] prefix) didn’t appear until 2022.
  • Line 45: [void _addToHistory(String operation)]: The prefix [_] also works on METHODS, not just on fields.
  • Line 60: [static int _lastId = 1000;]: Private fields and static methods also exist, using the same mechanism.
  • line 63: [WARNING] Dart does not have a “static initialization block” ([static { ... }]): a static field is limited to a direct initialization expression—for a computed initialization, the Dart idiom is a lazy static variable or a dedicated static method, never code that executes “on its own” when the class is loaded.

The result of the execution is as follows:

balance = 120.0
history of Dupont : [deposit of 50.0, withdrawal of 30.0]
nextId() = 1001
nextId() = 1002
nextId() = 1003

docs.title: 3.10.8. Conclusion
docs.text: Dart classes incorporate most of the TypeScript syntax (inheritance, [@override], getters/setters, static members), with one fundamental difference that runs throughout this chapter: prefix-based access restriction is a language rule that applies to the entire file, whereas it is merely a convention with no effect - a difference made visible by separating [Person] and [Teacher] into two distinct files.

docs.title: 3.11. Dart 3.x New Features
docs.text: The TypeScript course devotes three sections to recent updates in JavaScript: [New Features ECMAScript 2020–2024], [New Features in ECMAScript 2026], and [Temporal: the modern replacement for Date]. These new features are specific to JavaScript/TypeScript and have no direct equivalent in Dart (Temporal, in particular, does not need to be ported: [DateTime] already covers, in Dart, most of what Temporal brings to JavaScript, and has been discussed throughout this course—for example, in excep_01.dart). This section replaces them with the most significant additions from Dart 3.0 (2023): [records], [pattern matching], [sealed] classes, and class modifiers—all features already used ahead of schedule in several previous scripts in this course (basics_01.dart, obj_07.dart...), and grouped together here for a comprehensive overview.

docs.title: 3.11.1. script [dart3_01_records]
docs.text:
// dart3_01_records.dart
// Dart 3.x new features (1/4): RECORDS (Dart 3.0, 2023).
// A Record is a composite, anonymous and immutable type, which groups
// several values WITHOUT needing to declare a class beforehand -
// useful in all the cases where basics_01.dart had to resort to a List
// [dynamic] (losing all type checking) to return "several
// values" from a function.
void main() {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 1) POSITIONAL records
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // the type (String, int, int) denotes "a record with 3 positional fields" -
  // each field keeps its own type, checked at compile time
  (String, int, int) f2() {
    return ("one", 0, 100);
  }

  final (label, code, quantity) = f2(); // direct destructuring at the call
  print("label=$label, code=$code, quantity=$quantity");

  // a record can also be handled without being destructured right away
  final result = f2();
  print("result=$result"); // automatic display: (one, 0, 100)
  print("result.\$1=${result.$1}"); // positional access: $1, $2, $3...

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) NAMED records
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // more readable than a positional record when the order of the fields is not
  // enough to find your way around
  ({String name, int age}) f3() {
    return (name: "Ada", age: 36);
  }

  final person = f3();
  print("person.name=${person.name}, person.age=${person.age}");
  // named destructuring - the shorthand notation [:name] extracts the
  // field [name] and names it [name] (like TypeScript's {lastName,
  // firstName} shorthand, already seen in obj_07.dart for classes)
  final (:name, :age) = person;
  print("name=$name, age=$age");

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) structural equality - [WARNING, difference with the other
  //    Dart objects] two records are equal ([==]) if their fields are
  //    equal one by one, EVEN if they are two different Record
  //    instances - unlike a List or an ordinary class
  //    (reminder: arr_01.dart, obj_01.dart), which compare by REFERENCE
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  print("(1, 2) == (1, 2) : ${(1, 2) == (1, 2)}"); // -> true !

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 4) typical use: replace an ad-hoc Map<String, dynamic> with a
  //    strongly typed record, for a "tailor-made" function result
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ({int sum, double average, int max}) statistics(List<int> values) {
    final s = values.reduce((a, b) => a + b);
    return (sum: s, average: s / values.length, max: values.reduce((a, b) => a > b ? a : b));
  }

  final stats = statistics([4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]);
  print("sum=${stats.sum}, average=${stats.average}, max=${stats.max}");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • [(String, int, int) f2() => ("one", 0, 100);]: A positional RECORD groups together several typed values without declaring a class—useful wherever basics_01.dart had to resort to a [List<dynamic>], thereby losing all type checking.
  • Line 31: [({String name, int age}) f3()]: a NAMED record, which is more readable than a positional variable when the field order alone is not sufficient to make sense of it.
  • Line 50: [(1, 2) == (1, 2)] is equivalent to [true] (line 50): two records are equal if their fields match one-to-one, even if they come from two different evaluations—unlike a [List] or an ordinary class, which compare by REFERENCE (reminder: arr_01.dart, obj_01.dart).
  • Line 56: [({int sum, double average, int max}) statistics(...)]: the most common practical use of a record—replacing an ad-hoc [Map<String, dynamic>] with a strongly typed, “custom” function result.

The result of the execution is as follows:

label=one, code=0, quantity=100
result=(one, 0, 100)
result.$1=one
person.name=Ada, person.age=36
name=Ada, age=36
(1, 2) == (1, 2) : true
sum=108, average=18.0, max=42

docs.title: 3.11.2. script [dart3_02_patterns]
docs.text:
// dart3_02_patterns.dart
// Dart 3.x new features (2/4): PATTERNS (pattern matching, Dart 3.0).
// Already encountered in this course (basics_01.dart for lists, obj_07.dart and
// dart3_01_records.dart for objects/records): this script groups them
// and goes further, with the pattern [switch] and guards ([when]).
void main() {
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 1) pattern switch EXPRESSION (and no longer just statement)
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // a [switch] can now be an EXPRESSION (it "evaluates to" a value),
  // with a [=>] syntax per case - much more concise than a series of
  // if/else - and the pattern can be a simple value, as here
  String describe(int grade) => switch (grade) {
        20 => "perfect",
        >= 16 && < 20 => "very good", // combined relational + logical pattern
        >= 12 && < 16 => "good",
        >= 10 && < 12 => "fair",
        _ => "insufficient", // "wildcard" pattern, equivalent of [default]
      };
  for (final n in [20, 17, 13, 10, 5]) {
    print("grade $n -> ${describe(n)}");
  }

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 2) matching on the SHAPE of a value (list, record...)
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  String describeList(List<int> values) => switch (values) {
        [] => "empty list",
        [var single] => "a single element: $single",
        [var first, var second] => "two elements: $first and $second",
        [var first, ..., var last] => "at least 3 elements, from $first to $last",
      };
  print(describeList([]));
  print(describeList([42]));
  print(describeList([1, 2]));
  print(describeList([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]));

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 3) if-case: tests and destructures in a single statement, without
  //    going through a full switch - handy for a single pattern
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  final Object input = (name: "Curie", age: 66);
  if (input case (name: String n, age: int a) when a >= 18) {
    // "when a >= 18" is a GUARD: the pattern only matches if the
    // additional condition is true
    print("$n is an adult (age=$a)");
  } else {
    print("does not match the expected pattern, or is a minor");
  }

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // 4) nested destructuring - combines all the levels seen above
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  final List<({String name, int age})> team = [
    (name: "Ada", age: 36),
    (name: "Grace", age: 85),
  ];
  for (final (:name, :age) in team) {
    print("$name, $age years old");
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 13–15: [String describe(int grade) => switch (grade) { 20 => ..., >= 16 && < 20 => ..., _ => ... };]: a [switch] can now be an EXPRESSION, with a combination of relational ([>= 16]) and logical ([&&]) patterns—the wildcard [_] acts as the [default].
  • line 31: [[var first, ..., var last] => ...]: filtering on the SHAPE of a list (empty, one element, two elements, or at least three via the elision [...]).
  • Lines 43–47: [if (input case (name: String n, age: int a) when a >= 18) { ... }]: [if-case] tests AND unpacks it into a single instruction, with a GUARD [when] for an additional condition.
  • Line 58: [for (final (:name, :age) in team)]: Record unpacking naturally combines with a [for-in] to iterate over a list of named records.

The result of the execution is as follows:

grade 20 -> perfect
grade 17 -> very good
grade 13 -> good
grade 10 -> fair
grade 5 -> insufficient
empty list
a single element: 42
two elements: 1 and 2
at least 3 elements, from 1 to 5
Curie is an adult (age=66)
Ada, 36 years old
Grace, 85 years old

docs.title: 3.11.3. script [dart3_03_sealed_classes]
docs.text:
// dart3_03_sealed_classes.dart
// Dart 3.x new features (3/4): SEALED classes (Dart 3.0) - to be
// combined with the pattern [switch] of dart3_02_patterns.dart.
//
// A [sealed] class can be extended (or implemented) ONLY by
// classes of the SAME .dart file - the compiler therefore knows, once
// and for all, the EXHAUSTIVE list of its possible subtypes. Combined with
// a [switch], this allows a check very close to TypeScript's "discriminated
// unions" (which do not exist in Dart as a
// type, but whose spirit - "one of these possible shapes, and no
// other" - is found here), with an additional advantage: the
// compiler REFUSES to compile a [switch] that would forget a case.
sealed class CalculationResult {}

class Success extends CalculationResult {
  final double value;
  Success(this.value);
}

class Failure extends CalculationResult {
  final String message;
  Failure(this.message);
}

// division that never throws an exception: it returns a CalculationResult,
// Success or Failure depending on the case
CalculationResult divide(double a, double b) {
  if (b == 0) {
    return Failure("division by zero");
  }
  return Success(a / b);
}

// [WARNING, key point] this switch has NO [_] (default) case - and
// yet it compiles: the Dart compiler knows, thanks to [sealed], that
// Success and Failure are the ONLY TWO possible subclasses of
// CalculationResult. If we added a 3rd subclass (e.g.: "InProgress")
// without updating this switch, the COMPILATION would fail ("non
// exhaustive") - a precious safety, which neither TypeScript nor JavaScript
// offer natively at this level.
String displayResult(CalculationResult result) => switch (result) {
      Success(value: var v) => "result = $v",
      Failure(message: var m) => "error: $m",
    };

void main() {
  print(displayResult(divide(10, 2)));
  print(displayResult(divide(10, 0)));

  // typical and very frequent use in modern Dart (notably with
  // Flutter): modelling the state of a network load - a preview that
  // will make full sense in the chapter "Dart's HTTP functions"
  for (final state in [
    LoadingInProgress(),
    LoadingSucceeded("data received"),
    LoadingFailed("timeout exceeded"),
  ]) {
    print(describeState(state));
  }
}

sealed class LoadingState {}

class LoadingInProgress extends LoadingState {}

class LoadingSucceeded extends LoadingState {
  final String data;
  LoadingSucceeded(this.data);
}

class LoadingFailed extends LoadingState {
  final String reason;
  LoadingFailed(this.reason);
}

String describeState(LoadingState state) => switch (state) {
      LoadingInProgress() => "loading...",
      LoadingSucceeded(data: var d) => "loaded: $d",
      LoadingFailed(reason: var r) => "failure: $r",
    };

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Line 13: [sealed class CalculationResult {}]: A class [sealed] can be extended ONLY by classes of the SAME file—the compiler therefore knows, once and for all, the EXHAUSTIVE list of its subtypes.
  • [switch (result) { Success(...) => ..., Failure(...) => ... }] WITHOUT [_] still compiles: the compiler knows that [Success] and [Failure] are the ONLY TWO possible subclasses - Adding a third subclass without updating this [switch] would make the COMPILATION FAIL (“non-exhaustive”).
  • When combined with the pattern-based [switch], [sealed] provides control very similar to the discriminated unions of TypeScript, with an additional advantage: this exhaustiveness is VERIFIED AT COMPILATION, whereas TypeScript offers it only if the developer enables and adheres to the corresponding option [strict].
  • [LoadingState] ([LoadingInProgress]/[LoadingSucceeded]/[LoadingFailed]) already foreshadows the use described in section [The HTTP functions in Dart], which models the state of a network call.

The result of the execution is as follows:

result = 5.0
error: division by zero
loading...
loaded: data received
failure: timeout exceeded

docs.title: 3.11.4. script [dart3_04_class_modifiers]
docs.text:
// dart3_04_class_modifiers.dart
// Dart 3.x new features (4/4): CLASS MODIFIERS (Dart 3.0) -
// [base], [interface], [final], [sealed] (already seen), [mixin class].
//
// Without a modifier, an ordinary Dart class can be: instantiated,
// extended (extends), AND used as an interface (implements) - from
// ANY file that imports it. These new modifiers
// allow the AUTHOR of a class to restrict, FROM ITS DECLARATION, what
// the other files are allowed to do with it - a control that
// TypeScript does not offer in this way (in TypeScript, "implements" on
// any existing class always works).
//
// [IMPORTANT NOTE] the restrictions below apply to files
// OUTSIDE the one where the class is declared (exactly as for [_],
// see classes/person.dart): inside THIS file, all
// uses remain possible, including those that another file could
// not do. The comments below specify, for each
// modifier, what would be refused FROM ANOTHER FILE.

// [base]: can be extended (extends) but not implemented (implements)
// from the outside. Guarantees that any subclass REALLY inherits the
// behaviour defined here (its methods cannot be
// "reimplemented from scratch" by another file that would merely
// respect the signature).
base class Vehicle {
  void start() => print("generic start");
}

// a subclass of a [base] class must itself be [base], [final]
// or [sealed]: otherwise, it could be implemented elsewhere (implements
// Car), which would indirectly break the "no external
// implementation" guarantee carried by [Vehicle] - the compiler therefore requires
// propagating the modifier along the whole hierarchy.
base class Car extends Vehicle {
  // extends: allowed, including from another file
}

// [interface]: can be implemented (implements) but not extended
// (extends) from the outside. It is the reverse of [base]: the
// user is required to provide THEIR OWN implementation of each method,
// without being able to reuse this one through inheritance - the closest
// Dart equivalent of a pure TypeScript "interface".
interface class LogService {
  void log(String message) => print("[log] $message");
}

class InMemoryLogService implements LogService {
  final List<String> messages = [];
  @override
  void log(String message) => messages.add(message);
}

// [final] (on a class): neither extended, nor implemented, nor "mixed in" from
// the outside - only direct INSTANTIATION remains possible. Useful for
// a class whose behaviour we want to guarantee will NEVER be
// diverted through inheritance or a fake implementation, wherever it is
// used.
final class Configuration {
  final String key;
  final String value;
  const Configuration(this.key, this.value);
}

// [sealed] (already seen in dart3_03_sealed_classes.dart): neither extended nor
// implemented from the outside, but in addition, the compiler knows the
// EXHAUSTIVE list of subtypes (useful with switch) - the
// strictest combination.

// [mixin class]: can be used both as a normal class
// (extends/instantiation) AND as a mixin (with) - before Dart 3, you
// had to choose between declaring a [class] OR a [mixin] separately,
// with different rules; [mixin class] brings both uses together.
mixin class Timestampable {
  DateTime? timestamp;
  void markNow() => timestamp = DateTime.now();
}

class Event with Timestampable {
  final String title;
  Event(this.title);
}

void main() {
  Car().start();

  final service = InMemoryLogService();
  service.log("first message");
  print(service.messages);

  const config = Configuration("theme", "dark");
  print("${config.key} = ${config.value}");

  final event = Event("launch")..markNow();
  print("${event.title} at ${event.timestamp}");
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 25: [base class Vehicle]: can be extended but not implemented from another file—ensures that any subclass ACTUALLY inherits the behavior defined here.
  • line 43: [interface class LogService]: the opposite of [base]—can be implemented but not extended from the outside; the closest Dart equivalent to a pure TypeScript interface.
  • line 58: [final class Configuration]: neither extended, implemented, nor “mixed” from the outside—only direct instantiation is possible.
  • line 73: [mixin class Timestampable]: can be used both as a normal class ([extends]/instantiation) and as a mixin ([with])—before Dart 3, you had to choose between [class] and [mixin] separately.
  • These restrictions apply only to files OUTSIDE the one where the class is declared—the same principle, this time at the class level, as the restriction by [_] at the field level (see classes/person.dart). This is a check that TypeScript does not provide in this way: [implements] always works there, on any existing class.

The result of the execution is as follows:

generic start
[first message]
theme = dark
launch at 2026-09-20 10:54:11.874911

docs.title: 3.11.5. Summary Table
docs.text:
Summary of the four Dart 3.x features presented in this section, and their typical uses:

  • [Records]: Group multiple typed values without a class—a “custom” function return, a typed alternative to an ad hoc [Map<String, dynamic>].
  • [Patterns] (pattern-based [switch], [if-case], [when] guards): Filter and deconstruct in a single expression—a concise alternative to a sequence of [if]/[else].
  • [Sealed classes]: model a CLOSED set of variants (one result, one state), with exhaustiveness verified at compile time in a [switch].
  • [Class modifiers] ([base], [interface], [final], [mixin class]): document and enforce, as soon as a class is declared, what other files are permitted to do with it.

docs.title: 5.1. Choosing HTTP Tools
docs.text:
Unlike JavaScript/TypeScript, which provides a [fetch] NATIVE function (both in the browser and in Node.js), Dart does NOT provide a high-level client in its standard library ([dart:io] exposes only a low-level [HttpClient], which is cumbersome to use directly). Two external packages together cover exactly the same ground as [fetch] and [axios] in the TypeScript course:

  • [package:http] (pub.dev/packages/http), maintained by the Dart team itself: a simple, low-level API, with no global configuration or interceptors—the role of [fetch].
  • [package:dio] (pub.dev/packages/dio): global configuration ([baseUrl], [timeout]), interceptors, enhanced error handling ([DioException.response])—the role of [axios].

docs.title: 5.2. The Tax Calculation Server
docs.text: All scripts in this chapter target the NestJS server installed in the previous chapter, at the address [http://localhost:3000/main.php]. Before testing the following scripts, verify that your NestJS server is running. For it to work, the Laragon tool must also be running.

docs.title: 5.2.1. [dart_fetch_01] script
docs.text:
// dart_fetch_01.dart
// Ports fetch-01.ts.
// Choice of HTTP tools in Dart: the [http] package (pub.dev/packages/http),
// maintained by the Dart team itself, plays the role of the native [fetch] of
// Node.js/the browser - a simple, low-level API, without
// global configuration or interceptors (unlike the [dio] package,
// which plays the role of [axios] - see dart_dio_01.dart).
import 'dart:convert';
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

// base URL of the tax calculation server (see the chapter
// "Installing a NestJS server")
const String baseUrl = 'http://localhost:3000/main.php';

// init session
Future<dynamic> initSession() async {
  // [difference with TypeScript] the [http] package has no
  // [timeout] option on the request itself: we limit the waiting time by
  // wrapping the Future with the [.timeout(...)] extension of dart:async,
  // which works on ANY Future (not only HTTP
  // requests) - a more general mechanism than fetch's
  // AbortSignal.timeout(), specific to the native fetch.
  final uri = Uri.parse(baseUrl).replace(queryParameters: {
    'action': 'init-session',
    'type': 'json',
  });
  try {
    // asynchronous request - http.get() returns a Future<http.Response>
    final stopwatch = Stopwatch()..start();
    final response = await http.get(uri).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 2));
    // [response] is the whole HTTP response of the server (HTTP
    // headers + body) - we display it to see its structure
    print("http response in Dart (duration=${stopwatch.elapsedMilliseconds}ms) : "
        "statusCode=${response.statusCode}");
    // we can access the HTTP headers
    print("response headers=${response.headers}");
    // [difference with TypeScript] unlike fetch, where response.json()
    // is a separate ASYNCHRONOUS method (a new Future), the body of the
    // http.Response is already fully available
    // SYNCHRONOUSLY (response.body, a String): http.get() has already waited for
    // the whole body before returning its result. jsonDecode() is therefore
    // not an asynchronous operation here.
    final object = jsonDecode(response.body);
    print("json response=$object, type=${object.runtimeType}");
    return object;
  } catch (error) {
    // we are here because the server responded with an error code, or
    // because the http client threw an exception (network unreachable,
    // timeout exceeded...)
    print("fetch error in Dart=${error.runtimeType}, $error");
    // we rethrow the error
    rethrow;
  }
}

// the main function runs the asynchronous function [initSession]
Future<void> main() async {
  try {
    print("HTTP request to the server in progress "
        "---------------------------------------------");
    final response = await initSession();
    print("success ---------------------------------------------");
    print("response=$response ${response.runtimeType}");
  } catch (error) {
    print("error ---------------------------------------------");
    print("error=$error");
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 30: [http.get(uri).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 2))]: the [http] package does not have a [timeout] option on the request itself - We limit the wait time by wrapping [Future] with the [.timeout(...)] method of dart:async, which works on ANY [Future], not just HTTP requests.
  • Line 43: [jsonDecode(response.body)]: Unlike [fetch], where [response.json()] is a separate ASYNCHRONOUS method, the body of a [http.Response] is already fully available SYNCHRONOUSLY ([response.body], a [String]): [http.get()] has already waited for the entire body before returning its result.

The result of the execution is as follows:

response headers={x-powered-by: Express, connection: keep-alive, keep-alive: timeout=5, set-cookie: connect.sid=s%3AWxLD5aAAWVIL6pinZyP75L4COQi837LW.NmwJehFDFeCvZ0p6CKHV9ybz9xNUvndTB7TYlKgp7s4; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax, date: Sun, 20 Sep 2026 09:47:30 GMT, content-length: 84, etag: W/"54-sE02l73cr4dRIJSanYxwhuhm21c", content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8}
