docs.title: 5.2.3. script [dart_fetch_03]
docs.text:
// dart_fetch_03.dart
// Ports fetch-03.ts: maximum delay and manual cancellation of an HTTP
// request.
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

// base URL of the tax calculation server (see http/README, the
// historical PHP server of the original course; here we directly target the
// NestJS server - see the chapter "Installing a NestJS server")
const String baseUrl = 'http://localhost:3000/main.php';

// example 1: request with a maximum delay, thanks to [.timeout(...)]
// (dart:async extension on any Future - see dart_fetch_01.dart)
Future<void> requestWithMaximumDelay() async {
  print("--- request with .timeout() ---");
  try {
    final response = await http
        .get(Uri.parse('$baseUrl?action=init-session&type=json'))
        // beyond 2 seconds, [.timeout] completes the Future with an error
        // with a [TimeoutException] - the Dart equivalent of
        // fetch's AbortSignal.timeout()
        .timeout(const Duration(seconds: 2));
    print("response = ${response.body}");
  } catch (error) {
    // if the server does not exist (a likely case in this exercise), or if
    // the delay is exceeded, [error] is a [TimeoutException] or a
    // [SocketException]/[ClientException] depending on the case
    print("error.runtimeType = ${error.runtimeType}, message = $error");
  }
}

// example 2: manual cancellation of a request, for example because
// the user changed their mind (e.g.: they retype in a search
// field).
//
// [WARNING, fundamental difference with TypeScript] the [http] package has no
// PER-REQUEST cancellation signal, like fetch's AbortSignal: the
// only way to cancel is to CLOSE THE CLIENT (http.Client.close()) as a
// whole, which cancels ALL the requests in progress on this client - you
// therefore need to create a client DEDICATED to the request you want to be able to cancel
// individually, rather than a client shared by the whole application.
Future<void> manuallyCancellableRequest() async {
  print("--- request cancelled manually ---");
  final client = http.Client();

  // we schedule a "business" cancellation after 10 ms (in a real
  // application, this would for example be a click on a "cancel" button)
  Future.delayed(const Duration(milliseconds: 10), () {
    print("manual cancellation triggered");
    client.close();
  });

  try {
    final response = await client.get(Uri.parse('$baseUrl?action=init-session&type=json'));
    print("response = ${response.body}");
  } catch (error) {
    // closing the client during a request in progress makes it fail with
    // a [ClientException]
    print("error.runtimeType = ${error.runtimeType}, message = $error");
  }
}

Future<void> main() async {
  await requestWithMaximumDelay();
  await manuallyCancellableRequest();
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • Line 21: [.timeout(const Duration(seconds: 2))] completes the failed [Future] with a [TimeoutException] that exceeded the time limit - the Dart equivalent of [AbortSignal.timeout()] for [fetch].
  • Line 35: [WARNING, key difference]—the [http] package has NO PER-REQUEST cancellation signal like [AbortController] for [fetch]: the only way to cancel is to CLOSE THE CLIENT ([http.Client.close()]) in its entirety, which cancels ALL pending requests on that client—hence the need to create a DEDICATED client for the request you want to be able to cancel individually.

The result of the execution is as follows:

--- request with .timeout() ---
response = {"action":"init-session","status":700,"response":"session started with type [json]"}
--- request cancelled manually ---
response = {"action":"init-session","status":700,"response":"session started with type [json]"}
manual cancellation triggered

docs.title: 5.2.4. script [dart_dio_01]
docs.text:
// dart_dio_01.dart
// Ports axios-01.ts and axios-02.ts.
// Choice of HTTP tools in Dart: the [dio] package (pub.dev/packages/dio)
// plays the role of [axios] - a global configuration (baseUrl, timeout),
// interceptors, enriched error handling (error.response, like
// axios): everything that the [http] package, closer to fetch, leaves to the
// calling code (see dart_fetch_01.dart).
import 'package:dio/dio.dart';

// a Dio instance configured once and for all, reused by all
// the calls - exactly the role of "axios.defaults" in TypeScript
final Dio dio = Dio(BaseOptions(
  baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000/',
  connectTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 2),
  receiveTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 2),
));

// init session
Future<dynamic> initSession({required String type}) async {
  try {
    // asynchronous request - dio.get() directly accepts
    // queryParameters, like axios.request({params: ...})
    final response = await dio.get('main.php', queryParameters: {
      'action': 'init-session',
      'type': type,
    });
    // the server's response is in [response.data] (already decoded into
    // Map/List by Dio if the Content-Type is JSON), exactly like
    // response.data in axios
    return response.data;
  } on DioException catch (error) {
    // the parameter [error] is a [DioException] - we display it to
    // see its structure (equivalent of the "console.log(axios error)"
    // commented out in axios-01.ts)
    if (error.response != null) {
      // the server signalled an error in the HTTP status but it
      // also sent a response: it is in [error.response!.data],
      // exactly like [error.response.data] in axios
      return error.response!.data;
    } else {
      // no response at all (network unreachable, timeout...) - we
      // rethrow the error
      rethrow;
    }
  }
}

Future<void> main() async {
  try {
    // 1st attempt, deliberately invalid (type='x' instead of 'json'),
    // to observe how the server - then dio - signal the error:
    // the server still responds (with a business error status), so
    // error.response.data is indeed filled, as in axios-01.ts
    print("HTTP request (invalid type) to the server in progress "
        "---------------------------------------------");
    final invalidResponse = await initSession(type: 'x');
    print("response=$invalidResponse ${invalidResponse.runtimeType}");

    // 2nd attempt, corrected (type='json'), like axios-02.ts
    print("HTTP request (corrected type) to the server in progress "
        "---------------------------------------------");
    final response = await initSession(type: 'json');
    print("success ---------------------------------------------");
    print("response=$response ${response.runtimeType}");
  } catch (error) {
    print("error ---------------------------------------------");
    print("error=$error");
  }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • Lines 12–15: [Dio(BaseOptions(baseUrl: ..., connectTimeout: ..., receiveTimeout: ...))]: a [Dio] instance configured once and for all, reused by all calls—exactly the role of [axios.defaults] in TypeScript.
  • [response.data]: the server’s response, which was already DECODED into [Map]/[List] by Dio if [Content-Type] is JSON, exactly like [response.data] in axios.
  • Lines 30–31: [on DioException catch (error) { if (error.response != null) ... }]: the same distinction as [error.response] in Axios between an error WITH a server response (business error status) and an error WITHOUT a response (network unreachable, timeout).

The result of the execution is as follows:

HTTP request (invalid type) to the server in progress ---------------------------------------------
response={action: init-session, status: 703, response: invalid parameter type=[x]} _Map<String, dynamic>
HTTP request (corrected type) to the server in progress ---------------------------------------------
success ---------------------------------------------
response={action: init-session, status: 700, response: session started with type [json]} _Map<String, dynamic>

docs.text:
// dart_dio_02.dart
// Ports axios-03.ts: chaining two HTTP requests - init-session, then
// authenticate-user (a POST with a body encoded as
// x-www-form-urlencoded).
import 'package:dio/dio.dart';

final Dio dio = Dio(BaseOptions(
  baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000/',
  connectTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 2),
  receiveTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 2),
));

Future<dynamic> initSession() async {
  try {
    final response = await dio.get('main.php', queryParameters: {
      'action': 'init-session',
      'type': 'json',
    });
    return response.data;
  } on DioException catch (error) {
    if (error.response != null) {
      return error.response!.data;
    }
    rethrow;
  }
}

Future<dynamic> authenticateUser(String user, String password) async {
  try {
    // POST request with an x-www-form-urlencoded body - Dio automatically
    // encodes a Map as x-www-form-urlencoded if the
    // Content-Type is specified in the [Options], exactly like qs.stringify(...)
    // + the manual header of axios-03.ts
    final response = await dio.post(
      'main.php',
      queryParameters: {'action': 'authenticate-user'},
      data: {'user': user, 'password': password},
      options: Options(contentType: Headers.formUrlEncodedContentType),
    );
    return response.data;
  } on DioException catch (error) {
    if (error.response != null) {
      return error.response!.data;
    }
    rethrow;
  }
}

// the main function runs the asynchronous functions one by one
Future<void> main() async {
  try {
    // init-session
    print("init-session action in progress "
        "---------------------------------------------");
    final response1 = await initSession();
    print("success ---------------------------------------------");
    print("response=$response1");
    // authenticate-user - [NOTE, as in the original TypeScript
    // course] this call starts from a new HTTP request, WITHOUT
    // automatically sharing the session cookie set by the server at
    // the previous step (neither Dio nor axios do it automatically on the
    // Node/Dart side): manual tracking of the session cookie is precisely the
    // subject of dart_dio_03.dart, which ports axios-04.ts.
    print("authenticate-user action in progress "
        "---------------------------------------------");
    final response2 = await authenticateUser('admin', 'admin');
    print("success ---------------------------------------------");
    print("response=$response2");
  } catch (error) {
    print("error ---------------------------------------------");
    print("error=$error");
  }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • line 38: [Options(contentType: Headers.formUrlEncodedContentType)]: Dio automatically encodes the [Map] passed to [data] into [x-www-form-urlencoded] as soon as this [Content-Type] is specified - the equivalent of [qs.stringify(...)] combined with the manual Axios header.
  • This call is a new HTTP request that does NOT automatically share the session cookie set by the server in the previous step—neither Dio nor axios does this automatically on the Dart/Node side: manual cookie tracking is the subject of the following script.

The result of the execution is as follows:

init-session action in progress ---------------------------------------------
success ---------------------------------------------
response={action: init-session, status: 700, response: session started with type [json]}
authenticate-user action in progress ---------------------------------------------
success ---------------------------------------------
response={action: authenticate-user, status: 103, response: [no session in progress. Start with action [init-session]]}

docs.title: 5.2.6. script [dart_dio_03]
docs.text:
// dart_dio_03.dart
// Ports axios-04.ts: manual tracking of the session cookie between two requests.
import 'package:dio/dio.dart';

final Dio dio = Dio(BaseOptions(
  baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000/',
  connectTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 2),
  receiveTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 2),
  // we disable the default validation of the HTTP status to be able to
  // inspect an error response ourselves (like error.response in
  // axios), without systematically going through a catch block
  validateStatus: (_) => true,
));

// session cookie
const String sessionCookieName = "connect.sid";
String sessionCookie = '';

Future<dynamic> getRemoteData(String path, {
  required String method,
  Map<String, dynamic>? queryParameters,
  Object? data,
  Options? options,
}) async {
  // for the session cookie - we add it ourselves to the headers of
  // each request, exactly like axios-04.ts
  final opts = (options ?? Options(method: method)).copyWith(
    method: method,
    headers: {
      ...?options?.headers,
      'Cookie': sessionCookie,
    },
  );
  // execution of the HTTP request
  final response = await dio.request(
    path,
    queryParameters: queryParameters,
    data: data,
    options: opts,
  );
  // we retrieve the session cookie if it exists - response.headers is a
  // Dio [Headers] object (not a simple Map like response.headers in
  // axios); response.headers['set-cookie'] returns a List<String>?
  final setCookie = response.headers['set-cookie'];
  if (setCookie != null) {
    // we look for the session cookie in this list
    for (final header in setCookie) {
      final result = RegExp('^($sessionCookieName.+?);').firstMatch(header);
      if (result != null) {
        // we store the session cookie
        sessionCookie = result.group(1)!;
        break;
      }
    }
  }
  // the server's response is in [response.data]
  return response.data;
}

Future<dynamic> initSession() {
  return getRemoteData(
    'main.php',
    method: 'GET',
    queryParameters: {'action': 'init-session', 'type': 'json'},
  );
}

Future<dynamic> authenticateUser(String user, String password) {
  return getRemoteData(
    'main.php',
    method: 'POST',
    queryParameters: {'action': 'authenticate-user'},
    data: {'user': user, 'password': password},
    options: Options(contentType: Headers.formUrlEncodedContentType),
  );
}

// the main function runs the asynchronous functions one by one
Future<void> main() async {
  try {
    print("init-session action in progress ----------------");
    final response1 = await initSession();
    print("success --------------------------");
    print("response=$response1");
    print("authenticate-user action in progress ---------");
    final response2 = await authenticateUser('admin', 'admin');
    print("success -------------------");
    print("response=$response2");
  } catch (error) {
    print("error ------------------");
    print("error=$error");
  }
}

Let’s break down this code:

  • Line 12: [validateStatus: (_) => true]: disables the default validation of status HTTP, so you can inspect an error response yourself without always having to go through a [catch] block—the same choice as axios-04.ts.
  • [response.headers['set-cookie']] returns a [List<String>?]: unlike [response.headers] in Axios (a simple object), Dio’s [response.headers] is a dedicated [Headers] object, whose indexing always returns a list.
  • Line 48: [RegExp('^($sessionCookieName.+?);').firstMatch(header)]: the session cookie is retrieved and stored manually, then reinserted into the [Cookie] header of each subsequent request—exactly the same pattern as axios-04.ts, adapted for Dio’s API.

The result of the execution is as follows:

init-session action in progress ----------------
success --------------------------
response={action: init-session, status: 700, response: session started with type [json]}
authenticate-user action in progress ---------
success -------------------
response={action: authenticate-user, status: 200, response: Authentication successful [admin, admin]}

docs.title: 5.2.7. Conclusion
docs.text: [package:http] and [package:dio] together cover the entire scope of [fetch] and [axios]: a low-level API close to the protocol, and a feature-rich API with global configuration and enhanced error handling. The specific differences ([timeout] being generic per [Future] rather than per request, lack of individual cancellation, lack of automatic cookie management) will be reflected, in concrete form, in the HTTP clients in the following chapter.
